fields.title: Portraits of Courage – Amy Carmichael
fields.subtitle: A Belfast Mission Hall, the Children of Dohnavur, and a Mother Called Amma
fields.description: A Christian biography of Amy Carmichael (1867–1951), the Irish missionary who went to South India in 1895, never came home, and spent more than half a century making a family at Dohnavur out of children whom nobody else would keep — beginning with one runaway girl from a temple household. Built chiefly on her own early books and checked against the record, it tells the real woman behind the legend: fearless and fierce, tender and sometimes imperious, honest about the cost of the work and about the people she opposed. All Scripture from the public-domain ASV (1901).

qa.question: What is this biography of Amy Carmichael about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of Amy Carmichael (1867–1951), the Irish missionary who founded the Dohnavur Fellowship in South India. It follows her from her childhood in Millisle, County Down, through the Welcome Hall for Belfast mill girls, Manchester, Robert Wilson’s home at Broughton Grange, fifteen months in Japan, and village evangelism in the Tinnevelly district, to the coming of a runaway child named Preena in 1901, the growth of the family at Dohnavur, her crippling fall in 1931, and her death in 1951.

qa.question: Who was Amy Carmichael?
qa.answer: She was a missionary from the north of Ireland who reached India in 1895 with the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society and stayed for fifty-five years without a furlough. After years of travelling the villages with a band of Indian women, she began in 1901 to shelter girls in danger of being dedicated to temples, and later boys as well. The children called her Amma, “mother.” She also wrote many books, including Things as They Are, Gold Cord and If.

qa.question: Did Amy Carmichael end the dedication of girls to temples?
qa.answer: No, and the book is careful about this. The practice was outlawed in the Madras Presidency by the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of October 1947, after a long campaign led above all by Indian reformers such as Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy and Moovalur Ramamirtham. Amy Carmichael’s contribution was to shelter children, one by one, for nearly fifty years, and her witness was one of many streams that fed the reform.

qa.question: How does the book handle the temple-children subject?
qa.answer: Honestly, but without graphic detail. It explains the long history of the temple women of South India, including their place in classical dance and music, and how the tradition had come by her day to involve the dedication of small girls to a life of exploitation. It also reports the criticism of historians such as Davesh Soneji that reform writing, missionary and Indian alike, did lasting harm to the hereditary communities concerned.

qa.question: Was Things as They Are controversial?
qa.answer: Yes. Published in 1903, it told readers at home that most days on the mission field ended as they began, and that conversion in caste India often cost everything. Some in England doubted it; later editions printed confirmatory notes from missionaries and from Pandita Ramabai. The biography also asks how the book would have read to a Hindu, noting that its language about Hinduism was often harsh and sometimes unfair.

qa.question: Does the book show her faults?
qa.answer: Yes. It shows a woman who could be imperious and slow to share authority, who wrote about Hinduism in terms common among missionaries of her day, and whose protectiveness at Dohnavur some observers saw as control. It tells of her painful parting with the young Stephen Neill in 1925. It also shows her courage, humour, tenderness and lifelong self-giving, and argues that the shadows are real but do not cancel the light.

qa.question: Which sources does the book use?
qa.answer: It quotes chiefly from her own early books, above all Things as They Are (1903), which is in the public domain. The standard biographies by Frank Houghton (1953) and Elisabeth Elliot (1987) are still in copyright and are used only for facts, never quoted. Where a well-known story rests only on later retelling, such as the coffee-stained skin or the place of her fall, the book says so.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning. The preface and introduction explain the sources and how the legend differs from the record; the chapters then follow her life in order, from Millisle and Belfast to Japan, Tinnevelly, Dohnavur and her last twenty years in one room. Appendix A gathers lessons from her life, Appendix B is a study guide for groups, Appendix C a chronology, and Appendix D a note on sources and corrections.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.”

— Matthew 18:14, ASV

The earlier volumes of this series told of a Chinese church leader who died in a Communist labour camp, an American who prayed his way through the villages of the Punjab, a Dutch watchmaker who hid Jews behind a false wall, a Scottish mill girl who went alone up the rivers of Calabar, an African bishop who had once been sold as a slave, an Indian widow who built a home for thousands of outcast women, an Oxford don who was found by God against his will, and an American widow who carried her small daughter into the Ecuadorian forest. This ninth volume tells the story of an Irish woman who went to South India in 1895, never came home, and spent more than half a century making a family out of children whom nobody else was able, or willing, to keep.

Amy Beatrice Carmichael was born in 1867 in Millisle, a village on the coast of County Down, and died in 1951 at Dohnavur, a village near the southern tip of India. Between those two places lie a Belfast mission hall for mill girls, a slum in Manchester, a country house in the Lake District, fifteen months in Japan, a few months in Ceylon, a bullock cart on the rutted roads of the Tinnevelly district, and a compound of red-tiled nurseries under the mountains, which grew in her lifetime into the Dohnavur Fellowship. The children there called her Amma, which in Tamil means “mother.” When she died, that one word was all they put over her grave.

A Link with the Last Volume

Readers who have come to this book from the volume before it will notice a thread between them. In 1987 Elisabeth Elliot published a long biography of Amy Carmichael, and took its title from a saying attributed to her, that missionary life is simply a chance to die. Elisabeth Elliot had read Amy Carmichael since her student years, and she found in her a writer who would not pretend. The two women never met. One was born in the reign of Queen Victoria and the other in the year of the General Strike. But they shared a conviction that a missionary story should be told as it happened, without the gilding that home audiences liked, and that God is honoured by the truth more than by a flattering account of his servants. This book tries to tell Amy Carmichael’s story in that spirit.

Why Courage?

Some of her courage was of the visible kind. She went out to Asia after a mission board had turned her down on grounds of health. She spent years travelling with a band of Indian women through villages where a foreign woman was a curiosity and the gospel was an offence. She took in a runaway child who belonged, by local custom, to a temple, knowing that the women who had kept her could bring the law down on her for doing it. For half a century she sheltered children at risk of the same fate, and she was threatened, slandered and taken to court for it.

But this book will suggest that there were quieter kinds of courage in her life, and that they may have cost her more. There was the courage to write home the truth when her readers wanted good news. Her first book about India, Things as They Are, published in 1903, told English Christians that most days on the mission field ended exactly as they began, and that conversion in caste India usually meant the loss of everything. Some readers in England did not believe her. There was the courage to stay. She never took a furlough in fifty-five years, and she buried many of the people she loved most in Indian soil. And there was the courage, in her last twenty years, of lying in one room in pain, unable to walk far, and going on with the work by prayer and by pen.

How This Book Is Written

Like the earlier volumes, this book tries to be honest about its sources. Amy Carmichael was a prolific writer, and her own books are the first source for her life. Those published before 1929, including Things as They Are (1903), Overweights of Joy (1906), Lotus Buds (1909) and Walker of Tinnevelly (1916), are in the public domain in the United States, and this book quotes from them, chiefly from Things as They Are, which is in the Ochorus library. Her later books, including Gold Cord (1932), her history of the Fellowship, and the little devotional book If (1938), are named so that readers can find them, but they are not quoted here, out of respect for the rights that may still attach to them in some countries.

The two standard biographies are Frank Houghton’s Amy Carmichael of Dohnavur, published in 1953 by a writer who was given access to her papers, and Elisabeth Elliot’s A Chance to Die. Both are still in copyright. This book has used them only as guides to facts and dates, and it does not quote or follow their wording. It tells her life in its own words. Where the sources disagree, or where a well-known story rests only on a later retelling, this book says so.

Two subjects need particular care. The first is the system of temple dedication that Amy Carmichael spent her life opposing, by which some girls in South India were given in childhood to temples and brought up to a life that ended, for many of them, in sexual exploitation. That is the hardest part of her story. This book handles it honestly, without graphic detail, and with respect for the Hindu people among whom she lived, most of whom had nothing to do with it and many of whom opposed it. Indian reformers fought it too, and it was Indian legislators who finally outlawed it. The second is that Amy Carmichael was a woman of her time and her empire. She sometimes wrote about Hinduism in language that is painful to read, and she ran Dohnavur with an authority that some who worked with her found hard to bear. A Christian biography should neither hide that nor make it the whole story.

Scripture in This Book

As in the earlier volumes, all Scripture is quoted from the American Standard Version of 1901, which is in the public domain. Each chapter opens with a passage that carries its theme. Amy Carmichael herself read the older Authorised Version, and where the words she remembered differ from the ASV, this book points it out.

The verse at the head of this preface is the end of a parable about a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to look for one that has gone astray. Jesus said, “it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.” Amy Carmichael built her life on that sentence. She was not a strategist of mass movements or a leader of crowds. Her work, as she saw it, was to go after one child, and then another, and then another, because each one mattered to God. This book is the story of how she did it, and of what it cost.

fields.title: Introduction: The Legend and Her Own Books
fields.body_html:
“For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.”

— 2 Corinthians 13:8, ASV

A Verse She Chose Herself

When Amy Carmichael sat down in 1902 to introduce her first book about India, she put a sentence of Paul’s at the head of it: “We can do nothing against the Truth, but for the Truth.” She quoted it from the Authorised Version, and it is the same sentence that stands, in the words of the American Standard Version, at the head of this chapter. Under it she wrote a short paragraph about her book. “This, the book, has tried to tell the Truth,” she said. “That is all it has to say about itself.”

It is a good standard for a biography, and it is the standard this book tries to keep. That is harder than it sounds, because Amy Carmichael has become a legend, and legends are not easily corrected.

The Legend

The popular story of her life is told in sermons, children’s books, devotional websites and missionary calendars, and much of it is true. She did grow up by the sea in County Down. She did gather mill girls into a hall in Belfast. She did go to Japan, and then to India, and she never came home. She did take in a little girl named Preena who had run away from a temple, and she did spend the rest of her life sheltering children. She did fall, in 1931, and spend her last twenty years largely confined to her room. She did write many books that are still in print.

But the legend has also grown in the telling. Some versions say that she rescued a thousand temple prostitutes, as if the children she sheltered were all taken out of temples. Most were not. Many were babies or small children brought to Dohnavur because they were thought to be in danger of being given to temples, and many others came for other reasons, as orphans, as unwanted daughters, or as the children of women who could not keep them. Some versions say that her work ended the dedication of girls to temples in India, or that the practice was outlawed in 1948 because of her. The law that ended it in the Madras Presidency was passed in October 1947, after a long campaign led by Indian reformers, above all the physician and legislator Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, and by members of the communities concerned. Missionaries had a part in the debate, but it was not their law.

Other stories are true in substance but uncertain in detail. The best-known story from her childhood, of a little girl praying for blue eyes and discovering in the morning that they were still brown, comes from her own memory, told late in life, and the ages given for it vary. The story of her staining her skin with coffee to pass unnoticed into places where a European could not go is told in many popular books; it is consistent with what she says about wearing Indian dress, but the details have been embroidered. The saying most often quoted from her, that “missionary life is simply a chance to die,” is widely attributed to her and gave Elisabeth Elliot the title of her book, but it is rarely given with a date or a source.

None of this makes her smaller. It is simply the kind of growth that happens to the stories of people who are loved. This book tries to separate what is known from what is told.

Her Own Books

The first source for her life is what she wrote herself. She wrote a great deal: books, booklets, poems, hymns, and a stream of letters to friends, to supporters, and to the members of her own Fellowship. The early books were mostly written from the field, in the form of letters or sketches, and they are vivid and immediate. From Sunrise Land (1895) collected her letters from Japan. Things as They Are (1903) told of village work in the Tinnevelly district, and its sequel Overweights of Joy (1906) set beside it the joys she felt the first book had not had room for. Lotus Buds (1909) described the first babies and small girls at Dohnavur and the system from which many of them had been kept. Walker of Tinnevelly (1916) was her memoir of the missionary with whom she worked for sixteen years. Later came biographies of Indian Christians, books of verse and devotion, and Gold Cord (1932), her own history of the Fellowship.

These books are invaluable, but they need to be read for what they are. They were written for supporters, and she shaped them. She changed names, often giving the people in them English translations of their Tamil names, such as Pearl-eyes, Star and Jewel of Victory, to protect them and to make them memorable. She sometimes compressed time. She wrote in the language of the Keswick holiness movement, in which every event was part of a spiritual battle, and in which the religion of her neighbours was often described as the work of the devil. And she was, by her own admission, a writer who left a great deal out. In Things as They Are she said repeatedly that she could not tell the whole truth, because it could not be printed.

The Biographers

The first full life, Frank Houghton’s Amy Carmichael of Dohnavur (1953), was written by a senior figure in the China Inland Mission, who was given access to her letters and papers. It is the source of many of the dates and details that later books repeat. It is also the work of an admirer, written within two years of her death for readers who loved her. Elisabeth Elliot’s A Chance to Die (1987) drew on Houghton, on the Dohnavur archives, and on interviews with people who had known Amy, and it is more willing to see her faults. Iain Murray’s Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes (2015) is a more recent life from within the same tradition. All three remain in copyright, and this book has used them for facts and not for their words.

Beside the biographies there is a smaller body of scholarly work. Historians of mission have looked at her place in the Keswick movement and at the long quarrel between her and the young Stephen Neill, later a bishop and a noted historian of Christian missions, who worked at Dohnavur for little more than a year in 1924 and 1925. Historians of South India have studied the reform movement against temple dedication, in which missionary writing, including hers, played a part. Some of them, notably Davesh Soneji, have argued that the reformers’ language did lasting harm to the hereditary communities of temple dancers and musicians, whose art and dignity were swept away along with the abuses. This book does not adopt every judgement of these scholars, but it has listened to them.

What This Book Is, and Is Not

This book is a narrative life. It follows Amy Carmichael from Millisle to Dohnavur, and it tries to give the people around her their due: her mother, who outlived her husband by nearly thirty years and let her eldest daughter go, first to another household and then to the far side of the world; Robert Wilson, the Quaker who treated her as a daughter; Thomas Walker, who taught her Tamil and fought beside her for sixteen years; Ponnammal, the young widow who led the women’s band; Arulai, the girl convert who became one of the pillars of Dohnavur; and the children themselves, so far as the sources let us see them.

It is not an account of her devotional teaching. Her poems and meditations deserve their own reading, and the best way to meet them is in her own books. The present book quotes her own words chiefly from Things as They Are, which readers can find complete in the Ochorus library, and it quotes sparingly.

Above all, this book does not try to make her a saint without shadows. She could be fierce, and she could be imperious. She sometimes wrote about Hinduism with a contempt that was common among missionaries of her day, and that Hindu readers had every reason to resent. She guarded the children of Dohnavur with a protectiveness that some observers saw as love and others as control. She was also brave, self-forgetting, funny, tender, and utterly given to the God she served. Paul said that he could do nothing against the truth, but only for it. A true portrait will serve her memory, and her Lord, better than a flattering one.

fields.title: Brown Eyes
fields.body_html:
“For thou didst form my inward parts: Thou didst cover me in my mother’s womb. I will give thanks unto thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: Wonderful are thy works; And that my soul knoweth right well.”

— Psalm 139:13-14, ASV

A Village by the Sea

Millisle is a small village on the eastern shore of the Ards peninsula in County Down, in the north of Ireland. It looks out across the Irish Sea, and on a clear day the hills of Galloway in Scotland can be seen on the horizon. In the middle of the nineteenth century it was a place of farms, fishing boats and mills, where the wind and the tide set the rhythm of the day. Amy Beatrice Carmichael was born there on 16 December 1867.

Her father, David Carmichael, was a miller, and so were the men of his family before him. The Carmichaels were of Scottish descent, like many of the Presbyterian families of County Down, whose ancestors had crossed the narrow sea in the seventeenth century. They ran flour mills, and in Amy’s childhood the business was prosperous. Her mother, Catherine Jane Filson, came from a family of similar background, and she was by every account a woman of warm and steady faith. Amy was the first of their seven children. Brothers and sisters followed in quick succession, and the house was full and noisy.

The family belonged to the Presbyterian church, and their faith was the faith of the Ulster Presbyterians of their day: serious, scriptural, and rooted in the Westminster Shorter Catechism, which children learned by heart. Sunday was kept with care. Family prayers were a fixed part of the day. The great Ulster revival of 1859 had swept through the province less than a decade before Amy was born, and it had left behind it a strong evangelical piety, with an expectation that faith would be personal, that conversion was real, and that the Bible spoke directly to the soul. It was in that atmosphere that Amy grew up.

The Shorter Catechism begins with a question that every Presbyterian child in Ulster could answer by heart: “What is the chief end of man?” The answer is: “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.” It is a sentence that holds together two things that later piety often pulled apart, duty and delight. Amy Carmichael would spend her life on the first half of it, in obedience that sometimes looked severe to those around her. But those who knew her best always spoke of the second half too: of the joy she found in God, in children, in birds and flowers and mountain streams, and of the gaiety that never quite left her even in pain. The catechism had given her both halves before she could understand either.

A Strong-Willed Child

She was, by all accounts, a lively and wilful little girl. The stories told of her childhood, most of which come from her own memory and from her family, show a child who was quick, imaginative, and not easily controlled. She loved the sea, the shore, the boats in the harbour and the open air. She was the eldest, and she led her brothers into adventures. She was also, from very early, a child who took prayer seriously, and who expected that God would answer it.

The discipline in the Carmichael house was firm, in the way of Victorian families, and Amy seems to have known it well. Later she would speak with gratitude of parents who were strict and loving at once, who expected obedience and also made the children feel deeply secure. She was not a meek child, and she was never a meek woman. But she learned at home that love and authority belong together, and that lesson, for good and for ill, shaped the way she would one day lead a household of her own.

The Prayer for Blue Eyes

The best-known story of her childhood is one she told herself, many years later. Her own eyes were brown, and she wished they were blue. Her mother had taught her that God hears and answers prayer, and so one night she asked him to change the colour of her eyes. In the morning she ran to the mirror, fully expecting to see blue eyes looking back at her. They were still brown. In the versions of the story that she told and that her biographers repeat, she was disappointed, but she also learned something that she never forgot: that no is an answer too. God had heard her; he had simply said no.

The ages given for the story vary, from about three to about five, and it is the kind of memory that grows in the telling. But it has lasted because of what came after. Decades later, in South India, Amy Carmichael wore Indian dress and, on some of her journeys, darkened her skin, so that she could move among people who would have closed their doors to a European. A woman with blue eyes would have been noticed at once. Brown eyes could pass. Whether she herself drew that connection at the time, or whether it was drawn later by those who told her story, it became one of the most loved parables of her life: a child’s prayer refused because God had a better answer in mind.

It is worth pausing over the parable, because it is easy to make it too neat. Not every unanswered prayer turns out, years later, to have a clear explanation. Amy Carmichael herself would pray many prayers in India that were not answered as she asked, for children who died, for friends who were not healed, for converts who went back. She learned to live without explanations. But the child at the mirror in Millisle had learned the first lesson of a long school: that God is not a vending machine, that he is free, and that his refusals can be trusted. The psalmist says that God formed us in our mother’s womb, and that we are “fearfully and wonderfully made.” The child who wanted different eyes was being taught, before she understood it, that she had been made as she was for a purpose.

Home and Its Shelter

The Carmichael home in Millisle was a comfortable one, at least in Amy’s early years, and the children would later be sent away to school. She remembered her childhood as a happy one, and she remembered both her parents with deep affection.

Two things about that home matter for the rest of her story. The first is that it was a home in which children were taken seriously as persons who could know God. Prayer was not something adults did on their behalf; it was something they did themselves. When Amy later insisted, against the habits of many missionaries of her day, that small Indian children could truly know and love Christ, and should be taught to pray in their own words, she was passing on what she had been given.

The second is that it was a home that would not last. Within a few years the business that supported it would decline, the family would move to Belfast, and David Carmichael would die young, leaving his widow with seven children and much less money. Amy’s childhood security was real, but it was brief. Perhaps that is one reason why, for the rest of her life, she poured so much of herself into giving security to children who had none.

The Sea

She never forgot the sea at Millisle. Many years later, in the hot plains of South India, she spent a short holiday by the sea with the young converts of her band, and in Things as They Are she described one of the boys standing on a rock in the surf, “the wind in his hair and his face wet with spray, rejoicing in it all.” The joy she took in that picture is the joy of a child who had grown up beside the water. A grown woman who had spent her early years running on the shore of the Irish Sea knew exactly what that boy was feeling.

She also learned, by the sea, the feeling of smallness that it gives, and the sense of a God whose works are wonderful. The mountains of the Western Ghats, under which she spent most of her life, would give her something similar, and she loved them. But the first great things she knew were the sky and the sea of County Down.

What Was Given

It would be wrong to read too much of the later woman back into the little girl. Most of what is told of Amy Carmichael’s childhood comes from her own memories, written or spoken long afterwards, when she knew how the story had turned out, and from relatives who told it in the light of what she became. Childhood memories are selected, and the ones we keep are the ones that fit.

But some things seem clear. She was born into a family of faith, and she never had to discover the Bible as a stranger. She was the eldest of a large family, used to leading and used to responsibility. She was strong-willed, imaginative, and quick to feel. She had been taught that God hears prayer, and she had learned, at a mirror one morning, that hearing is not the same as granting. And she had been formed, as the psalm says, by a God who did not make mistakes about the colour of a child’s eyes.

Many years later, those who knew her at Dohnavur remembered her laughter as much as her seriousness. She liked fun, she liked games, and she liked to tease. The wilful girl from Millisle had not disappeared; she had been brought under a stronger will. The next step in that process would come at a boarding school in Yorkshire, when she was fifteen.

fields.title: Harrogate
fields.body_html:
“Jehovah appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.”

— Jeremiah 31:3, ASV

A School in Yorkshire

In the early 1880s, when Amy was about twelve, her parents sent her across the sea to a girls’ boarding school in Harrogate, in Yorkshire. Harrogate was a spa town, prosperous and respectable, full of hotels and pump rooms where the well-to-do came to drink the sulphurous waters. The school she attended was run on Methodist lines, which is a reminder that the Carmichaels, though Presbyterians, did not draw tight boundaries around their evangelical faith. What mattered to them was that their daughter would be well taught, and taught in a Christian setting.

It was a long way from Millisle. For a girl who loved the shore and the open air, the regulated life of a Victorian boarding school, with its bells, its walks in pairs and its rules, cannot have been easy. Amy was clever, but she was not a model pupil. The stories that survive from these years show her as she had been at home: high-spirited, inclined to lead, and impatient with rules she thought pointless.

The Comet

One story from Harrogate has been told so often that it has become part of the legend, and it is worth telling with a little caution. In the autumn of 1882 one of the brightest comets of the century, now known as the Great September Comet, was in the newspapers and could be seen in the early morning sky. The girls of the school wanted to see it, and they were forbidden to stay up. According to the story, which her biographers took from her own later recollection, Amy organised a party of girls to slip out of bed and watch for it at night, and when they were found out she was very nearly sent home in disgrace.

Whether every detail is accurate, the story fits everything else we know about her. She was not a girl who accepted limits easily, and she was a born organiser. Years later she would gather hundreds of children into a well-ordered community, and she would be the one setting the rules. Those who think of her only as the saintly invalid of her last years should remember the girl who wanted to see the comet.

A Children’s Mission

The most important event of her schooldays came in 1883, when she was fifteen. A children’s mission was held in Harrogate, of a kind that was then common in Britain. The Children’s Special Service Mission had been founded in 1867, the year of Amy’s birth, to hold meetings for children and young people, on beaches in the summer and in schools and halls through the year. Its speakers told Bible stories, taught simple choruses, and spoke plainly about the love of Christ and the need to respond to it.

The movement had begun in a small way. Its founder, Josiah Spiers, had started holding meetings for children in London, and soon afterwards he gathered a crowd of children on a beach in North Wales by writing a text in the sand. The idea spread quickly, and by the 1880s the mission’s workers were a familiar sight at the seaside in summer and in schools through the year. They were mostly lay people, many of them young, and they spoke to children as if what children thought and chose really mattered. That was less common in Victorian Britain than it should have been. To be addressed in that way, as someone capable of a real response to God, could be a powerful thing for a child.

Amy later said that it was at such a meeting that she put her trust in Christ for herself. The details of what was said have been retold in different ways, and some later accounts add a hymn or a particular moment of silence that cannot now be checked. What she remembered was the substance. She had known about Jesus all her life. She had prayed since she was a small child. But at fifteen, in a school far from home, she came to understand that the love of God was meant for her personally, and she received it.

It may seem strange to speak of conversion in a girl who had grown up in such a devout home, and some Christians would hesitate to use the word. But it was the language of her tradition, and she meant something real by it. There is a difference between living inside a faith and owning it. Many children of Christian homes cross that line so quietly that they cannot name the day. Others, like Amy, remember a time and a place. Neither way is better than the other. What matters is that the faith of the parents becomes the faith of the child.

An Everlasting Love

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the prophet Jeremiah, speaking to a people in exile: “Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.” It is a verse about the initiative of God. The love comes first, and it is everlasting, which means it was there before the people knew it. The drawing comes after, and it is done with kindness, not force.

That is a good description of what happened to Amy Carmichael at Harrogate. She did not discover a God who had been absent. She discovered that a God who had always been present had been drawing her all along. Her later writing is full of this sense of being drawn, of being wooed rather than driven. It was a long way from the hell-fire that frightened some Victorian children into faith. She would one day teach small Indian girls that Jesus loved them, and she would refuse to frighten them into believing it.

It is worth noticing, too, that this decisive moment came through a children’s mission. Amy Carmichael never forgot that she had been reached as a child, by people who took children seriously enough to speak to them about God. When she later found herself responsible for hundreds of children, she did not treat them as too young for real faith. She believed that a child could know Christ, and she organised a whole community around that belief.

The End of School

Her time at Harrogate did not last much longer. The Carmichael business was in difficulty. The flour mills of the north of Ireland faced hard competition in the 1870s and 1880s, as cheap grain and flour came in from abroad and the old local mills struggled to keep up, and David Carmichael’s fortunes declined. About 1883 the family moved to Belfast, and Amy was brought home from school. Accounts differ on the exact year, and on whether the move came before or after the worst of the losses, but the direction is clear. The comfortable life of Millisle was ending.

In Belfast her father seems to have tried to make a new start, and for a time the family still lived in a respectable part of the city. But money was tighter than before, and the children who had been growing up as the sons and daughters of a prosperous miller were growing up instead as the children of a struggling one. For Amy, the eldest, that meant responsibility. She was expected to help her mother with the younger children, and she did.

A Girl of Her Time

It is easy to forget how limited the options were for a girl like Amy in the 1880s. A daughter of a middle-class Presbyterian family in Belfast was expected to help at home, to do charitable work, and in due course to marry. Higher education for women was only just beginning, and few women from her background went to university. A career outside the home was unusual and, for many families, faintly disreputable. Missionary service abroad was one of the very few ways in which a single woman could do serious work in the world, and even that was only beginning to open to women on their own.

Amy Carmichael did not yet know that she would be a missionary. She did not yet know what she would do at all. But she came home from Harrogate with two things that would shape the rest of her life. She had a personal faith, which she knew to be hers and not merely her parents’. And she had a strong will that was beginning to be brought under the control of something stronger than itself. The comet had shown the will; the children’s mission had shown the faith. The next years in Belfast would show what happened when the two came together.

A Reflection

Christian biographies often hurry past their subjects’ conversions, as if the important part were what they did afterwards. But for Amy Carmichael the moment at Harrogate was the root of everything. She was not, in later life, a woman who talked much about her own experiences. She preferred to point to Christ. But when she did look back, she saw her whole life as the story of being drawn, step by step, by a love that had been there before she knew it.

The verse from Jeremiah was spoken to Israel at a time of loss, when the nation had been carried into exile and the old securities were gone. It was not a promise that the losses would be undone. It was a promise that love would hold. Amy was about to lose a great deal: her father, her family’s comfort, and much of the life she had expected. What she had gained at fifteen would have to carry her through it.

She had a personal faith, which she knew to be hers and not merely her parents’. And she had a strong will that was beginning to be brought under the control of something stronger than itself. The comet had shown the will; the children’s mission had shown the faith. The next years in Belfast would show what happened when the two came together. But when she did look back, she saw her whole life as the story of being drawn, step by step, by a love that had been there before she knew it. The verse from Jeremiah was spoken to Israel at a time of loss, when the nation had been carried into exile and the old securities were gone. It was not a promise that the losses would be undone. It was a promise that love would hold. Amy was about to lose a great deal: her father, her family’s comfort, and much of the life she had expected. What she had gained at fifteen would have to carry her through it.

fields.title: Gold, Silver, Costly Stones
fields.body_html:
“But if any man buildeth on the foundation gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, stubble; each man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself shall prove each man’s work of what sort it is.”

— 1 Corinthians 3:12-13, ASV

Belfast

The Belfast to which the Carmichaels moved in the early 1880s was a city growing at astonishing speed. In the course of the nineteenth century it had changed from a modest port into one of the great industrial cities of the British Isles. Its linen mills were among the largest in the world. Its shipyards were beginning to build the great liners. Its population had multiplied many times over within living memory, and it was still climbing. Rows of narrow brick houses spread out from the mills along the Falls Road and the Shankill, and tens of thousands of women and girls walked to work each morning in the dark.

The Carmichaels did not live among them. They took a house in a respectable district, and they worshipped at Rosemary Street Presbyterian Church, one of the old congregations of the city centre. For a time, at least, life went on in much the way it had in Millisle. But the family business was failing, and the money that had once seemed secure was draining away.

Her Father’s Death

In 1885 David Carmichael died. He was still in middle life, and his death was a shock to the whole family. Amy was seventeen. She was the eldest of seven children, and her mother was left with a large family, a failing business, and debts. The comfortable years were over.

We know less than we would like about Amy’s grief. She did not write much about it, and her biographers have little to go on beyond the fact itself and its consequences. But it is clear that her father’s death changed her position in the family. She became, in a real sense, her mother’s partner, sharing the responsibility for the younger children and for the household. It was a role she seems to have taken on without complaint, and it prepared her, in ways she could not have foreseen, for the role she would one day take on at Dohnavur.

It is worth noting, too, that a long and painful illness entered her life at about this time. She began to suffer from neuralgia, a condition of the nerves that brought attacks of severe pain, sometimes lasting for days or weeks and leaving her exhausted and unable to work. It would trouble her for the rest of her life. In an age before modern painkillers, there was little that doctors could do for it. It would be the reason a mission board turned her down, and it would be her companion in every place she lived.

A Sunday Morning

The most famous story of Amy’s Belfast years is one she told herself, long afterwards, as the moment when the direction of her life changed. It happened on a dull Sunday morning, as the family was walking home from church. Amy and two of her brothers saw an old woman, poor and ragged, struggling along the street with a heavy bundle. They turned and helped her, taking her arms and carrying her load. It was not a dignified sight, and the respectable people who were coming out of church at the same time could see them. Amy later admitted that she felt hot with embarrassment.

As they passed a fountain in the street, words came into her mind with such force that she turned to see who had spoken them. They were the words of Paul from the third chapter of First Corinthians, in the Authorised Version she knew: “gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble.” Every man’s work, the passage goes on, shall be made manifest, for the day shall declare it, and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is. There was nobody there. The fountain splashed, the people walked on, and the boys and their sister went on with the old woman. But when she got home, Amy went to her room and stayed there for some time alone. She said later that she settled something with God that day.

The ASV, quoted at the head of this chapter, renders “precious stones” as “costly stones,” but the meaning is the same. Paul is talking about the work that Christians build on the foundation of Christ. Some of it will last, and some of it will burn. The test is not how it looks to other people but how it stands in the fire of God’s judgement. On that Sunday morning, a girl who had been embarrassed to be seen helping a poor woman in the street was suddenly confronted with the question of what she was building with her life. Respectability, she realised, was wood, hay and stubble. The love that bends down to carry an old woman’s bundle was gold.

It is a story that has been told so often that it is easy to tidy it up. She did not become a different person overnight. She went on caring about what people thought of her, and she would struggle with pride for the rest of her life, as she freely admitted. But from that morning, as she told it, she knew where the line ran. She would rather be seen with the poor, and look foolish, than be admired and build with stubble.

The Glasgow Meeting

A second turning point came in 1886, when she was eighteen. She travelled to Glasgow to attend a convention for the deepening of spiritual life, of the kind that the Keswick Convention had made popular. These meetings, which had begun in the English Lake District in 1875, taught that Christians need not live in constant defeat by sin, and that by trusting Christ and yielding themselves entirely to him they could know a life of rest and victory. The teaching was sometimes called “the higher life” or “holiness,” and it drew large crowds, especially among evangelical Anglicans, Presbyterians and Quakers.

The convention at Keswick itself had been founded by the vicar of St John’s, Keswick, Canon Thomas Harford-Battersby, together with a Quaker businessman from the neighbouring countryside named Robert Wilson. Its motto was “All one in Christ Jesus,” and it deliberately brought together Christians of different denominations under one tent each summer. Amy did not yet know Robert Wilson. Within a few years he would be the most important older friend of her life, and his house would be her home.

Amy had come with a sense of need. She was finding the Christian life a struggle. According to her own account, the speakers at the meeting did not help her much. What reached her, near the end, was a short prayer offered by the chairman, which drew on the closing words of the letter of Jude, where Christ is praised as the one who is able to keep his people from falling. In the ASV the verse reads, “Now unto him that is able to guard you from stumbling, and to set you before the presence of his glory without blemish in exceeding joy.” She said afterwards that she went out of the hall with the knowledge that he was able to keep her, and that this was enough.

That conviction stayed at the centre of her faith. She was not a theologian, and she did not spend much time on the debates that the Keswick teaching provoked, about how complete the victory over sin could be in this life. What she took from it was simpler: that Christ himself was the keeper, and that the life of faith was a life of trusting him rather than straining after holiness in one’s own strength. It was a teaching that would carry her through much that was to come.

A Life Begins to Turn

The two experiences, on the Belfast street and in the Glasgow hall, belong together. One was about service: what she would build. The other was about strength: how she would be kept. Together they gave her a direction and a source of power for it.

She began at once to look for ways to serve. She started meetings for the children of the neighbourhood, and she visited the poor. She joined in the work of the city mission. And she began to notice the girls who walked past her church every morning on their way to the mills, wrapped in shawls because they could not afford hats, and who never came inside. The next chapter tells what she did about them.

The Fire That Proves

Paul’s image of the fire is a sobering one. It is not about salvation; he says plainly that the one whose work is burned up will be saved, “yet so as through fire.” It is about the value of what we do with our lives. Much that looks impressive will not survive the test, and much that looks small will. An old woman’s bundle, carried through the streets of Belfast on a wet Sunday, may outlast a great deal of religious activity.

Amy Carmichael spent the rest of her life measuring her work by that test. She was suspicious of statistics, of large claims, of success that could be photographed and reported. She cared about whether the work was real, whether the converts were true, and whether the children were loved. In the most famous passage of her later writing, she would ask herself again and again whether her love was the love of Calvary, and if not, what it was worth. That searching habit of mind began on the Sunday morning by the fountain, when a girl in her teens, embarrassed by the company she was keeping, heard Paul’s words and knew that God was looking not at how her work appeared, but at what it was made of.

fields.title: The Shawlies
fields.body_html:
“Then the master of the house being angry said to his servant, Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor and maimed and blind and lame.”

— Luke 14:21, ASV

Girls in Shawls

In the Belfast of the 1880s, a woman’s headgear told the world where she stood. A lady wore a hat or a bonnet. A servant wore a cap. A mill girl, who could afford neither, wrapped a shawl around her head and shoulders against the rain and walked to work like that. People called them “shawlies,” and the word was not a compliment.

There were thousands of them. The linen industry of Belfast depended on women and girls, many of whom started work in their early teens, some as “half-timers” even younger. They worked long hours in the spinning rooms and weaving sheds, where the air was hot and wet to keep the flax supple, and where the noise of the machinery was deafening. Their wages were low. Their health suffered from the damp, the dust and the long hours on their feet. Many of them came from families that had moved to the city from the countryside in search of work, and many lived in crowded houses in the narrow streets near the mills.

Few of them went to church. The churches of Belfast were full on Sunday mornings, but they were full of people in hats. A girl in a shawl would have felt out of place in a respectable congregation, and many congregations would have made her feel it. The gulf between the churchgoing classes and the working poor was wide in every British city, and in Belfast it was sharpened by the divisions of class within each denomination.

The First Class

Amy Carmichael noticed them. Exactly how it began is not certain, but by the mid-1880s she was running a Sunday morning class for shawlies in a hall belonging to Rosemary Street Presbyterian Church. It was a bold thing to do. Some members of the congregation were not pleased to see their premises filled with mill girls, and the girls themselves were wary at first of a young lady from a good family who wanted to teach them the Bible.

But they came, and they kept coming. Amy was not much older than many of them, and she seems to have had a gift, from the start, for treating people as people rather than as objects of charity. She taught them the Bible, sang with them, and prayed with them. She also tried to help them in practical ways. The class grew until the hall was too small, and it went on growing.

It is worth asking why. Amy had no training as a teacher or an evangelist. She was shy in some ways, and she would never be a great public speaker. But she cared intensely about the girls in front of her, and they could tell. Years later, in India, people would notice the same thing: that she had a way of making each person feel that she or he mattered to her, and to God. It was not a technique. It was the fruit of the Sunday morning by the fountain, when she had learned that an old woman’s bundle was worth more than other people’s good opinion.

A Hall for the Shawlies

As the class outgrew its room, Amy began to pray for a building of its own. The story of how the prayer was answered is one of the best known of her early life. She saw an advertisement in The Christian, a widely read evangelical weekly, for a building made of corrugated iron that could be put up to hold about five hundred people, at a cost of five hundred pounds. Iron halls of this kind, sometimes called tin tabernacles, were common at the time; they were cheap and quick to erect, and many mission congregations began in them.

Five hundred pounds was a very large sum, far beyond anything the Carmichael family could now afford. But, according to the account handed down, a Christian woman named Kate Mitchell heard of the need and gave the whole amount, and a mill owner gave a piece of land on which to put it, at the corner of Cambrai Street and Heather Street, off the Shankill Road. The hall was built, and it was named the Welcome. Sources differ on when it opened: some give 1887, and others say that it was opened at the beginning of 1889. The later date seems more likely to be the date of the formal opening, though the work had begun some years before.

The name said everything. This was to be a place where the shawlies would be welcome, not tolerated. Amy was firm about who it was for. It was not to become another middle-class mission hall, filled with the respectable poor and the comfortable rich. It was for the girls from the mills.

The Work Grows

At the Welcome Hall the work spread out in many directions. There were Bible classes and Sunday meetings, and, by the accounts that survive, gatherings during the week as well, meant to meet the girls where they were and not only on Sundays. Amy was not the only worker; others joined her, and she seems to have been as good at drawing in helpers as at drawing in the girls. But she was the centre of it, and she poured herself into it.

The hall outlived her by a long time. It still stands in Belfast, now as Welcome Evangelical Church, and a centre in her name tells her story to visitors. It is a modest monument. But there is something fitting about it. The first permanent fruit of Amy Carmichael’s ministry was a corrugated iron hall built for girls who were too poor to wear hats.

What She Learned

The Welcome Hall years taught Amy Carmichael things she would use for the rest of her life. She learned that the gospel was for the poor, and that the poor would come if they were truly welcomed. She learned that faith and practical care belonged together. She learned to organise, to lead others, and to keep a work going week after week. And she learned, perhaps for the first time, the pattern of prayer and provision that would mark her whole life. She had prayed for a hall, she had not asked anyone for money, and the money had come.

That last point needs to be handled carefully. Amy Carmichael came to believe very firmly that the needs of God’s work should be made known to God in prayer, and not to people by appeals. She learned this partly from the example of George Müller of Bristol, who had run orphan houses for thousands of children on that principle, and from Hudson Taylor and the China Inland Mission. In later years Dohnavur would never make appeals for money, and she would point to its survival as evidence that God answers prayer. But it is worth remembering that the Welcome Hall was paid for by a wealthy woman who heard about it, and that the principle of not asking did not mean that nobody knew. Christians who share her convictions have sometimes been accused of asking by not asking, by telling stories of need in a way that invites a response. Amy was aware of the danger, and she tried hard to avoid it. Whether she always succeeded is a fair question, and one she would have asked herself.

The Feast in the Parable

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from a parable of Jesus about a great supper. The invited guests made excuses and did not come, and the master of the house, angry at their refusal, sent his servant out into the streets and lanes of the city to bring in the poor, the maimed, the blind and the lame. When there was still room, he sent him out again, to the highways and hedges, to compel people to come in, so that his house would be filled.

It is a parable about the generosity of God and about the strange guest list of his kingdom. The respectable, who had every reason to come, stayed away. The poor, who had no claim on the master at all, were brought in. The servant’s job was simply to go out and bring them.

The young woman who built a hall for the shawlies of Belfast had understood that parable. She did not wait for the mill girls to find their way into the churches. She went out to them, and she made a place for them. It would not be the last time. In India, she would go out to the villages, and later she would make a place for children who had nowhere else to go. The Welcome Hall was the first of her houses of welcome. It was not the last.

A Call Beyond Belfast

By 1889 the Welcome Hall was well established, and Amy might have spent her life there. Many women of her background did spend their lives in exactly this kind of work, running mission halls and Bible classes in their home cities, and it was valuable and honourable work. But the Carmichael family’s circumstances were changing again. Their financial troubles had not ended with her father’s death, and in 1889 the family left Belfast. Amy and her mother went to Manchester, where a new opening for mission work among mill girls had been offered to them. She handed over the Welcome Hall to others. She was twenty-one, and she was about to discover that the work she loved could be taken from her as suddenly as it had been given.

In later years Dohnavur would never make appeals for money, and she would point to its survival as evidence that God answers prayer. But it is worth remembering that the Welcome Hall was paid for by a wealthy woman who heard about it, and that the principle of not asking did not mean that nobody knew. Christians who share her convictions have sometimes been accused of asking by not asking, by telling stories of need in a way that invites a response. The invited guests made excuses and did not come, and the master of the house, angry at their refusal, sent his servant out into the streets and lanes of the city to bring in the poor, the maimed, the blind and the lame. It is a parable about the generosity of God and about the strange guest list of his kingdom. The respectable, who had every reason to come, stayed away. The poor, who had no claim on the master at all, were brought in. The servant’s job was simply to go out and bring them. The young woman who built a hall for the shawlies of Belfast had understood that parable. She did not wait for the mill girls to find their way into the churches. She went out to them, and she made a place for them. It would not be the last time. In India, she would go out to the villages, and later she would make a place for children who had nowhere else to go. The Welcome Hall was the first of her houses of welcome. It was not the last. A Call Beyond Belfast By 1889 the Welcome Hall was well established, and Amy might have spent her life there. Many women of her background did spend their lives in exactly this kind of work, running mission halls and Bible classes in their home cities, and it was valuable and honourable work. But the Carmichael family’s circumstances were changing again. Their financial troubles had not ended with her father’s death, and in 1889 the family left Belfast. Amy and her mother went to Manchester, where a new opening for mission work among mill girls had been offered to them. She handed over the Welcome Hall to others. She was twenty-one, and she was about to discover that the work she loved could be taken from her as suddenly as it had been given.

fields.title: The Dear Old Man
fields.body_html:
“God setteth the solitary in families: He bringeth out the prisoners into prosperity; But the rebellious dwell in a parched land.”

— Psalm 68:6, ASV

Manchester

In 1889 Amy Carmichael and her mother moved to Manchester. The rest of the family was scattering. The Carmichael fortunes had not recovered, and the younger children were making their own way; in time several of them would emigrate and make their lives overseas. For Amy and her mother, Manchester offered a fresh start and a new field of work. They had been invited to help in a mission among the mill workers of the city, and Amy threw herself into it with all the energy she had brought to the Welcome Hall.

Manchester was the first industrial city of the world. Its cotton mills had made it rich and famous, and they had also made parts of it among the most wretched places in Britain. Ancoats, the district where the earliest great mills had been built, was a byword for overcrowding, dirt and poverty. Its streets were narrow and dark, its houses damp, its air thick with smoke. Mill girls lived there in great numbers, and so did the poorest of the city’s poor.

Amy chose to live among them. She took a room in the district, in a house that, by the accounts that survive, was dirty and infested with vermin, so that she would be near the people she wanted to reach. It was an unusual thing for a young woman of her background to do, and it showed the same instinct that would later lead her to wear Indian dress and live in an Indian village. She wanted to be among people, not above them.

Breakdown

The work in Manchester did not last long. Amy’s health, already uncertain, could not stand the strain. The neuralgia that had troubled her in Belfast grew worse, and the long hours, the poor food, and the foul air of Ancoats wore her down. Within months she was exhausted and ill, and she had to stop.

It was a bitter experience. She had given up the Welcome Hall to come to Manchester, and now she could not do the work she had come for. She had to accept that there were limits to what her body could bear, and that zeal alone would not carry her. It was the first of many such lessons. Again and again in her life, illness would stop her, or slow her, or send her somewhere she had not planned to go. She never found it easy to accept, but she came to believe that God used it.

Robert Wilson

It was at this low point that an old friend stepped in. Robert Wilson was a Quaker, a Cumberland businessman, and one of the founders of the Keswick Convention. He was a much older man, a widower who, by the usual account, had lost both his wife and his only daughter, and he lived at Broughton Grange, a country house near Cockermouth, with his grown sons. Amy had met him through the convention movement, probably in 1887, and he had taken a warm interest in her. Now, seeing her worn out by the work in Manchester, he invited her to come and stay at Broughton Grange.

She went in 1890, and she stayed. What began as a convalescence became a new life. Robert Wilson came to treat her as a daughter, and she came to treat him as a father. She called him by an affectionate nickname, “the Dear Old Man,” and in her letters often simply “D.O.M.” In time she began to use his name alongside her own, and her early books were published under the name Amy Wilson-Carmichael. She was never legally adopted, but the relationship was, for both of them, real and deep.

Her mother agreed to the arrangement, and that too was an act of generosity. Catherine Carmichael was a widow, and Amy was her eldest daughter. To let her go to another household was to give something up. But she seems to have seen that her daughter needed rest, and that Robert Wilson needed companionship, and that the arrangement might serve them both. It was not the last time that she would let Amy go.

A School of Another Kind

Broughton Grange was a school for Amy in a way that Harrogate had never been. Robert Wilson was at the heart of the Keswick movement, and through him she met many of the leading evangelical figures of the day. Missionaries on furlough, speakers at the convention, and leaders of mission societies came and went at the house. She heard their stories, listened to their discussions, and saw the needs of the world through their eyes. Among them, she would later meet or hear Hudson Taylor, founder of the China Inland Mission, whose appeal for workers had already stirred her at Keswick in 1887.

She also absorbed something of the Quaker spirit of her adopted father. Robert Wilson was a man of quiet, practical faith, and he valued silence and waiting on God. The Keswick Convention he had helped to found was deliberately interdenominational; its motto was “All one in Christ Jesus.” Amy, the Presbyterian girl who had been schooled among Methodists and who would later work with Anglicans, took that spirit to heart. Dohnavur would never belong to a single denomination, and she would insist that its members be united by their love for Christ rather than by their church labels.

At Broughton Grange she learned, too, the practical business of running a large household. She helped Robert Wilson with his correspondence, acted as his companion, and in many ways ran his home. It was experience that she would draw on later, when she found herself at the head of a household of hundreds.

A Missionary Age

The years Amy spent at Broughton Grange were years of extraordinary missionary enthusiasm in the English-speaking churches. In 1885 seven young men from Cambridge, among them a famous cricketer, had sailed for China with Hudson Taylor’s mission, and their story had been told in every evangelical newspaper. In America, the Student Volunteer Movement had taken as its watchword “the evangelization of the world in this generation,” and thousands of students were signing pledges to go overseas. Women were beginning to go out in large numbers, not only as missionaries’ wives but as missionaries in their own right, to teach, to nurse, and to visit women in their homes where no man could go.

The Keswick Convention was caught up in this movement and helped to drive it. Its teaching on surrender, on giving the whole of oneself to Christ, led naturally to the question of where Christ wanted that self to be given. Speakers at the convention appealed for missionaries, and the convention began to consider whether it should send missionaries of its own. By the late 1880s missionary meetings had become part of the convention week, and before long it would form a committee to send missionaries of its own. Robert Wilson was at the centre of these discussions, and Amy, living in his house, heard them all.

She was not yet thinking of going herself. Her health was poor, and she had a home and a duty at Broughton Grange. But the air she breathed there was full of the needs of the world, and of the conviction that those needs were a summons to every Christian who heard of them. Sooner or later, the question would become personal.

Set in a Family

The verse at the head of this chapter says that “God setteth the solitary in families.” It is a verse about the care of God for those who are alone: the orphan, the widow, the stranger, the prisoner. Amy Carmichael was not exactly solitary in 1890. She had a mother and brothers and sisters who loved her. But her father was dead, her family was scattering, her health had broken, and her work had been taken from her. In Robert Wilson’s house, God gave her a new family at the moment she needed it.

She would spend much of her life doing the same for others. At Dohnavur she would gather children who had no family at all, or whose families could not or would not keep them, and make them into a family. She insisted that it was a family, not an institution. The children were not inmates or cases; they were sons and daughters, brothers and sisters. She was their Amma. It is not too much to say that she was passing on what she had received at Broughton Grange, where an old man had taken in a worn-out young woman and made her his daughter.

The Shadow of a Question

There is one more thing to say about the Broughton Grange years, and it would come to matter a great deal. Robert Wilson came to depend on Amy, and he hoped that she would stay with him. He was growing old, and she had become the light of his home. When, two years later, she believed that God was calling her to go overseas, she faced a painful choice between the call and the man who had been a father to her.

Some of those around them thought she should stay. Robert Wilson needed her; she had a duty to him; there were plenty of people who could go to the mission field, but only one who could care for him. It was a reasonable argument, and Amy felt its force. The next chapter tells how she resolved it, and what it cost her and him. But it is worth noticing that the question arose because the relationship was so real. Amy Carmichael was not a woman who sat lightly to human love. She loved deeply, and she would have to learn, again and again, what it meant to put Christ first without loving others less.

For now, in 1890 and 1891, she was at peace. She had a home, a father, and work to do, and she was recovering her strength. She was also listening, though she did not yet know for what.

fields.title: “Go Ye”
fields.body_html:
“And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to the whole creation.”

— Mark 16:15, ASV

13 January 1892

Amy Carmichael remembered the date for the rest of her life. On 13 January 1892, a winter evening at Broughton Grange, she was alone in her room when, as she later described it, the words “Go ye” came to her with a clarity and authority that she could not mistake. She had heard the great commission read and preached all her life. She had heard missionary speakers at Keswick and in Robert Wilson’s drawing room. She had read reports from China and India and Africa. But this time, she said, the words were addressed to her.

It is worth being careful about what this means. Amy Carmichael was not given to claiming visions or voices, and she was suspicious of Christians who were. She did not say that she heard an audible voice. She said that a familiar command of Christ became, on a particular evening, a personal command, impossible to evade. Many Christians have known something similar: a verse read a hundred times that suddenly becomes alive, and will not let go. For Amy, it was the words of the risen Jesus at the end of Mark’s Gospel: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to the whole creation.”

A Letter to Her Mother

The next day she wrote to her mother. It must have been one of the hardest letters she ever wrote. Her mother was a widow, living with reduced means, and Amy was her eldest daughter. Her father’s death had made the family depend on one another, and Amy had been her mother’s right hand. Now she was asking her mother’s blessing to go to the other side of the world, quite possibly never to return.

Catherine Carmichael’s reply has been preserved, and the biographies print it. It is a remarkable letter, from a woman who had already lost a great deal. She did not try to hold her daughter back, and she did not lay her own needs before her. She gave her daughter up to God, freely and with thanksgiving. Amy kept the letter for the rest of her life.

The willingness of Christian parents to let their children go has always been one of the hidden costs of missionary work. The missionary gets the stories and the honour; the parents get the empty chair and the long silences between letters. Catherine Carmichael would die in England in 1913, and the daughter she had given up would not be with her. Her letter of 1892 was an act of faith as costly as anything her daughter did.

The Dear Old Man’s Grief

Robert Wilson found the news harder to bear. He had come to depend on Amy, and he loved her as a daughter. He was growing old, and her going would leave his house empty again. There were friends who told Amy plainly that her duty lay at Broughton Grange, and that it was wrong to leave an old man who needed her. Some of them thought she was being selfish, dressing up a desire for adventure in the language of a divine call.

Amy felt the force of these arguments. She did not leave lightly, and she suffered over the decision. But she was convinced that the call was real, and that to refuse it would be disobedience. In the end, Robert Wilson himself gave his consent, though it cost him a great deal to do so. He would continue to support her, write to her, and pray for her for the rest of his life, and she would continue to call him her father.

It is easy to tell such stories as if the right choice were obvious. It was not. Jesus himself spoke of the duty to care for parents, and condemned those who used religious language to evade it. Amy Carmichael was choosing between two goods, and she knew it. That she chose to go does not mean that those who urged her to stay were wrong to care about the old man. It means that she was convinced, after much prayer, that God was asking her to go, and that he would care for Robert Wilson in her absence. Whether she was right is a question that only faith can answer. She believed she was, and the rest of her life was the evidence she offered.

The China Inland Mission

Her first thought was of China. She had heard Hudson Taylor speak, and she had been moved by his appeals for workers for the vast interior of China, where there were millions who had never heard the gospel. The China Inland Mission was the kind of mission that appealed to her. It accepted workers from different denominations, it made no appeals for money, it asked its missionaries to wear Chinese dress and live as close to the people as possible, and it expected them to trust God for their needs. Everything about it matched her convictions.

In 1892 she applied to the mission and went to London to its training home for women candidates. There she shared in the life of the house, studied, and prepared to sail. But the mission required its candidates to pass a medical examination, and Amy did not pass. The doctors judged that her health, and above all the neuralgia that so often laid her low, made her unfit for the rigours of life in inland China. The door was closed.

It was a severe disappointment. She had been certain of the call, and now the very mission whose principles she most admired had turned her down. She went back to Broughton Grange, uncertain of what to do next. It must have seemed to some of her friends that the matter had been settled: she was not strong enough, and she should stay at home. But she did not believe the call had been withdrawn. She believed only that one door had shut.

The Keswick Missionary

The next door opened from an unexpected direction. The Keswick Convention had been discussing for some time whether it should support missionaries of its own, and it now formed a committee to do so. Amy Carmichael became the first missionary it sent out. Arrangements were made for her to join the work of Barclay Buxton, an Anglican missionary of the Church Missionary Society who was leading an evangelistic work in western Japan, around the town of Matsue. Buxton was himself a Keswick man, and the connection was natural.

It was, in some ways, an odd arrangement. Amy was not a member of the Church Missionary Society, and she was not formally attached to any mission board. She was going out on the support of a convention, to work alongside a mission whose structures she did not belong to. Her health had just been judged unequal to missionary life by one of the most experienced missions in the world. Some observers must have thought it unwise. But she was sure that she was meant to go, and those who sent her shared her confidence.

She sailed for the East in March 1893, travelling with a small party of women missionaries bound for China. She was twenty-five. She had never been further from home than England, and she had no training in languages or in cross-cultural work. What she had was a conviction that she had been sent, a faith that had been tested by loss and illness, and a capacity for love that had already been proved among the shawlies of Belfast and the mill girls of Manchester.

Single Women Abroad

It is easy now to forget how new it was for a single woman to go overseas as a missionary in her own right. For most of the nineteenth century the Protestant missionary was a man, often accompanied by a wife who worked as hard as he did but whose work was rarely recognised. Single women began to go out in significant numbers only from the 1860s onward, and at first they went mostly to teach in schools or to visit women in their homes, the so-called zenana work, in societies where a male missionary could not enter the women’s quarters of a house. Societies were formed especially for this purpose, among them the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society, founded in 1880, which Amy Carmichael would one day join.

By the 1890s the numbers were growing rapidly, and in some missions single women outnumbered the men. But their position was still uncertain. They were often paid less than men, they were usually excluded from the councils that made decisions, and they were expected to defer to the senior male missionaries of their stations. Many of them found ways to do remarkable work within these limits, and a few, like Mary Slessor in Calabar, found ways to step outside them. Amy Carmichael would prove to be one of the few. But in March 1893 she was simply a young woman of uncertain health, going out under an unusual arrangement to a country whose language she did not know.

Go Ye

The great commission at the end of Mark’s Gospel is addressed to the eleven disciples, but Christians have always heard it as addressed to the whole church. “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to the whole creation.” It is not a command to be successful. It is a command to go, and to tell.

Amy Carmichael would later write, in Things as They Are, of the long days of village work in which nothing seemed to happen, and she would hold on to that commission as the reason for going on. “He said ‘Go, tell,’” she wrote, “and we have come and are telling, and we meet Him as we ‘go and tell.’” The last part of that sentence is the key to her whole life. She did not go out of a sense of duty only, though duty mattered to her. She went because she believed that the one who sent her would be found on the road. She had found him on a winter evening at Broughton Grange, and she would look for him in Japan, in India, and in every village and nursery she ever entered.
