She had heard Hudson Taylor speak, and she had been moved by his appeals for workers for the vast interior of China, where there were millions who had never heard the gospel. The China Inland Mission was the kind of mission that appealed to her. It accepted workers from different denominations, it made no appeals for money, it asked its missionaries to wear Chinese dress and live as close to the people as possible, and it expected them to trust God for their needs. Everything about it matched her convictions. In 1892 she applied to the mission and went to London to its training home for women candidates. There she shared in the life of the house, studied, and prepared to sail. But the mission required its candidates to pass a medical examination, and Amy did not pass. The doctors judged that her health, and above all the neuralgia that so often laid her low, made her unfit for the rigours of life in inland China. The door was closed. It was a severe disappointment. She had been certain of the call, and now the very mission whose principles she most admired had turned her down. She went back to Broughton Grange, uncertain of what to do next. It must have seemed to some of her friends that the matter had been settled: she was not strong enough, and she should stay at home. But she did not believe the call had been withdrawn. She believed only that one door had shut. The Keswick Missionary The next door opened from an unexpected direction. The Keswick Convention had been discussing for some time whether it should support missionaries of its own, and it now formed a committee to do so. Amy Carmichael became the first missionary it sent out. Arrangements were made for her to join the work of Barclay Buxton, an Anglican missionary of the Church Missionary Society who was leading an evangelistic work in western Japan, around the town of Matsue. Buxton was himself a Keswick man, and the connection was natural. It was, in some ways, an odd arrangement. Amy was not a member of the Church Missionary Society, and she was not formally attached to any mission board. She was going out on the support of a convention, to work alongside a mission whose structures she did not belong to. Her health had just been judged unequal to missionary life by one of the most experienced missions in the world. Some observers must have thought it unwise. But she was sure that she was meant to go, and those who sent her shared her confidence. She sailed for the East in March 1893, travelling with a small party of women missionaries bound for China. She was twenty-five. She had never been further from home than England, and she had no training in languages or in cross-cultural work. What she had was a conviction that she had been sent, a faith that had been tested by loss and illness, and a capacity for love that had already been proved among the shawlies of Belfast and the mill girls of Manchester. Single Women Abroad It is easy now to forget how new it was for a single woman to go overseas as a missionary in her own right. For most of the nineteenth century the Protestant missionary was a man, often accompanied by a wife who worked as hard as he did but whose work was rarely recognised. Single women began to go out in significant numbers only from the 1860s onward, and at first they went mostly to teach in schools or to visit women in their homes, the so-called zenana work, in societies where a male missionary could not enter the women’s quarters of a house. Societies were formed especially for this purpose, among them the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society, founded in 1880, which Amy Carmichael would one day join. By the 1890s the numbers were growing rapidly, and in some missions single women outnumbered the men. But their position was still uncertain. They were often paid less than men, they were usually excluded from the councils that made decisions, and they were expected to defer to the senior male missionaries of their stations. Many of them found ways to do remarkable work within these limits, and a few, like Mary Slessor in Calabar, found ways to step outside them. Amy Carmichael would prove to be one of the few. But in March 1893 she was simply a young woman of uncertain health, going out under an unusual arrangement to a country whose language she did not know. Go Ye The great commission at the end of Mark’s Gospel is addressed to the eleven disciples, but Christians have always heard it as addressed to the whole church. “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to the whole creation.” It is not a command to be successful. It is a command to go, and to tell. Amy Carmichael would later write, in Things as They Are, of the long days of village work in which nothing seemed to happen, and she would hold on to that commission as the reason for going on. “He said ‘Go, tell,’” she wrote, “and we have come and are telling, and we meet Him as we ‘go and tell.’” The last part of that sentence is the key to her whole life. She did not go out of a sense of duty only, though duty mattered to her. She went because she believed that the one who sent her would be found on the road. She had found him on a winter evening at Broughton Grange, and she would look for him in Japan, in India, and in every village and nursery she ever entered.

fields.title: Sunrise Land
fields.body_html:
“From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same Jehovah’s name is to be praised.”

— Psalm 113:3, ASV

Matsue

Amy Carmichael reached Japan in the spring of 1893, after a voyage by way of Shanghai. Japan was then a country in the middle of headlong change. Only forty years earlier it had been closed to the outside world. Now, under the Meiji government, it was building railways and factories, writing a constitution, and sending its young men abroad to study. Christian missionaries had been allowed to work openly for about two decades, and the churches were small but growing. In the larger cities there were mission schools and congregations, but in the countryside, especially on the western side of the main island, the gospel was still almost unknown.

The Christian story in Japan was older than the Meiji era, and darker. Roman Catholic missionaries had arrived in the sixteenth century, and for a time hundreds of thousands of Japanese had become Christians. Then, in the early seventeenth century, the faith was banned, and it was hunted down with great cruelty for more than two hundred years. Believers were tortured and killed; suspected Christians were made to tread on images of Christ and Mary to prove that they had renounced him. Some communities kept their faith in secret, handing it down through generations without priests or Scriptures. Public notice boards forbidding Christianity were taken down only in 1873, twenty years before Amy arrived. When she spoke of Christ in a Japanese home, she was speaking of a name that many older people had been taught from childhood to fear.

Barclay Buxton had gone to that western coast a few years before. He was a member of a well-known English evangelical family, an Anglican clergyman of independent means, and a man shaped, like Amy, by the Keswick movement. He had settled in Matsue, an old castle town on the shore of a lake in the province of Izumo, and had gathered a band of Japanese and English workers who travelled through the towns and villages of the region preaching the gospel. It was to this band that Amy came.

The work suited her temperament. It was evangelistic, it was carried out in teams, it involved travelling to places where the gospel had not been heard, and it depended on prayer. Buxton believed, as she did, in a close partnership with the Japanese believers, and much of the most effective work was done by Japanese Christians. Amy herself could not speak the language, and she depended on Japanese fellow workers to interpret for her, among them a young Christian woman whom she called Misaki San. With them she visited homes, held meetings for women, and travelled into the countryside. It was humbling work for someone who wanted to speak for herself, and it taught her how much the gospel in any country depends on its own people.

Letters from Sunrise Land

We know a good deal about Amy’s months in Japan because she wrote long letters home, which were later collected and published in 1895 as From Sunrise Land, her first book. The letters are lively, observant and often funny. They describe journeys by kuruma, the Japanese rickshaw, meetings with women and enquirers, and the strangeness and beauty of the country. They also show a young missionary learning hard lessons about herself.

The best-known of those lessons, as she told it later, came on a visit to an old woman who was ill and who seemed to be on the point of believing. Amy had gone in her ordinary English clothes, which included a pair of fur-lined gloves against the cold. As she spoke, she noticed the old woman’s attention wandering to the gloves. The moment passed, and the woman did not respond. Amy went home convinced that her foreign clothes had come between the woman and the gospel, and she resolved from then on to wear Japanese dress. Whatever the exact details, the lesson stayed with her. In India she would wear a sari, and she would ask the members of her Fellowship to dress as the people around them did. She did not believe that clothes could save anyone. But she believed that they could get in the way.

Learning the Hard Way

Not everything went well. Japanese is a difficult language, and Amy made slow progress. Working through an interpreter was frustrating, and she felt keenly her inability to speak directly to the people she wanted to reach. The climate did not suit her. The damp cold of the Japanese winter and the humid heat of summer brought on her neuralgia, which she began to call her “Japanese head.” There were weeks when she could do nothing at all.

There were also spiritual struggles. Amy came to Japan with high expectations, shaped by the Keswick teaching on faith and victory. She prayed for definite results, and sometimes she saw them. But she also saw much that discouraged her: people who listened politely and went away unchanged, enquirers who drew back, and the slowness of the work. She learned, as every missionary learns, that the field is not the platform, and that the stories told at conventions are only part of the truth. It was a lesson she would later put into a whole book.

The Cave

One of the most important moments of her time in Japan was not about the work at all. Many years later, she told a younger colleague about a day when she had gone alone to a cave in the hills to pray. She was troubled by the prospect of a life alone. She was in her twenties; she had chosen a path that would very probably mean she would never marry; and she was afraid of the loneliness of the years ahead. In the cave, she said, she brought the fear to God, and she received an assurance from the words of a psalm, which she knew in the Authorised Version: “none of them that trust in him shall be desolate.”

The verse is the last line of Psalm 34. In the American Standard Version it reads a little differently: “none of them that take refuge in him shall be condemned.” The two translations bring out different sides of the Hebrew word, which carries the sense of being held guilty and also of being left desolate and bereft. Amy took from it the promise that she would not be left alone. She did not say that she was never lonely afterwards; she was, often. But she said that the promise held, and that she never again doubted that God would be enough for her.

The story is told only in her later recollection, and like many such memories it may have been shaped by the years. But it rings true to the rest of her life. She never married. She formed deep friendships, and she gathered a family of hundreds, but she lived without the companionship of a husband, and she knew what that meant. Her writing about singleness, in later years, was neither sentimental nor bitter. It was the writing of someone who had faced the question squarely in a cave in Japan, and found an answer she could live with.

Fifteen Months

Amy Carmichael stayed in Japan for about fifteen months. By the summer of 1894 her health had broken down badly, and she was exhausted. She decided that she must leave, at least for a time. She went first to Shanghai, and then, believing that she was being guided, on to Ceylon. The decision was made quickly, and she did not consult the committee that had sent her before making it. Some of those at home were dismayed. To them it looked as if the Keswick missionary had simply left her post.

It is fair to ask what Japan had amounted to. In terms of visible results, not very much: some meetings, some conversations, a small number of people who professed faith, and a book of letters. She herself seems to have felt that she had failed. But Japan had taught her lessons she would use for the rest of her life: about dress and identification, about the slowness of real work, about the importance of indigenous workers, and about loneliness and the faithfulness of God. Barclay Buxton’s band was also an early model of the kind of community she would later build: a group of men and women, foreign and local, living simply and working together in prayer.

From the Rising of the Sun

The psalm at the head of this chapter speaks of the name of God being praised from the rising of the sun to its going down. Japan, the land of the rising sun, was the first place where Amy Carmichael saw that promise begin to come true in a place far from her own. She saw Japanese men and women turn to Christ and become fellow workers. She saw that the gospel was not English, or Irish, or Western, but belonged to every people under the sun.

She would spend most of her life in India, and her months in Japan are often passed over quickly in her story. But they were the first test of her call, and in some ways the hardest. She went out with no experience, no language, and poor health, under an arrangement that some thought unwise, and she came away ill and uncertain. Yet she did not doubt that she had been sent, or that she would be sent again. The next stage of the journey would be short, and it would end, unexpectedly, back in England.

fields.title: A Door Shut, a Door Opened
fields.body_html:
“Trust in Jehovah with all thy heart, And lean not upon thine own understanding: In all thy ways acknowledge him, And he will direct thy paths.”

— Proverbs 3:5-6, ASV

Ceylon

Amy Carmichael arrived in Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, in the late summer of 1894. She was ill, tired, and uncertain of her future, and she had come without the approval of the committee that had sent her to Japan. To some of her friends at home it looked like a mistake: a young woman acting on impulse, mistaking her own restlessness for the leading of God. She herself believed that she had been guided, and that she was meant to be in Ceylon, at least for a time.

Her stay there was short, and we know comparatively little about it. She was received by Christian friends, she recovered some of her strength, and she took part in evangelistic work, speaking at meetings and visiting homes. The island was warm, green and beautiful, and its people, Sinhalese and Tamil, were of many faiths: Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians. For the first time, she was among Tamil-speaking people, though she could not yet have known that Tamil would become the language of her life.

It is tempting to see the Ceylon months as a bridge to India, and in a sense they were. But at the time they must have felt more like a pause, or a detour. She did not know where she was going. She had left Japan, she had not been accepted by any mission board, and her health was as poor as ever. If she had a plan, it was simply to obey day by day and wait for the next step to become clear.

News from Broughton Grange

The next step came in a form she did not expect. Late in 1894 news reached her that Robert Wilson had suffered a stroke. He was an old man, and it seemed possible that he would not recover. Amy did not hesitate. She left Ceylon at once and sailed for England, arriving home towards the end of the year.

Robert Wilson recovered, at least in part, and lived for another ten years. Amy stayed with him at Broughton Grange through his convalescence, and for some months it seemed that her missionary career might be over. She had gone out to Japan and come back ill; she had gone to Ceylon and come back to nurse an invalid. Some of those who had criticised her for leaving him in the first place must have felt that events had proved them right.

But she did not believe that the call had been withdrawn. She had been told to go, and she had gone; that she had come back did not mean that she was meant to stay. She waited, and she prayed, and she watched for a door to open.

The Zenana Society

The door that opened in 1895 was the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society. It had been founded in 1880 to send women missionaries to work among women in India and China, especially in the zenanas, the secluded women’s quarters of high-caste homes, where no male missionary could go. It was an Anglican society, and Amy was not an Anglican, but its leaders knew of her through the Keswick connection, and they were willing to accept her.

The question of health came up again. On medical advice it was agreed that if she were to go to India at all, she should go to Bangalore, in the south, where the climate on the high plateau was cooler and healthier than on the plains. It was a sensible precaution, and Amy accepted it. She was to go to Bangalore, learn the language, and see whether her health would bear the strain. Nobody, least of all Amy herself, knew that she was going to India for good.

Robert Wilson gave his consent again. It must have been even harder the second time. He was older and weaker, and he knew now what it meant to lose her. But he let her go, and he continued to support her with his letters and his prayers until his death in 1905.

Sailing for India

In October 1895 Amy Carmichael sailed for India. She was twenty-seven. She arrived at Madras, on the south-east coast, in November, and travelled inland to Bangalore. She did not know it, but she would never see Britain again. She would spend the remaining fifty-five years of her life in India, and she would never take a furlough. In an age when missionaries normally went home every few years to rest, to report and to raise support, her staying would become one of the things she was known for.

It was not, at first, a deliberate decision. She did not sail in 1895 with a vow never to return. The decision grew out of circumstances: the work she found herself doing, the children who came to depend on her, the dangers that would face them if she left, and her own conviction that she was needed where she was. In later years it hardened into a principle, and she encouraged the members of her Fellowship to think carefully before going home. But in 1895 she was simply a young missionary of uncertain health, going out on trial, to a station she had not chosen, for a society she did not belong to by tradition.

India in 1895

The India to which she sailed was ruled by the British Crown, which had taken over the government of the country from the East India Company after the great rising of 1857. The south of the peninsula was governed from Madras as the Madras Presidency, alongside a number of princely states whose rulers kept a measure of independence under British oversight. British rule was at its height, and to most Britons it seemed permanent. But the Indian National Congress had been founded ten years earlier, Indian newspapers were debating self-government, and educated Indians were asking hard questions about the foreign power that ruled them and the foreign religion that so many of its people professed.

Hinduism itself was in a period of ferment. Reformers were challenging child marriage, the treatment of widows and the rigidities of caste, while others were defending the old ways with new confidence against both the reformers and the missionaries. Christianity was, in most of India, the faith of a small minority. In a few places, however, it had taken root in whole communities, and one of those places was the Tinnevelly district in the far south, where Amy Carmichael would spend almost all of her life. She knew none of this in detail when she landed. She would learn it slowly, and partly by painful experience.

Guidance and Its Mysteries

The story of Amy Carmichael’s path from Broughton Grange to Bangalore raises questions about guidance that Christians have always found difficult. She believed she was called to China, and China would not have her. She went to Japan, and her health broke down. She went to Ceylon, believing herself guided, and was called home within months. She went to India because a doctor thought the climate would suit her. If one were to tell the story only by its outward events, it would look like a series of false starts.

She did not see it that way. She saw it as a path along which God had been leading her, step by step, even when she could not see where it went. The verse at the head of this chapter says, “Trust in Jehovah with all thy heart, And lean not upon thine own understanding: In all thy ways acknowledge him, And he will direct thy paths.” It does not say that the path will be straight, or that its turnings will make sense at the time. It says that God will direct it.

That is a hard kind of faith. It is easy to say afterwards that the false starts were part of the plan. It is much harder to go on trusting while the path is winding and the destination is unclear. Amy Carmichael was not always sure, in 1894 and 1895, that she was doing the right thing. She was criticised, and she sometimes doubted herself. But she kept acknowledging God in the decisions she made, and she kept moving when the next step became clear. In later years she would often counsel others not to try to see the whole road, but to take the next step in obedience.

It is worth adding a word of caution. Not every winding path ends well, and not every sense of guidance is reliable. Amy’s decision to leave Japan without consulting those who had sent her was, in the view of some who loved her, not well handled, and the criticism she received was not all unfair. Faith in God’s guidance does not excuse us from the ordinary duties of consultation and accountability. Amy learned that too, in time, though she never found it easy to submit her own sense of God’s will to the judgement of others.

What She Carried

When Amy Carmichael landed at Madras in November 1895, she carried with her more than she knew. She carried the faith of her parents and the conversion of Harrogate, the lesson of the fountain and the assurance of Glasgow. She carried the experience of the Welcome Hall and the hard lesson of Manchester. She carried the interdenominational spirit of Keswick and the quiet faith of Robert Wilson. She carried the lessons of Japan about dress and identification, and the promise received in a cave that she would not be left desolate. And she carried her neuralgia, which went with her everywhere.

She did not carry a plan. She did not know about the temple children, or Dohnavur, or the family she would gather. She knew only that she had been sent, and that she was going. The rest, as she would have said, was in other hands.

The Zenana Society The door that opened in 1895 was the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society. It had been founded in 1880 to send women missionaries to work among women in India and China, especially in the zenanas, the secluded women’s quarters of high-caste homes, where no male missionary could go. It was an Anglican society, and Amy was not an Anglican, but its leaders knew of her through the Keswick connection, and they were willing to accept her. The question of health came up again. On medical advice it was agreed that if she were to go to India at all, she should go to Bangalore, in the south, where the climate on the high plateau was cooler and healthier than on the plains. It was a sensible precaution, and Amy accepted it. She was to go to Bangalore, learn the language, and see whether her health would bear the strain. Nobody, least of all Amy herself, knew that she was going to India for good. Robert Wilson gave his consent again. It must have been even harder the second time. He was older and weaker, and he knew now what it meant to lose her. But he let her go, and he continued to support her with his letters and his prayers until his death in 1905. Sailing for India In October 1895 Amy Carmichael sailed for India. She was twenty-seven. She arrived at Madras, on the south-east coast, in November, and travelled inland to Bangalore. She did not know it, but she would never see Britain again. She would spend the remaining fifty-five years of her life in India, and she would never take a furlough. In an age when missionaries normally went home every few years to rest, to report and to raise support, her staying would become one of the things she was known for. It was not, at first, a deliberate decision. She did not sail in 1895 with a vow never to return. The decision grew out of circumstances: the work she found herself doing, the children who came to depend on her, the dangers that would face them if she left, and her own conviction that she was needed where she was. In later years it hardened into a principle, and she encouraged the members of her Fellowship to think carefully before going home. But in 1895 she was simply a young missionary of uncertain health, going out on trial, to a station she had not chosen, for a society she did not belong to by tradition. India in 1895 The India to which she sailed was ruled by the British Crown, which had taken over the government of the country from the East India Company after the great rising of 1857. The south of the peninsula was governed from Madras as the Madras Presidency, alongside a number of princely states whose rulers kept a measure of independence under British oversight. British rule was at its height, and to most Britons it seemed permanent. But the Indian National Congress had been founded ten years earlier, Indian newspapers were debating self-government, and educated Indians were asking hard questions about the foreign power that ruled them and the foreign religion that so many of its people professed. Hinduism itself was in a period of ferment. Reformers were challenging child marriage, the treatment of widows and the rigidities of caste, while others were defending the old ways with new confidence against both the reformers and the missionaries. Christianity was, in most of India, the faith of a small minority. In a few places, however, it had taken root in whole communities, and one of those places was the Tinnevelly district in the far south, where Amy Carmichael would spend almost all of her life. She knew none of this in detail when she landed. She would learn it slowly, and partly by painful experience. Guidance and Its Mysteries The story of Amy Carmichael’s path from Broughton Grange to Bangalore raises questions about guidance that Christians have always found difficult. She believed she was called to China, and China would not have her. She went to Japan, and her health broke down. She went to Ceylon, believing herself guided, and was called home within months. She went to India because a doctor thought the climate would suit her. If one were to tell the story only by its outward events, it would look like a series of false starts. She did not see it that way. She saw it as a path along which God had been leading her, step by step, even when she could not see where it went. The verse at the head of this chapter says, “Trust in Jehovah with all thy heart, And lean not upon thine own understanding: In all thy ways acknowledge him, And he will direct thy paths.” It does not say that the path will be straight, or that its turnings will make sense at the time. It says that God will direct it. That is a hard kind of faith. It is easy to say afterwards that the false starts were part of the plan. It is much harder to go on trusting while the path is winding and the destination is unclear. Amy Carmichael was not always sure, in 1894 and 1895, that she was doing the right thing. She was criticised, and she sometimes doubted herself. But she kept acknowledging God in the decisions she made, and she kept moving when the next step became clear. In later years she would often counsel others not to try to see the whole road, but to take the next step in obedience. It is worth adding a word of caution. Not every winding path ends well, and not every sense of guidance is reliable. Amy’s decision to leave Japan without consulting those who had sent her was, in the view of some who loved her, not well handled, and the criticism she received was not all unfair. Faith in God’s guidance does not excuse us from the ordinary duties of consultation and accountability. Amy learned that too, in time, though she never found it easy to submit her own sense of God’s will to the judgement of others. What She Carried When Amy Carmichael landed at Madras in November 1895, she carried with her more than she knew. She carried the faith of her parents and the conversion of Harrogate, the lesson of the fountain and the assurance of Glasgow. She carried the experience of the Welcome Hall and the hard lesson of Manchester. She carried the interdenominational spirit of Keswick and the quiet faith of Robert Wilson. She carried the lessons of Japan about dress and identification, and the promise received in a cave that she would not be left desolate. And she carried her neuralgia, which went with her everywhere. She did not carry a plan. She did not know about the temple children, or Dohnavur, or the family she would gather. She knew only that she had been sent, and that she was going. The rest, as she would have said, was in other hands.

fields.title: Bangalore
fields.body_html:
“And be not fashioned according to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is the good and acceptable and perfect will of God.”

— Romans 12:2, ASV

The Garden City

Bangalore in 1895 was a pleasant place for a European to live. It stood on the Deccan plateau about three thousand feet above the sea, and its climate was mild compared with the burning plains around it. The British had built a large military cantonment there, with wide roads, gardens, churches, clubs and bungalows, and the town was popular with officers, officials and their families. It was also a centre of missionary work, with schools, churches and mission houses belonging to several societies.

It was to this place that Amy Carmichael came at the end of 1895, to learn Tamil and to see whether her health would bear life in India. She was soon ill. Within a short time of arriving she was struck down by fever, and for weeks she was too weak to study or work. It was not an encouraging start, and it confirmed the fears of those who had doubted whether she should have come at all.

A Disappointment

When she recovered, she found herself disturbed by something more troubling than illness. She had come to India expecting to find missionaries who were wholly given to their work, living simply among the people and burning with zeal for the gospel. What she found in Bangalore, as she saw it, was something else. Many of the missionaries lived much as other Europeans did. They had large houses and servants, they kept up English social customs, they spent time on tennis and calls and the round of station life, and they kept themselves socially apart from the Indian people among whom they worked. Some of them, she felt, had lost the fire that had brought them out.

She was young, and she was not always fair. It is easy for a newcomer to judge those who have spent years in a hard climate and have learned, sometimes through painful experience, what they need to survive. Rest and recreation were not luxuries for missionaries in India; many of them died young or broke down because they did not take enough. The social life of a station was also, for many, the only support they had. Amy would later learn to be more understanding of the weaknesses of fellow workers, though she never lost her dislike of what she saw as worldliness in missionary life.

But her unease was not simply youthful censoriousness. It grew from a real conviction, which she would hold all her life, that the gospel could not be credibly preached by people who lived as if the world were their home. She wrote later, in Things as They Are, about the gulf between the missionary and the people. “We are still up above to them; not on a level, not one of themselves,” she wrote. She admired those who had tried to close the gap, and she knew that it could never be closed completely. “No matter how far you may go,” she wrote, “there is always a distance you cannot cover—yards or inches it may be, but always that fatal hiatus.” The question of how near she could get would occupy her for years.

A Question About Converts

There was another thing that troubled her in Bangalore. She met Indian Christians, many of whom had been Christians for generations, and she found that their faith did not always look like the faith she had known in Belfast and at Keswick. Some seemed to her to be Christians in name only. The missionaries around her, she felt, too readily counted church members as converts, and too rarely asked whether lives had really been changed.

This too was a judgement she would later have to soften and refine. Indian Christianity, like Christianity everywhere, included the earnest and the nominal, and the missionary societies knew it as well as she did. Eugene Stock, the historian of the Church Missionary Society, said as much in the preface he wrote for her first book about India in 1903: “Hereditary Christianity in India is much like hereditary Christianity at home.” But Amy’s concern was not wrong. She wanted to see real conversion, and she distrusted anything that looked like religious statistics without spiritual reality. That concern would shape the way she worked in the villages, and later the way she received children and workers at Dohnavur.

Tamil

Meanwhile she was learning Tamil. It is one of the great classical languages of the world, with a literature that goes back two thousand years, and it is notoriously difficult for English speakers. It has sounds that do not exist in English, a grammar built on very different principles, and a written form with its own script. It also has a gulf between the literary language and the spoken language of ordinary people, so that a learner must master two registers at once.

Amy found it hard. She was not a natural linguist, and her illnesses interrupted her studies. But she was determined, and she had a great motive: she wanted to speak to people directly, without the interpreter she had depended on in Japan. Over the following years she became fluent, and she came to love the language. She wrote Tamil hymns and poems, gave Tamil names to the children of Dohnavur, and in her English books she often translated Tamil words and proverbs for her readers. One of them stands at the end of the note she wrote for a later edition of Things as They Are: “to the Mighty One,” as the Tamil proverb says, “even the blade of grass is a weapon.”

With the language came names. In the villages she would be called the Missie Ammal, a mixture of English and Tamil meaning something like “the missionary lady,” and the glossary she later printed for English readers explained that Amma, “Mother,” was used by all women speaking to one another and by girls speaking to women. It was an ordinary word of courtesy. Within a few years it would become, for hundreds of children, the only name they had for her.

Thomas Walker

The person who did most to help her, and who changed the direction of her life, was Thomas Walker. He was a missionary of the Church Missionary Society who had been working in the Tinnevelly district, in the far south of India, since the 1880s. He was a fine Tamil scholar, a teacher of Indian clergy and evangelists, and a much-loved speaker at conventions for the deepening of spiritual life. By the usual account Amy met him and his wife while they were away in the hills, and Walker agreed to help her with her Tamil.

It was the beginning of a partnership that would last sixteen years, until Walker’s death in 1912. Amy admired him enormously. He was a disciplined, scholarly and humble man, and he combined a deep personal devotion with a hard-headed realism about the work. He had little patience with sentimental reports or inflated numbers. He was also, by temperament, a man who was not easily impressed, and the young Irishwoman with her intensity and her poor health was not an obvious recruit. But he saw in her a real gift and a real call, and he took her seriously.

In 1896 Amy left Bangalore and went to the Tinnevelly district to live and work with the Walkers. It was an unusual arrangement. She remained a missionary of the Zenana Society, but she was to work under the direction of a missionary of another society, in a place her own society had not chosen. It was the kind of arrangement that only made sense because of the people involved, and it would last, in one form or another, for the rest of Walker’s life. When Amy wrote his biography in 1916, she called it simply Walker of Tinnevelly.

Not Fashioned According to This World

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s appeal to the Christians at Rome: “be not fashioned according to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.” The word Paul uses for being fashioned suggests being pressed into a mould. He is warning against letting the surrounding culture shape the Christian life, and calling instead for a transformation that comes from within.

Amy Carmichael’s months in Bangalore were in a sense a confrontation with that verse. She saw, or thought she saw, a missionary community that had been pressed into the mould of British colonial life, and she was determined not to be pressed into it herself. In the years that followed she would reject much of that life: the European dress, the social round, the separation from Indian people. She would wear a sari, eat Indian food, live in Indian houses, and adopt many Indian customs.

But there is a subtler point in Paul’s words, and Amy would come to feel it in time. It is possible to resist one mould and be pressed into another. A missionary who rejects the colonial club can still carry colonial attitudes in her heart; a reformer who rejects worldliness can still be shaped by pride. The transformation Paul speaks of is not achieved by changing one’s clothes, important as that may be. It is the work of God renewing the mind. Amy Carmichael’s life would show both sides of this: a remarkable freedom from many of the habits of her time, and a sharing in some of its assumptions that she never fully saw. She left Bangalore having learned what she did not want to become. She was about to learn, in the villages of Tinnevelly, what she was meant to be.

fields.title: The Starry Cluster
fields.body_html:
“And they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.”

— Daniel 12:3, ASV

The Far South

The Tinnevelly district, now Tirunelveli, lies at the southern tip of the Indian peninsula, where the land narrows towards Cape Comorin. To the west rise the Western Ghats, a wall of mountains that catches the monsoon rains and sends them down in rivers across the plain. To the east the land falls away in a great red plain dotted with palmyra palms, rice fields watered by tanks, small towns and hundreds of villages, to the sea. It is hot for most of the year, and dry for much of it. In Amy Carmichael’s day most people lived by farming, by climbing the palmyra palms for their sap, or by trades handed down through their castes.

It was also one of the few places in India where Christianity had taken deep root. Protestant missionaries had worked there since the eighteenth century, and in the early nineteenth century the German missionary Charles Rhenius, working for the Church Missionary Society, had seen large numbers of people, especially among the palmyra-climbing Shanar community, now known as Nadars, become Christians. Whole villages had come over together, and Christian villages with their own churches and schools had grown up across the district. By the 1890s the Christian community in Tinnevelly numbered tens of thousands, served by Anglican missions of two societies, by Indian pastors, and by catechists and schoolmasters in many villages.

But it was still a small minority. Eugene Stock, introducing Amy’s first book about the district, reckoned that there were about twenty Hindus to every Christian. Most of the Christians came from a handful of communities, and the caste Hindus of the district, especially the higher castes, had remained largely untouched. The Christian presence was strong enough to be familiar, and familiar enough to be resented. To a high-caste Hindu family, conversion to Christianity meant joining the people of lower castes who had already done so, and losing caste, family and inheritance in the process.

With the Walkers

Amy came to Tinnevelly in 1896 and lived at first with the Walkers at Palamcottah, the chief mission centre of the district. Later they moved to Pannaivilai, a village in the east of the district, where Walker had charge of a wide area of country and of the training of Indian Christian workers. Amy studied Tamil under Walker’s guidance, and as her Tamil improved she began to go out into the villages.

Walker was a demanding teacher. He expected her to learn the language properly, not just enough to get by, and he insisted on accuracy. He was also a model of the kind of missionary she wanted to be: someone who lived for the work, who knew the people and their language deeply, who prayed, and who did not exaggerate. Mrs. Walker, whom Amy’s books call simply “the Ammal,” became a close friend and, in many ways, a second mother.

The Band

The work Amy took up was itinerant evangelism among women. With a small group of Indian Christian women she travelled from village to village, staying for days or weeks in one area and then moving on, visiting homes, talking with women, singing, and telling the story of Jesus. In her books she called them the Band, and its members the Band Sisters. They became known in Tamil by a name that has been translated as “the Starry Cluster,” and the image stuck.

The women of the band were the heart of the work. They knew the language and the customs, they could go into homes where a foreigner would not be welcome, and they could speak of their own experience of Christ in a way that a foreigner could not. Amy described in Things as They Are how much depended on this. “To hear one of their own people saying, with evident sincerity, ‘One thing I know, that whereas I was blind now I see,’” she wrote, “makes them look at each other and nod their heads sympathetically.” She called it the “simple witness,” and she believed that nothing told more.

The leading member of the band was Ponnammal, a young widow from a Christian family. In Tamil society a widow was expected to live a hidden and restricted life, and even in Christian families some of those expectations lingered. Ponnammal broke with them to join the band, and she became one of its most effective workers and Amy’s closest Indian friend. Amy would later write her life, and she would mourn her deeply when she died. Other women joined over the years, some of them, like Ponnammal, widows; others young converts who had come out of Hindu families at great cost. Amy lived with them, travelled with them, ate with them and prayed with them, and the band became a kind of family, the first of several she would build.

On the Road

Things as They Are is full of the texture of these journeys. The band travelled by bandy, a springless bullock cart with a mat roof, over roads that were often nothing but ruts. “Crash and tumble went the bandy,” Amy wrote, describing an afternoon when the floods were out and the cart rolled into a pool, so that “the water swished in at the lower end and floated our books out quietly.” They fished the books out and went on, “somewhat damp, but happy.”

In the villages they were a sensation. Amy wore Indian dress, but she could not do without a sun hat, which marked her out at once. On one occasion a little girl caught sight of the hat through the end of the cart and ran to tell the village: “A great white man is here! Oh what an appalling spectacle!” Amy enjoyed the story, and enjoyed even more the contrast with a magazine article at home which claimed that Indian women thought the lady missionary fairer and more divine than anything they had ever imagined. “Was it not an appalling spectacle?” the villagers said instead. In another chapter she mentioned the hat again, calling it “the only foreign thing about me which was visible—oh that I could dispense with it!”

The women they met asked endless questions. Was she married or a widow? Why did she wear no jewels? Where were her relations? Why had she left them? What did the government pay her? Why did she not oil her hair? Amy recorded these questions with humour and patience, and she knew that they had to be answered before anything else could be said. “If we ignore their desires,” she wrote of the women’s natural curiosity, “we defeat our own.”

Humdrum

But the heart of Things as They Are is not the comedy of the road. It is the hardness of the work. Day after day the band visited homes, told the story of Jesus, and saw nothing happen. People listened politely, or stared, or laughed, or wandered away. A girl at a potter’s wheel asked whether, if she joined the Christian way, she would get a new sari and good curry every day. An old woman, on the point of interest, drew back when she understood that following Christ would mean the end of her place in her family. The men of one village forbade their children to learn to read lest they be drawn to the missionaries.

Amy called one chapter “Humdrum,” and she meant it. “There have been times of late,” she wrote, “when I have had to hold on to one text with all my might: ‘It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful.’ Praise God, it does not say ‘successful.’” She refused to dress up the work for readers at home. “Most days in real life,” she wrote, “end exactly as they began, so far as visible results are concerned.”

That honesty was costly. Supporters at home wanted encouraging news, and missionary magazines were full of it. To write that most days ended as they began was to risk discouraging the people whose prayers and gifts sustained the work. But Amy believed that the truth would produce better prayer than a pleasant fiction. She also believed, and this is easy to miss, that faithfulness without visible success was itself a kind of joy. “There is joy in the doing of it,” she wrote of the humdrum work, “there is joy in just obeying.”

Caste

The great obstacle, as Amy came to see it, was caste. The Hindu social order divided people into thousands of hereditary communities, each with its own occupation, customs and rules about food, marriage and contact with others. To belong to a caste was to belong to a people: to have a place, a trade, a family, and a network of obligations and protections. To break caste, by eating with people of other castes or by joining a religion that ignored caste, was to lose all of that.

Amy did not think that every Hindu who heard the gospel was indifferent to it. She met people who seemed to be moved, and who asked questions that showed real interest. But again and again she saw that interest die when the cost became clear. “However tenderly you tell it,” she wrote, “the keen Hindu mind soon perceives the drift of it all—Redemption must mean loss of Caste.” A potter told her that he could not imagine a potter changing his caste; his caste was his trade, his life, and everything he knew. “Caste and religion!” she wrote. “They are so mixed up that we do not know how to unmix them.”

Modern readers will want to be careful here. Amy wrote about caste as a missionary, convinced that it was a barrier to the gospel and a source of cruelty. She was not wrong that it caused great suffering, especially to those at the bottom of the hierarchy, and many Indian reformers of her day, Hindu as well as Christian, said the same. But she also tended, like most missionaries of her time, to see caste only from the outside, as a system of bondage, and to miss the sense of identity, belonging and mutual care that it also gave. The Indian Christian churches, moreover, were not free of caste themselves; in Tinnevelly, as elsewhere, caste divisions persisted among Christians, a fact that Amy acknowledged and grieved over. She would later insist that at Dohnavur there should be no caste distinctions at all, and she held to that with great firmness.

Stars

To the west rise the Western Ghats, a wall of mountains that catches the monsoon rains and sends them down in rivers across the plain. To the east the land falls away in a great red plain dotted with palmyra palms, rice fields watered by tanks, small towns and hundreds of villages, to the sea. It is hot for most of the year, and dry for much of it. In Amy Carmichael’s day most people lived by farming, by climbing the palmyra palms for their sap, or by trades handed down through their castes. It was also one of the few places in India where Christianity had taken deep root. Protestant missionaries had worked there since the eighteenth century, and in the early nineteenth century the German missionary Charles Rhenius, working for the Church Missionary Society, had seen large numbers of people, especially among the palmyra-climbing Shanar community, now known as Nadars, become Christians. Whole villages had come over together, and Christian villages with their own churches and schools had grown up across the district. By the 1890s the Christian community in Tinnevelly numbered tens of thousands, served by Anglican missions of two societies, by Indian pastors, and by catechists and schoolmasters in many villages. But it was still a small minority. Eugene Stock, introducing Amy’s first book about the district, reckoned that there were about twenty Hindus to every Christian. Most of the Christians came from a handful of communities, and the caste Hindus of the district, especially the higher castes, had remained largely untouched. The Christian presence was strong enough to be familiar, and familiar enough to be resented. To a high-caste Hindu family, conversion to Christianity meant joining the people of lower castes who had already done so, and losing caste, family and inheritance in the process. With the Walkers Amy came to Tinnevelly in 1896 and lived at first with the Walkers at Palamcottah, the chief mission centre of the district. Later they moved to Pannaivilai, a village in the east of the district, where Walker had charge of a wide area of country and of the training of Indian Christian workers. Amy studied Tamil under Walker’s guidance, and as her Tamil improved she began to go out into the villages. Walker was a demanding teacher. He expected her to learn the language properly, not just enough to get by, and he insisted on accuracy. He was also a model of the kind of missionary she wanted to be: someone who lived for the work, who knew the people and their language deeply, who prayed, and who did not exaggerate. Mrs. Walker, whom Amy’s books call simply “the Ammal,” became a close friend and, in many ways, a second mother. The Band The work Amy took up was itinerant evangelism among women. With a small group of Indian Christian women she travelled from village to village, staying for days or weeks in one area and then moving on, visiting homes, talking with women, singing, and telling the story of Jesus. In her books she called them the Band, and its members the Band Sisters. They became known in Tamil by a name that has been translated as “the Starry Cluster,” and the image stuck. The women of the band were the heart of the work. They knew the language and the customs, they could go into homes where a foreigner would not be welcome, and they could speak of their own experience of Christ in a way that a foreigner could not. Amy described in Things as They Are how much depended on this. “To hear one of their own people saying, with evident sincerity, ‘One thing I know, that whereas I was blind now I see,’” she wrote, “makes them look at each other and nod their heads sympathetically.” She called it the “simple witness,” and she believed that nothing told more. The leading member of the band was Ponnammal, a young widow from a Christian family. In Tamil society a widow was expected to live a hidden and restricted life, and even in Christian families some of those expectations lingered. Ponnammal broke with them to join the band, and she became one of its most effective workers and Amy’s closest Indian friend. Amy would later write her life, and she would mourn her deeply when she died. Other women joined over the years, some of them, like Ponnammal, widows; others young converts who had come out of Hindu families at great cost. Amy lived with them, travelled with them, ate with them and prayed with them, and the band became a kind of family, the first of several she would build. On the Road Things as They Are is full of the texture of these journeys. The band travelled by bandy, a springless bullock cart with a mat roof, over roads that were often nothing but ruts. “Crash and tumble went the bandy,” Amy wrote, describing an afternoon when the floods were out and the cart rolled into a pool, so that “the water swished in at the lower end and floated our books out quietly.” They fished the books out and went on, “somewhat damp, but happy.” In the villages they were a sensation. Amy wore Indian dress, but she could not do without a sun hat, which marked her out at once. On one occasion a little girl caught sight of the hat through the end of the cart and ran to tell the village: “A great white man is here! Oh what an appalling spectacle!” Amy enjoyed the story, and enjoyed even more the contrast with a magazine article at home which claimed that Indian women thought the lady missionary fairer and more divine than anything they had ever imagined. “Was it not an appalling spectacle?” the villagers said instead. In another chapter she mentioned the hat again, calling it “the only foreign thing about me which was visible—oh that I could dispense with it!” The women they met asked endless questions. Was she married or a widow? Why did she wear no jewels? Where were her relations? Why had she left them? What did the government pay her? Why did she not oil her hair? Amy recorded these questions with humour and patience, and she knew that they had to be answered before anything else could be said. “If we ignore their desires,” she wrote of the women’s natural curiosity, “we defeat our own.” Humdrum But the heart of Things as They Are is not the comedy of the road. It is the hardness of the work. Day after day the band visited homes, told the story of Jesus, and saw nothing happen. People listened politely, or stared, or laughed, or wandered away. A girl at a potter’s wheel asked whether, if she joined the Christian way, she would get a new sari and good curry every day. An old woman, on the point of interest, drew back when she understood that following Christ would mean the end of her place in her family. The men of one village forbade their children to learn to read lest they be drawn to the missionaries. Amy called one chapter “Humdrum,” and she meant it. “There have been times of late,” she wrote, “when I have had to hold on to one text with all my might: ‘It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful.’ Praise God, it does not say ‘successful.’” She refused to dress up the work for readers at home. “Most days in real life,” she wrote, “end exactly as they began, so far as visible results are concerned.” That honesty was costly. Supporters at home wanted encouraging news, and missionary magazines were full of it. To write that most days ended as they began was to risk discouraging the people whose prayers and gifts sustained the work. But Amy believed that the truth would produce better prayer than a pleasant fiction. She also believed, and this is easy to miss, that faithfulness without visible success was itself a kind of joy. “There is joy in the doing of it,” she wrote of the humdrum work, “there is joy in just obeying.” Caste The great obstacle, as Amy came to see it, was caste. The Hindu social order divided people into thousands of hereditary communities, each with its own occupation, customs and rules about food, marriage and contact with others. To belong to a caste was to belong to a people: to have a place, a trade, a family, and a network of obligations and protections. To break caste, by eating with people of other castes or by joining a religion that ignored caste, was to lose all of that. Amy did not think that every Hindu who heard the gospel was indifferent to it. She met people who seemed to be moved, and who asked questions that showed real interest. She was not wrong that it caused great suffering, especially to those at the bottom of the hierarchy, and many Indian reformers of her day, Hindu as well as Christian, said the same. She would later insist that at Dohnavur there should be no caste distinctions at all, and she held to that with great firmness. fields.title: The Cost of One Soul
fields.body_html:
“Jesus said, Verily I say unto you, There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or mother, or father, or children, or lands, for my sake, and for the gospel’s sake, but he shall receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.”

— Mark 10:29-30, ASV

“With Persecutions”

The promise of Jesus at the head of this chapter is one of the most generous in the Gospels. Those who leave home and family for his sake will receive a hundredfold, in this life as well as the next: houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, lands. But tucked into the middle of the list are two words that are easy to read past: “with persecutions.” The hundredfold comes, but it comes with suffering attached.

In the villages of Tinnevelly at the end of the nineteenth century, those two words were not a footnote. For a Hindu of caste, especially a girl or a young woman, to become a Christian was to leave house and family in the most literal sense. It could also mean danger. Amy Carmichael spent the years from about 1897 to 1901 learning what that meant, not from books but from the people she came to love. Much of Things as They Are is about them.

Seeds and Opposition

By the late 1890s the work of the band was beginning to show some fruit. Here and there, in villages across the district, individuals were showing real interest in the gospel. They were few, and most of them were young: boys in their teens, girls even younger. They listened when the band came, asked questions, learned texts and hymns, and sometimes said openly that they believed.

The response of their families and communities was swift. Amy described it in a chapter she called “The Prey of the Terrible,” after a verse in Isaiah about captives being delivered from the mighty. A girl who listened in the shadow of a doorway was sent away to relatives and then, it was said, carried off over the mountains. A clever boy of seventeen who took the gospel’s part in an argument with village elders was suddenly married and sent away. Another girl, known to be an enquirer, was passed from village to village among her relatives until she was too frightened to show any interest at all. “It is often like that,” Amy wrote. “Just at the point where the soul-poise is so delicate that the lightest touch affects it, something, someone, pushes it roughly, and it trembles a moment, then falls—on the wrong side.”

It is important to read these stories fairly. The families who did these things were not monsters. From their point of view, a son or daughter who became a Christian was being lost to them, their caste and their gods, and was bringing disgrace on the whole family. To break caste was, in their eyes, one of the worst things a person could do, and the effects would fall not only on the convert but on brothers and sisters whose marriages might become impossible. Many of the families acted out of love and fear as much as out of hostility. Amy knew this. She wrote of a boy whose father, who “loved him dearly,” nerved himself to flog his son, and of a mother who sat with her hair undone and wailed the death-wail for a son who had gone to the Christians. She did not pretend that the cost fell only on the converts.

Children Who Could Not Be Kept

There was a further difficulty, and it was legal. Under the law of British India, a minor could not leave her parents or guardians to live with others, and a missionary who sheltered an under-age convert against her family’s wishes could be prosecuted. The law was there for good reason: it protected children from being taken from their families by anyone with a claim on them, and missionaries were not exempt. Amy accepted the principle. “It would never do,” she wrote, “if anyone could decoy away a mere child from her parents or natural guardians.”

But she found its working cruel. When a convert came, the police had to be told, and one of the first questions was age. If a girl could prove that she was over sixteen, and in some cases eighteen, she was free to choose. If she could not, she had to go back. In the villages there were often no birth registers, and the horoscope that recorded a child’s birth was kept by the family, who could refuse to produce it or produce a false one. “The whole burden of proof lies upon us,” Amy wrote, and she felt it as an injustice.

She told the story of one girl, whom she called Treasure, who was eager to be baptised and was ready to stand before a judge and say so. Amy had to tell her that unless her age could be proved, the missionaries had no power to protect her, and that it would be worse for her if she came and was then sent back. Amy remembered the tears in the girl’s eyes, and the question she asked: “Would God let them take me away? Would He not take care of me?” Treasure stayed at home, and suffered for her faith there. Amy did not soften the account of what she suffered, and she left the reader with the question.

The First to Come Out

Not all the stories ended in loss. In these years a small number of converts did come out of their homes and join the band, some of them girls who were old enough to choose, others who came with the consent, however reluctant, of their families. They became the core of Amy’s first household. In Things as They Are she gave them translated names: Victory, Jewel of Victory, Golden, Star, Pearl and others. They lived with her and the Walkers, learned, prayed, and went out with the band to tell others what had happened to them.

One of the most important of them was Arulai, a girl from a Hindu family who came to faith in these years and came to live with Amy. Arulai would grow into one of the most trusted leaders of the Dohnavur Fellowship, and Amy came to rely on her as on few others. Her story is a reminder that the work of these years was not only loss. Some of the seeds that seemed so fragile became trees.

The cost to the converts was nonetheless real. They had left their families, often without their blessing. They had lost their place in their communities. They lived as members of a small, embattled Christian household, dependent on the missionaries and on one another. Some of them had to endure years of hostility from their families, and some were never reconciled. In such circumstances it was not surprising that some fell away. Amy wrote that converts were “a responsible joy,” and she meant both words.

Two Boys

One story from these years shows both the joy and the cost more clearly than any other. Two boys from Hindu families had come to faith and joined the household. The younger was an only son, heir to considerable property. When he decided to follow Christ, his father flogged him twice, and when he finally left home his relatives came in a crowd to the bungalow and sat in a circle around him, pleading with him to return. They offered him a house, lands, his inheritance at once, and a bride with a rich dowry, and they promised him freedom to worship as he pleased if only he would come back and save his caste. “I will not go back,” he said.

A year or so later both boys were baptised together, with others, during a holiday by the sea. Amy called them Shining of Victory and Shining of Life. A few weeks later both died of cholera, one after the other, in the same order in which they had gone down into the water. The younger boy died in the presence of his parents and of Hindu neighbours who taunted him that this was his reward for breaking caste. Too weak to say much, he pointed upward and tried to sing a line from one of the band’s choruses. His mother wailed; his father stood silent, looking at his son.

Amy did not pretend to understand it. “Was it worth the pain it cost?” she asked. “Such a short time to witness, was it worth while?” Her answer was not an argument but a statement of faith. In their short time each boy had found one other boy, who might never have been found if the cost had been counted too great. And she believed that if the boys themselves could be asked, “they would tell you Jesus’ welcome made it far more than worth while.” It is the answer of the promise at the head of this chapter: a hundredfold, with persecutions, and in the world to come eternal life.

Publicity and Peril

One lesson of these years would shape the rest of Amy’s life as a writer and as the head of a mission. She learned that publicity could be dangerous. Supporters at home wanted stories of converts, with names and pictures, and missionary magazines printed them gladly. But in Tinnevelly, she found, a convert whose story was told could be traced, and a family that learned of a child’s interest in Christianity could act to stop it. “A certain connection has been observed between publicity and peril,” she wrote, and “we have learned by experience to fear any attempt to photograph spiritual fruit.”

That was why she changed names in her books, and why she sometimes left stories untold. It was also one of the roots of the reticence that would later mark Dohnavur, which made no appeals, published few details, and guarded its children from visitors and cameras. Critics sometimes saw that reticence as secrecy, or as a way of avoiding scrutiny. For Amy, it began as a way of protecting people whose lives might depend on it.

A Question for Readers

Modern readers may find these chapters of Things as They Are hard to read, and not only because of what they describe. Amy wrote as a partisan. She believed that Hinduism held its people in spiritual bondage, and she described Hindu families who opposed conversion as instruments of the devil. She did not often stop to ask how the same events looked from the other side, or to acknowledge that Christian families, too, have sometimes responded to a child’s change of faith with fury and cruelty. Some of the worst stories she reported came to her second-hand, and she could not verify them.

Yet she was not simply a polemicist. She recorded the courtesy, hospitality and intelligence of the Hindu people she met, and she often wrote of them with affection. She admitted the faults of Indian Christians and of missionaries. And she was right about something that is easy to forget in a more comfortable age: that for many people in many places, following Christ has meant losing everything else. Jesus did not hide that cost from his disciples. Amy Carmichael did not hide it from her readers. The next chapter tells how one small girl, who had nothing at all to lose, found her way to the Christian household at Pannaivilai, and changed the direction of Amy’s life.

fields.title: Pearl-Eyes
fields.body_html:
“Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: The helpless committeth himself unto thee; Thou hast been the helper of the fatherless.”

— Psalm 10:14, ASV

A Child at the Church Door

On an evening in early March 1901, a little girl was found alone outside the church at Pannaivilai. It was getting dark. She was about seven years old, with tumbled hair and frightened eyes, and she did not belong to the village. A Christian woman found her there and, rather than send her home in the dark, took her into her own house for the night. In the morning the child insisted that she wanted to see a particular foreign lady, and the woman, guessing who she meant, brought her to the mission bungalow.

The date usually given for her arrival at the bungalow is 7 March 1901. Amy Carmichael was sitting reading on the verandah when they came. The child ran straight to her, climbed onto her knee without the least fear, and began to tell her story. Her name, Amy wrote in her first account of it, was Pearl-eyes, and she wanted to stay there always. “I have come to stay,” she said.

In Amy’s later books and in all the biographies the child is called by her Tamil name, Preena. Her account in that book is the earliest we have, and the closest to the events, and this chapter follows it.

Her Story

The story the child told, as Amy recorded it, was this. Her mother had given her, as a baby, to women attached to a temple in a nearby town, whom Amy calls the Servants of the gods. She had grown up in their house. She was not happy there; nobody loved her. Some months before, the woman who kept her had burned her little fingers as a punishment for some childish fault, and she had run away. She knew that her mother lived in a town about twenty miles to the east, and she set out to walk there. Some kind people on the road let her travel with them, and after three days she reached the town, where she searched the streets, describing her mother to strangers, until she found her. “My mother cried,” she told Amy. But the temple woman had followed her, and her mother gave her up again.

Back in the temple house, the child overheard the women talking about her. She was soon to be “married to the god,” the phrase used for the ceremony by which a girl was formally dedicated to a temple, or, as they put it, “tied to a stone.” She did not understand all that it meant, but she understood enough to be terrified. Amy recorded what she did next. She ran into the temple, slipped past the priests, stood before the image of the god in the dim shrine, clasped her hands and prayed to it, “Let me die! A child of six or seven had been burned by the woman who was supposed to care for her, and had run twenty miles to find a mother who sent her back.

Within hours the women from the temple house arrived. Walker, whom Amy calls the Iyer, asked who they were. Out of sight of the woman, the child sobbed that if she refused they would catch her and punish her dreadfully, and she showed the cuts on her skin where she had been punished before. Then she came back, stood before them all, and cried, “I won’t! I won’t!” The crowd went away.

The danger was not over. The temple women said they would write to the child’s mother, who had legal authority over her. One of them accused the child of being a thief, a common charge in such disputes, which could be used to bring the police; the sum in question turned out to be fourpence halfpenny, which the missionaries paid. There was talk of a plot to snatch her back. For weeks the household never let her out of sight.

It is important to understand what Amy and the Walkers were risking. Under the law, the child belonged to her mother, and through her mother to the women to whom she had been given. To keep her against their will was, on the face of it, to take a minor from her lawful guardians, which was a criminal offence. Amy noted in her account that if the facts could be proved, “the Government would be on our side in such a matter,” because the dedication of minors to temples for an immoral life was already, in principle, against the law. “Only the great difficulty might be to prove it.”

That would be the pattern of the next half-century. The law of British India did forbid the sale or disposal of minors for prostitution, and courts had sometimes held that dedicating a girl to a temple for such a life fell under that law. But proof was almost impossible to obtain. The ceremonies were religious; the arrangements were made within families; the girls were usually too young to testify; and the communities concerned closed ranks against outsiders. Missionaries who took in such children could find themselves accused of kidnapping, and some were. Amy and the Walkers decided to keep Pearl-eyes and take the consequences. The early sources do not say whether the temple women ever went to law over her, but she was not taken back.

Fourpence Halfpenny

The child stayed, and she quickly became part of the household. Amy described her playing with dolls, setting out leaves and flowers in rows, cooking imaginary meals of sand with three pebbles for a hearth and a shell for a pot, and inviting the missionaries and her doll to dine. When she first arrived at the Christian woman’s house she had refused the curry and rice she was offered, drawing herself up and asking whether she, a child of good caste, could be asked to break her caste. A few weeks later she was playing at church with her doll and insisting that it should have its collection too.

Amy recorded one exchange that she treasured. Some weeks after the excitement of the first day, she was teaching the child the text about being redeemed “not with corruptible things, as silver and gold,” and explaining how much Jesus had paid for us. The child interrupted. “Oh yes, I understand!” she said. “I know how much you paid for me—fourpence halfpenny!”

Attracted by the Influence

Amy called the chapter in which she told this story “Attracted by the Influence.” The phrase came from a letter by Thomas Ragland, a Cambridge scholar who had worked as a missionary in Tinnevelly half a century earlier, and whose life Amy would later write. Ragland had tried to express the worth of a single soul in the language of astronomy, and had written of the soul of the poorest outcast as a body with mass and weight enough to draw down the Creator of the heavens to save it. Amy took up the image. Nowhere, she wrote, did she see the glory of God more than in “chapters of life which show Him bending down from the circle of the earth, yea rather, coming down all the way to help it, ‘attracted by the influence’ of the need of a little child.”

She also saw the hand of God in the timing. If the child had come to Pannaivilai a few weeks earlier, when the missionaries were away, there would have been nobody to protect her. If the Christian woman had taken her home that first night, she would have been lost. Amy listed these “touches that tell how God cares,” and they are the heart of her account. The psalm at the head of this chapter says that God sees mischief and spite, that the helpless commit themselves to him, and that he has been “the helper of the fatherless.” Amy believed she had seen that verse acted out on her verandah.

The Beginning

Amy Carmichael always regarded the coming of Preena as the beginning of the work for which she is remembered. Until then her attention had been on the women of the villages and the converts of the band. She had heard of the temple children, and had seen them playing in courtyards near the temples, “gracious little maidens,” she wrote, “winsome in their ways.” But she had felt powerless. “One longs to help the little things,” she wrote, “but no hand of ours can stretch over the wall and lift even one child out.”

Now a child had climbed over the wall by herself. Amy began to ask questions: how many such children there were, how they came to the temples, what happened to them, and whether anything could be done. The answers would occupy her for the rest of her life. Preena herself grew up in Amy’s household and stayed with the family that grew around her. She had come, as she said, to stay.
