fields.title: Dohnavur
fields.body_html:
“The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; Yea, I have a goodly heritage.”

— Psalm 16:6, ASV

Under the Mountains

Dohnavur lies on the plain at the foot of the Western Ghats, in the far south-west of the old Tinnevelly district, a few miles from the boundary of what was then the princely state of Travancore. Amy Carmichael described its setting in the first pages of Things as They Are: “The Western Ghauts sweep down to the sea in curves. Dohnavur is in one of the last of these curves. There are no proper roads running under the mountains, only rough country ruts crossing the plain.” The mountains rise steeply behind the village, blue in the morning and purple at dusk, and in the monsoon their streams come down in white threads. On the plain below are rice fields, palmyra palms and the great irrigation tanks that the people call lakes.

Amy loved the place from the first. She found in it something of the hills and waters of the English Lake District, where she had lived with Robert Wilson. Near one village, she wrote, “the Red Lake lies at the mountain foot; we call it Derwentwater, but there are palms and bamboos, and there is no Friar’s Crag.” It was a homesick joke, and a tender one. She would live within sight of those mountains for fifty years.

A Village with a History

Dohnavur was not an ordinary Tamil village. It had been founded in the 1820s as a Christian settlement by Charles Rhenius, the German missionary whose work had done so much to plant the church in Tinnevelly. Converts who had been driven out of their own villages by persecution were given land and a place to live where they could practise their faith in safety. The money for the land came, according to the village’s own tradition, from a Prussian nobleman, Count Dohna, and the village was named after him. It had a church, a school and a Christian community that by Amy’s day had been there for three generations.

It was, in other words, a place of refuge from the start. Amy and the Walkers did not create its character; they inherited it. When the household that grew up around Amy began to shelter children who had nowhere else to go, it was continuing, in a new form, the purpose for which the village had been founded.

The Old Testament law appointed cities of refuge, scattered through the land of Israel, to which a person in danger of vengeance could flee and be safe until justice was done. They were not prisons, and they were not fortresses; they were places where the vulnerable could live under protection. The image was a familiar one in Amy Carmichael’s tradition, and it fits Dohnavur well. In its earliest days it had sheltered converts whose own villages would not let them live. In her day it would shelter children whom the custom of their communities had marked out for a life they had not chosen. A refuge is only as good as its gate, and Amy would guard the gate of Dohnavur, for better and sometimes for worse, with all her strength.

The Move

The Walkers and Amy had spent time at Dohnavur in 1900, and it is that period of work in “the south of the South” that much of Things as They Are describes. After Preena’s coming in March 1901 at Pannaivilai, they made a more permanent move. Thomas Walker took on responsibilities there, including, by the usual account, the training of young Indian men for Christian service, and in 1901 the whole household moved there: the Walkers, Amy, the women of the band, the converts, and now Preena.

Nobody intended at the time that Dohnavur would become the centre of a large work. Walker had come to teach, and Amy and the band expected to go on with their village evangelism, using Dohnavur as a base. But the household was changing. Within a short time after Preena came, other children began to arrive: girls who had been in danger of temple dedication, girls whose families could not or would not keep them, and in time babies. Amy found that she could not travel with the band and care for small children at the same time. The children needed a home, and the home needed a mother.

A Nursemaid?

The shift was not universally welcomed. Amy had come to India as an evangelist, and some of her fellow missionaries thought she was wasting her gifts. Caring for small children was work that Indian women could do, they felt, and a missionary who could speak Tamil and preach the gospel ought to be out in the villages. Her biographers record that some people said, in effect, that she had given up the work of a missionary to become a nursemaid.

Amy felt the force of the criticism, and she felt the loss of the itinerant work, which she loved. But she came to believe that God had given her a new task. The children who came to her had been rescued from a system that, as she saw it, destroyed both body and soul. They needed not only shelter but a Christian upbringing, and that could not be done by visiting. It needed a home, day after day and year after year. She came to believe that caring for children for Christ’s sake was as spiritual a work as preaching, and that the washing of a baby could be an act of worship. That conviction runs through all her later writing about Dohnavur, and she lived by it from 1901 onward.

It is worth pausing on that change, because it says something about her. She was a woman of strong will and clear plans, and the plan had been village evangelism. When the children came, she let the plan go. She did not abandon evangelism; the children were taught the gospel, and many of them would become Christian workers themselves. But she accepted that God’s purposes for her were not the ones she had chosen. It is one thing to say “not my will but thine”; it is another to give up the work one loves for a work one never asked for. Amy did it, and she never looked back.

The Shape of a Household

In these early years the household at Dohnavur was small. There were the Walkers and Amy; the women of the band, including Ponnammal; the girl converts, including Arulai; and a growing number of small children. They lived in simple buildings near the church, adapted for the purpose and gradually added to. Life followed a pattern of work, prayer, teaching and play. The women of the band still went out to the villages when they could, but more and more of their time was taken up with the children.

From the beginning Amy was determined that the household should be a family and not an institution. She was suspicious of the orphanages and boarding schools that many missions ran, with their rows of beds and uniforms and regimented routines. She wanted the children to grow up as Indian children in an Indian home, with Indian food, Indian dress and Tamil as their language. She wanted them to be loved individually, and she wanted them to love one another. Above all she wanted them to know Christ, not as a subject taught in school, but as a person known in daily life.

She also wanted to keep them safe. The children who came to Dohnavur had been taken, in many cases, out of the reach of people who regarded them as their property, and who might try to recover them by force, by stealth or by law. That meant watchfulness. It meant that the household could not be entirely open to visitors, and that the children were not free to wander. In these early years the watchfulness was necessary and obvious. In later years, as the work grew and the dangers changed, some observers would question whether the walls of Dohnavur, both literal and figurative, had grown higher than they needed to be. That question will return later in this book.

Visitors and a Book

In 1901 and 1902 the household had visitors from home, two women friends who came to India for some months to see the work for themselves. They travelled with the band, shared in the life of the household, and saw, as Amy put it, “the fight as it is.” One of them was a keen photographer, whom the Tamils called the Picture-catching Missie Ammal, and whose pictures would illustrate the book that came out of their visit. Sitting on the floor of the verandah, Indian fashion, the two visitors urged Amy to gather the letters she had written home and make them into a book, so that others could see what they had seen. Amy was reluctant. She had little time, she said, and the world had many books. But they offered to do the hard work of editing, and she agreed. The book they made was Things as They Are. Its story is the subject of the next chapter.

A Goodly Heritage

The psalm at the head of this chapter is a psalm of contentment. “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; Yea, I have a goodly heritage.” The lines are the measuring lines used to divide land, and the psalmist is saying that the portion God has given him is a good one. But the psalm also makes clear that the real heritage is God himself: “Jehovah is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup” (Psalm 16:5, ASV).

Amy Carmichael’s portion, from 1901, was a village on a hot plain at the foot of the mountains, a household of converts and children, and a work she had not chosen. She would spend the rest of her life there. She came to love it as her home, and she found in it, as she would have said, a goodly heritage. But she would also have said that the heritage was not Dohnavur. It was the Lord who had led her there.

She did not abandon evangelism; the children were taught the gospel, and many of them would become Christian workers themselves. But she accepted that God’s purposes for her were not the ones she had chosen. It is one thing to say “not my will but thine”; it is another to give up the work one loves for a work one never asked for. Amy did it, and she never looked back. The Shape of a Household In these early years the household at Dohnavur was small. There were the Walkers and Amy; the women of the band, including Ponnammal; the girl converts, including Arulai; and a growing number of small children. They lived in simple buildings near the church, adapted for the purpose and gradually added to. Life followed a pattern of work, prayer, teaching and play. The women of the band still went out to the villages when they could, but more and more of their time was taken up with the children. From the beginning Amy was determined that the household should be a family and not an institution. She was suspicious of the orphanages and boarding schools that many missions ran, with their rows of beds and uniforms and regimented routines. She wanted the children to grow up as Indian children in an Indian home, with Indian food, Indian dress and Tamil as their language. She wanted them to be loved individually, and she wanted them to love one another. Above all she wanted them to know Christ, not as a subject taught in school, but as a person known in daily life. She also wanted to keep them safe. The children who came to Dohnavur had been taken, in many cases, out of the reach of people who regarded them as their property, and who might try to recover them by force, by stealth or by law. That meant watchfulness. It meant that the household could not be entirely open to visitors, and that the children were not free to wander. In these early years the watchfulness was necessary and obvious. In later years, as the work grew and the dangers changed, some observers would question whether the walls of Dohnavur, both literal and figurative, had grown higher than they needed to be. That question will return later in this book. Visitors and a Book In 1901 and 1902 the household had visitors from home, two women friends who came to India for some months to see the work for themselves. They travelled with the band, shared in the life of the household, and saw, as Amy put it, “the fight as it is.” One of them was a keen photographer, whom the Tamils called the Picture-catching Missie Ammal, and whose pictures would illustrate the book that came out of their visit. Sitting on the floor of the verandah, Indian fashion, the two visitors urged Amy to gather the letters she had written home and make them into a book, so that others could see what they had seen. Amy was reluctant. She had little time, she said, and the world had many books. But they offered to do the hard work of editing, and she agreed. The book they made was Things as They Are. Its story is the subject of the next chapter. A Goodly Heritage The psalm at the head of this chapter is a psalm of contentment. “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; Yea, I have a goodly heritage.” The lines are the measuring lines used to divide land, and the psalmist is saying that the portion God has given him is a good one. But the psalm also makes clear that the real heritage is God himself: “Jehovah is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup” (Psalm 16:5, ASV). Amy Carmichael’s portion, from 1901, was a village on a hot plain at the foot of the mountains, a household of converts and children, and a work she had not chosen. She would spend the rest of her life there. She came to love it as her home, and she found in it, as she would have said, a goodly heritage. But she would also have said that the heritage was not Dohnavur. It was the Lord who had led her there.

fields.title: Things as They Are
fields.body_html:
“but we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.”

— 2 Corinthians 4:2, ASV

A Battle-Book

Things as They Are: Mission Work in Southern India was published in London by Morgan and Scott in April 1903. It was not a long book by the standards of the day, but it was an unusual one. It was made up of letters and sketches that Amy Carmichael had written home over about two years, gathered and arranged by the two friends who had visited her, and illustrated with their photographs. Each chapter was headed by quotations from missionaries of earlier generations, which Amy said were “meant to be read, not skipped,” and were “more worthful than anything else in it.”

She was clear about what kind of book it was. “The book is a battle-book,” she wrote in her introduction, “written from a battle-field where the fighting is not pretty play but stern reality.” She advised readers to take its harder chapters “alone in some quiet place with God.” And she explained its title. Her friends had urged her to “tell about things as they actually are,” and she had tried. But she felt that she had failed, because the reality she wanted to show was spiritual and invisible, and what she could describe was only its outward effects. She called those effects, borrowing a poet’s phrase, “the Dust of the Actual.” The book, she said, “only touches the Dust.”

What the Book Said

Most of Things as They Are is about the ordinary work of the band: the journeys by bullock cart, the visits to homes, the questions of the village women, the long afternoons in which nothing happened. It is often funny and always vivid. But underneath the anecdotes it makes an argument that was unwelcome to many readers at home. The argument was that the evangelisation of caste Hindus in South India was very hard and very slow; that most people who heard the gospel did not want it; that those who did often paid for it with the loss of everything; and that missionary reports which suggested otherwise were misleading.

She said this directly. “Do not, we entreat you, expect to hear of us doing great things, as an everyday matter of course,” she wrote. “Do not expect every true story to dovetail into some other true story and end with some marvellous coincidence or miraculous conversion.” She mocked, gently, the article which claimed that Indian women thought the lady missionary more divine than anything they had imagined, and another which said that Indian women never smiled. “We were surprised to hear it,” she wrote. “We had not noticed it.” She was as impatient with the sentimental picture of the longing heathen as with the triumphalist picture of the converted nation.

And in the later chapters she wrote about things that most missionary books left out: the persecution of converts, the deaths of some of them, and the dedication of girls to temples. She wrote about these things carefully, without lurid detail, and she said repeatedly that she was leaving most of it out. But she did not leave out the fact of them.

Too Dark?

A story is often told that the manuscript was first sent to a missionary society or a publisher, who returned it with the advice that it was too dark and should be toned down, and that Amy refused to change anything but the title. The story is widely repeated, and it fits the book’s own account of itself, but its details are hard to verify. What is certain is that Amy knew the book would be thought too harrowing, because she said so in the book. In the chapter called “Married to the God,” about a little girl taken to a temple, she wrote:

“We are told to modify things, not to write too vividly, never to harrow sensitive hearts. Friends, we cannot modify truth, we cannot write half vividly enough; and as for harrowing hearts, oh that we could do it!”

That passage is the heart of the book. She was not writing to shock for its own sake. She was writing because she believed that Christians at home would not pray as they ought unless they knew what they were praying about. “Oh, to care,” she wrote, “and oh for power to make others care, not less but far, far more!”

Eugene Stock’s Preface

The book carried a preface by Eugene Stock, the editorial secretary of the Church Missionary Society and its historian, one of the most respected figures in the missionary world. His endorsement mattered, and he gave it without reserve. “I do not think the realities of Hindu life have ever been portrayed with greater vividness than in this book,” he wrote, “and I know that the authoress’s accuracy can be fully relied upon.” He added a sentence that has often been quoted since: “What she says is the truth, and nothing but the truth; but it is not the whole truth—that she could not tell. If she wrote it, it could not be printed. If it were printed, it could not be read.”

Stock also made a point that is easily forgotten. He said that the picture was drawn “without prejudice, with all sympathy, with full recognition of what is good.” And he admitted that missionaries had themselves to blame for some of the false impressions at home, because reports naturally dwelt on encouraging cases. “It is not a book to be read with a lazy kind of sentimental ‘interest,’” he wrote. “It is a book to send the reader to his knees—still more to her knees.”

Doubt and Confirmation

The book sold well. It was reprinted in August 1903, and again in the following years. But it also provoked doubt. Some readers in England could not believe that things were as bad as she said. Some called the book pessimistic. Others objected not to its facts but to its argument: that it was wrong to draw children away from their parents, or to break up families in the name of religion.

Amy took the objections seriously. In a chapter called “Three Objections” she set them out fairly. Readers had asked by what right missionaries pressed their religion on people who did not want it, and whether a convert should not stay at home and live quietly as a Christian there, rather than divide her family by leaving. One correspondent had written that girls who left their parents “richly deserve all they suffer.” Amy did not dismiss these questions. “We frankly admit that these objections and proposals are naturally reasonable,” she wrote, “and that what they state is perfectly true.” She agreed that the right thing was for a convert to live among her own people, and she called the breaking of family ties “a very cruel thing.” Her answer was that in caste society, as she had seen it, a convert was often not allowed to live at home as a Christian, and that she could not tell such a one to give up Christ.

When the fourth edition was being prepared, a number of experienced missionaries from other parts of South India sent notes confirming the book’s accuracy, and they were printed at the front of later editions. A Baptist missionary among the Telugus wrote that there was not a line in it “that cannot be duplicated in this Telugu Mission.” Others agreed. One of the notes came from an Indian woman whose voice carried more weight than any missionary’s. Pandita Ramabai, the Marathi scholar and reformer who had founded a home for widows and famine girls at Mukti, and whose life is told in the sixth volume of this series, wrote: “While I was reading Things as They Are, I fancied I was living my old life among Hindus over again. I can honestly corroborate everything said in regard to the religious and social life of the Hindus.”

A Hindu Reader’s View

A fair account of the book must also ask how it would have read to a Hindu. Amy Carmichael wrote as an evangelical missionary, convinced that the religion around her was the work of spiritual darkness. She called one chapter “Deified Devilry.” She described images of the gods as hideous, and temple festivals as revelry. She spoke of Hindu ascetics and priests in harsh terms. She sometimes generalised from the worst things she had seen or heard to the religion as a whole, as when she wrote that the practices she described were “Hinduism—not in theory of course, but in practice.”

A devout Hindu reading those pages would have had every reason to object. Hinduism is not one thing but many, and most Hindus in Tinnevelly, as everywhere, had nothing to do with the abuses she described and would have condemned them. Hindu reformers of her own generation were campaigning against child marriage, the mistreatment of widows, and the very temple practices that she attacked, and they did so in the name of a purer Hinduism. Missionary writing that blamed the religion itself for every evil made their work harder, and fed a resentment of Christianity that has not disappeared.

It is only fair to add that Amy was capable of seeing beyond her own polemic. She wrote with real admiration of the intelligence, courtesy and humour of many of the Hindus she met. She recorded their objections honestly, and sometimes conceded their force. She described the grief of Hindu parents with compassion. And her purpose was not to win an argument but to rouse prayer. But the reader today is right to notice the hard edges of the book, and to read them as part of the history, not as the last word on the people she lived among.

The Manifestation of the Truth

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Paul’s defence of his own ministry. He had renounced craftiness, he said, and would not handle the word of God deceitfully; instead, “by the manifestation of the truth” he commended himself to every person’s conscience before God. It was a claim to honesty, in a world where religious teachers were often suspected of trickery.

Things as They Are was Amy Carmichael’s attempt to live by that verse. She would not commend the missionary cause by pleasant fictions. She would tell the truth, as far as she could see it and as far as it could be printed, and leave the result to God. She did not see everything, and she sometimes saw through the lens of her own convictions. But the book’s honesty about the work itself, its slowness, its failures and its cost, was rare in its time, and it remains bracing today. Three years later, wanting to show the other side of the picture that the first book had not had room for, she published a sequel called Overweights of Joy. The title said that the joys outweighed the sorrows. She never said the sorrows were unreal.

fields.title: Servants of the Gods
fields.body_html:
“Deliver them that are carried away unto death, And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back. If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this; Doth not he that weigheth the hearts consider it? And he that keepeth thy soul, doth not he know it?”

— Proverbs 24:11-12, ASV

A Hard Chapter

This chapter is about the system from which many of the children of Dohnavur were sheltered. It is the hardest part of Amy Carmichael’s story to tell well, because it is easy to tell it badly in two opposite ways. It can be told as a lurid tale of heathen wickedness, in which a brave missionary rescues innocent girls from evil priests. Or it can be told as a story of missionary prejudice, in which a foreign woman misunderstood and slandered an ancient tradition of sacred art. Neither version is true. This chapter tries to tell it plainly, without graphic detail, and with fairness to everyone involved.

The Temple Women

For many centuries, in many parts of India and especially in the south, some temples had women attached to them who were dedicated to the service of the deity. In Tamil they were known by several names; in English they came to be called devadasis, from a Sanskrit word meaning “servant of god,” and Amy Carmichael translated their Tamil title as “Servants of the gods.” A girl was dedicated in a ceremony that was spoken of as a marriage to the god, after which she could never marry a man and so, as the people said, could never be widowed. That was why their presence was considered auspicious at weddings and festivals.

The tradition had a long and in some ways distinguished history. Inscriptions from the great temples of the Chola period record the endowment of hundreds of temple women, and in some periods they held property, were educated when most women were not, and were the custodians of the classical traditions of dance and music. The dance that is now known around the world as Bharatanatyam descends in large part from their art. Communities of hereditary temple dancers and musicians, with their own family structures and inheritance through the female line, were part of the social fabric of South India for many generations.

But by the nineteenth century the tradition had changed in many places, and its connection with sexual relationships outside marriage had become central. A woman dedicated to a temple could not marry, and in practice many such women entered relationships with patrons, sometimes long-term and recognised, sometimes not. Girls were dedicated in childhood. Some came from hereditary families; others were given by parents who had made a vow, or who could not support them, or were bought from poor families, or were adopted by older temple women to carry on their household. Whatever the arrangement, the girl had no say in it. By the time she was old enough to understand, her life had been decided for her.

What Amy Saw

Amy Carmichael did not set out to study this system. She stumbled on it, as she put it, through the children. She had seen little girls playing in the courtyards near the temples, “gracious little maidens, winsome in their ways,” and had heard that some of them had been bought as infants. In Things as They Are she described meeting a bright child in a village who asked to come home with her, and then, a few days later, seeing two men leading the same child away to be “married to the god.” She wrote that the men’s faces haunted her all night.

She had met the child once before, in her own village, and the memory of that meeting is one of the most striking passages in the book. Amy had been talking with the girl’s grandmother, a learned old woman who could recite page after page of the Tamil classics and who preferred to sing Hindu verses to her visitor and explain them, rather than listen to Christian ones. “Consider the age of our great Religion, consider its literature—millions of stanzas!” the old woman said. While they talked, the little girl came and stood by the verandah and joined in the verses her grandmother was chanting, going on through stanza after stanza while Amy listened in astonishment. Then she ran off laughing to play. Amy’s comment was brief: “And this was the child. All that brightness, all that intelligence, ‘married to a god.’” It is worth noticing what the passage shows without meaning to: a family of real culture and learning, a grandmother proud of a great literary tradition, and a child of quick intelligence. Amy did not think the people around her were savages. She thought that something terrible was being done within a world that was in many ways refined, and that was what made it so hard to bear.

After Preena came, she began to inquire systematically. She wanted to know how many girls were involved, how they were obtained, where they came from, and what happened to them. It was difficult and sometimes dangerous work. The subject was not discussed with outsiders, and certainly not with a foreign woman associated with the Christians. Information had to be gathered patiently, through Indian Christian helpers, through people who were willing to talk, and through official records such as the census of 1901, which Amy later drew on in Lotus Buds.

On some of these inquiries, it is said, she went in disguise. She already wore Indian dress, and popular accounts say that she darkened her skin, with coffee or some other stain, so that she could pass unnoticed in places where a European face would have closed every door. The details have been embellished, and should not be pressed. But it is clear that she went to great lengths to learn the truth, and that she took real risks in doing so.

What she learned convinced her that very large numbers of girls were involved across the Madras Presidency, and that many of them were destined, from early childhood, for a life of sexual exploitation in the name of religion. She did not publish the details. She said, again and again, that what she knew could not be printed. But she believed she knew enough to act.

Not a Western Discovery

It is important to say clearly that Amy Carmichael was not the first or the only person to oppose the dedication of girls to temples, and that the campaign which eventually ended it was led above all by Indians.

From the 1890s an “anti-nautch” movement, named after the Anglo-Indian word for a dance performance, had been campaigning against the hiring of temple dancers at social functions, and it drew support from Indian social reformers as well as from missionaries. In the early twentieth century Indian reformers in the Madras Presidency took up the cause in earnest. The most important of them was Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, the first woman to serve in the Madras Legislative Council, who in the late 1920s brought forward a resolution and then a bill to end the dedication of girls to temples. She had family ties to the communities concerned, and she argued her case in medical, moral and religious terms. Another powerful voice was Moovalur Ramamirtham, who came from a devadasi family herself and campaigned for decades, in the self-respect movement, for the freedom of women in her community to marry and live as they chose.

The campaign took many years. It was finally successful in October 1947, two months after Indian independence, when the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act was passed. Other states passed similar laws later, some of them much later, and the practice persisted illegally in some regions for decades. Amy Carmichael lived to see the Madras Act passed. She had spent nearly half a century working towards the same end, but the law was the achievement of Indian legislators and campaigners, and it should be remembered as theirs.

The Other Side

There is one more thing to say, and fairness requires it. Not everyone in the communities concerned welcomed the reform. Associations of hereditary temple artists protested against the bill, arguing that their community was being slandered for the sins of some, that their art and their livelihood were being destroyed, and that they had a right to their own way of life. Historians of South India have shown that the abolition, whatever its benefits, also brought real losses to these communities. Their dance was taken up and refashioned by others, often from higher castes, while the women who had carried it for generations were stigmatised and impoverished. Some scholars, notably Davesh Soneji, have argued that missionary writing, including Amy Carmichael’s, helped to fix a picture of these women as nothing but victims or prostitutes, and that this picture did lasting harm to their descendants.

A Christian reader may disagree with some of that argument. The children Amy sheltered were not consenting adults choosing a way of life; they were small girls whose futures had been decided for them, and there is ample evidence that many such girls were abused. But the critique is a needed reminder that the women of these communities were human beings with their own voices and their own dignity, and that the language used about them, by missionaries and by Indian reformers alike, was often cruel. The real people behind the “system” deserve to be remembered as people, and not only as a problem.

Deliver Them

The verse at the head of this chapter is one that Amy Carmichael might have taken as her charter. “Deliver them that are carried away unto death,” it says, “And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back.” The next verse removes the excuse of ignorance: “If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this; Doth not he that weigheth the hearts consider it?” Once we know, we are responsible.

That was how Amy saw it. Once she knew what she believed she knew, she could not unknow it, and she could not do nothing. She did not have the power to change the law, and she did not try to lead a public campaign. What she could do was to take in children, one at a time, and give them a home. It was a small response to a large evil. But she believed that God weighed hearts, and that he would ask what she had done with what she knew. She spent the rest of her life answering that question.

If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this; Doth not he that weigheth the hearts consider it? And he that keepeth thy soul, doth not he know it?” — Proverbs 24:11-12, ASV A Hard Chapter This chapter is about the system from which many of the children of Dohnavur were sheltered. It is the hardest part of Amy Carmichael’s story to tell well, because it is easy to tell it badly in two opposite ways. It can be told as a lurid tale of heathen wickedness, in which a brave missionary rescues innocent girls from evil priests. Or it can be told as a story of missionary prejudice, in which a foreign woman misunderstood and slandered an ancient tradition of sacred art. Neither version is true. This chapter tries to tell it plainly, without graphic detail, and with fairness to everyone involved. The Temple Women For many centuries, in many parts of India and especially in the south, some temples had women attached to them who were dedicated to the service of the deity. In Tamil they were known by several names; in English they came to be called devadasis, from a Sanskrit word meaning “servant of god,” and Amy Carmichael translated their Tamil title as “Servants of the gods.” A girl was dedicated in a ceremony that was spoken of as a marriage to the god, after which she could never marry a man and so, as the people said, could never be widowed. That was why their presence was considered auspicious at weddings and festivals. The tradition had a long and in some ways distinguished history. Inscriptions from the great temples of the Chola period record the endowment of hundreds of temple women, and in some periods they held property, were educated when most women were not, and were the custodians of the classical traditions of dance and music. The dance that is now known around the world as Bharatanatyam descends in large part from their art. Communities of hereditary temple dancers and musicians, with their own family structures and inheritance through the female line, were part of the social fabric of South India for many generations. But by the nineteenth century the tradition had changed in many places, and its connection with sexual relationships outside marriage had become central. A woman dedicated to a temple could not marry, and in practice many such women entered relationships with patrons, sometimes long-term and recognised, sometimes not. Girls were dedicated in childhood. Some came from hereditary families; others were given by parents who had made a vow, or who could not support them, or were bought from poor families, or were adopted by older temple women to carry on their household. Whatever the arrangement, the girl had no say in it. By the time she was old enough to understand, her life had been decided for her. What Amy Saw Amy Carmichael did not set out to study this system. She stumbled on it, as she put it, through the children. She had seen little girls playing in the courtyards near the temples, “gracious little maidens, winsome in their ways,” and had heard that some of them had been bought as infants. In Things as They Are she described meeting a bright child in a village who asked to come home with her, and then, a few days later, seeing two men leading the same child away to be “married to the god.” She wrote that the men’s faces haunted her all night. She had met the child once before, in her own village, and the memory of that meeting is one of the most striking passages in the book. Amy had been talking with the girl’s grandmother, a learned old woman who could recite page after page of the Tamil classics and who preferred to sing Hindu verses to her visitor and explain them, rather than listen to Christian ones. “Consider the age of our great Religion, consider its literature—millions of stanzas!” the old woman said. While they talked, the little girl came and stood by the verandah and joined in the verses her grandmother was chanting, going on through stanza after stanza while Amy listened in astonishment. Then she ran off laughing to play. Amy’s comment was brief: “And this was the child. All that brightness, all that intelligence, ‘married to a god.’” It is worth noticing what the passage shows without meaning to: a family of real culture and learning, a grandmother proud of a great literary tradition, and a child of quick intelligence. Amy did not think the people around her were savages. She thought that something terrible was being done within a world that was in many ways refined, and that was what made it so hard to bear. After Preena came, she began to inquire systematically. She wanted to know how many girls were involved, how they were obtained, where they came from, and what happened to them. It was difficult and sometimes dangerous work. The subject was not discussed with outsiders, and certainly not with a foreign woman associated with the Christians. Information had to be gathered patiently, through Indian Christian helpers, through people who were willing to talk, and through official records such as the census of 1901, which Amy later drew on in Lotus Buds. On some of these inquiries, it is said, she went in disguise. She already wore Indian dress, and popular accounts say that she darkened her skin, with coffee or some other stain, so that she could pass unnoticed in places where a European face would have closed every door. The details have been embellished, and should not be pressed. But it is clear that she went to great lengths to learn the truth, and that she took real risks in doing so. What she learned convinced her that very large numbers of girls were involved across the Madras Presidency, and that many of them were destined, from early childhood, for a life of sexual exploitation in the name of religion. She did not publish the details. She said, again and again, that what she knew could not be printed. But she believed she knew enough to act. Not a Western Discovery It is important to say clearly that Amy Carmichael was not the first or the only person to oppose the dedication of girls to temples, and that the campaign which eventually ended it was led above all by Indians. From the 1890s an “anti-nautch” movement, named after the Anglo-Indian word for a dance performance, had been campaigning against the hiring of temple dancers at social functions, and it drew support from Indian social reformers as well as from missionaries. In the early twentieth century Indian reformers in the Madras Presidency took up the cause in earnest. The most important of them was Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, the first woman to serve in the Madras Legislative Council, who in the late 1920s brought forward a resolution and then a bill to end the dedication of girls to temples. She had family ties to the communities concerned, and she argued her case in medical, moral and religious terms. Another powerful voice was Moovalur Ramamirtham, who came from a devadasi family herself and campaigned for decades, in the self-respect movement, for the freedom of women in her community to marry and live as they chose. The campaign took many years. It was finally successful in October 1947, two months after Indian independence, when the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act was passed. Other states passed similar laws later, some of them much later, and the practice persisted illegally in some regions for decades. Amy Carmichael lived to see the Madras Act passed. She had spent nearly half a century working towards the same end, but the law was the achievement of Indian legislators and campaigners, and it should be remembered as theirs. The Other Side There is one more thing to say, and fairness requires it. Not everyone in the communities concerned welcomed the reform. Associations of hereditary temple artists protested against the bill, arguing that their community was being slandered for the sins of some, that their art and their livelihood were being destroyed, and that they had a right to their own way of life. Historians of South India have shown that the abolition, whatever its benefits, also brought real losses to these communities. Their dance was taken up and refashioned by others, often from higher castes, while the women who had carried it for generations were stigmatised and impoverished. Some scholars, notably Davesh Soneji, have argued that missionary writing, including Amy Carmichael’s, helped to fix a picture of these women as nothing but victims or prostitutes, and that this picture did lasting harm to their descendants. A Christian reader may disagree with some of that argument. The children Amy sheltered were not consenting adults choosing a way of life; they were small girls whose futures had been decided for them, and there is ample evidence that many such girls were abused. But the critique is a needed reminder that the women of these communities were human beings with their own voices and their own dignity, and that the language used about them, by missionaries and by Indian reformers alike, was often cruel. The real people behind the “system” deserve to be remembered as people, and not only as a problem. Deliver Them The verse at the head of this chapter is one that Amy Carmichael might have taken as her charter. “Deliver them that are carried away unto death,” it says, “And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back.” The next verse removes the excuse of ignorance: “If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this; Doth not he that weigheth the hearts consider it?” Once we know, we are responsible. That was how Amy saw it. Once she knew what she believed she knew, she could not unknow it, and she could not do nothing. She did not have the power to change the law, and she did not try to lead a public campaign. What she could do was to take in children, one at a time, and give them a home. It was a small response to a large evil. But she believed that God weighed hearts, and that he would ask what she had done with what she knew. She spent the rest of her life answering that question.

fields.title: Lotus Buds
fields.body_html:
“He will feed his flock like a shepherd, he will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and will gently lead those that have their young.”

— Isaiah 40:11, ASV

The Elf

Before there were nurseries at Dohnavur, there was one small girl who would not keep still. In Things as They Are Amy Carmichael gave a whole chapter to Pearl-eyes, whom she nicknamed the Elf, “because it exactly describes her.” It is the happiest chapter in the book, and it shows a side of Amy that her more solemn admirers have sometimes missed.

The Elf, she wrote, was “a very wilful, truthful, exasperating, fascinating little Oriental.” She hated her share of the housework, which was ten minutes’ polishing of brass water-pots, until she made a discovery: “Satan doesn’t come very close to me if I sing all the time I’m rubbing the brasses. He runs away when he hears me sing, so I sing very loud, and that keeps him away. Satan doesn’t like hymns.” She liked to be first, and to choose the game, and when the other children would not play it her way she walked off. And every evening she said her prayers in Amy’s room, counting her sins on the fingers of one hand and her blessings on the other.

Amy recorded one of those prayers in full. The Elf confessed that she had been cross with another girl, but added that the other girl had been wrong too, “so it was only half a sin.” She confessed a quarrel with some smaller children, but noted that they had asked her forgiveness and she had forgiven them, “so that is three bad things and two good things to-day.” She thanked God for a cardboard box, some sweets, some rags from the waste-paper basket for her dolls’ clothes, and a piece of soap the size of a walnut. And she asked, as she always did, to be kept safe through the night from “the bites of snakes and scorpions, and all other noxious creatures.” Some time afterwards, Amy noted dryly, a nest of scorpions was discovered within six yards of the Elf’s sleeping mat, and none of them had disturbed her.

There were two other small girls in the household at the time, whom Amy called the Imp and Tangles, and the three of them argued theology with the energy of children who had just discovered it. Amy reported one of their conclusions, which, she said, “would shock the orthodox.” Obedience, the children had decided, was not so important as love. Orpah had obeyed her mother-in-law when Naomi told her to go home, and she went. Ruth had been told four times to go, and would not. Yet God blessed Ruth more than Orpah, because she loved her mother-in-law. “So obedience is not so important as love.” Amy had spent the previous day, she confessed, labouring to explain to them the necessity of obedience. It is a lovely picture of a missionary being taught by her pupils, and of a teacher who was humble enough, and amused enough, to write it down.

The Elf also brought Amy questions that were not childish at all. One morning she had prayed earnestly to be kept from being naughty, and within an hour she had been naughty again; she had looked at the clock and seen. “How was it I was naughty when I wanted to be good?” she asked. “So what is the use of praying?” Amy recognised the question. It was Paul’s question in the seventh chapter of Romans, and it was her own question at the Glasgow convention years before. She did not pretend it was easy to answer.

These pages matter because they show how Amy saw the children. They were not cases, or trophies, or victims to be pitied. They were persons, with their own wills and their own humour, their own theology and their own sins. She delighted in them, and she let her readers delight in them too.

Babies

In the years after Preena came, the household at Dohnavur began to change in a way that Amy had not foreseen. At first the children who came were girls old enough to walk and talk, like Preena herself. But Amy learned that the girls most at risk were often very young, and that the time to save a child from dedication was before it happened, sometimes in infancy. From about 1904 babies began to come. Some were brought by mothers or relatives who could not keep them and who preferred that they should go to the Christians rather than to a temple. Some came through Indian Christian helpers who learned of children in danger. Some came by ways that Amy never fully described, for the safety of everyone involved.

Babies were a different matter from older children. They needed milk, and in a world without safe infant formula that meant wet nurses, Indian women who were paid to nurse them. They needed constant care. And they died. Infant mortality in South India at the beginning of the twentieth century was very high, and babies who had been separated from their mothers, often after neglect or a hard journey, were especially vulnerable. Many of the babies who came to Dohnavur in its early years did not survive. Amy grieved over every one of them, and she learned, through bitter experience, how much skill and care it took to keep a newborn alive in that climate.

She learned too that babies could not be cared for in a corner of a missionary bungalow. Over the following years nurseries were built: simple buildings, open to the air, each with a group of small children and the women who cared for them. The compound grew, and with it the need for workers, for money, for food and for medicine. A household of converts was turning into something much larger.

Lotus Buds

In 1909 Amy published a book about the babies and small girls of Dohnavur. She called it Lotus Buds. The lotus grows in muddy water and opens into a flower of great beauty, and in Indian religious imagery it is a symbol of purity rising out of the mire. Amy used the image for the children, who had come, many of them, out of a dark place, and whom she hoped to see open into lives of beauty.

The book was handsomely produced, with fifty photographs of the children taken at Dohnavur, and it was the most carefully illustrated of her early books. In a chapter about the photographs she admitted, with some amusement, that they did not do the children justice; the babies were wary of the photographer, and their lively faces stiffened as soon as the camera appeared. The book also returned to the subject of temple dedication, drawing on official figures to show how many girls might be involved, but it did so with restraint. Its main purpose was to make readers love the children, and to pray for them and for the many others who were not safe.

Three years earlier she had published Overweights of Joy, a sequel to Things as They Are, which told of the joys of the work as frankly as the first book had told of its sorrows. The two books together give a picture of the years between 1901 and 1909 that is neither triumphant nor despairing. There were many losses: converts who went back, babies who died, children who could not be saved. There were also great joys: children who grew, converts who stood firm, and a household that was beginning to feel like a family.

Gentle Leading

The verse at the head of this chapter is one of the most tender in the Old Testament. Isaiah, comforting a people in exile, describes God as a shepherd who “will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and will gently lead those that have their young.” The picture is of strength used gently: a shepherd strong enough to carry the lambs, and wise enough not to drive the ewes too hard.

Amy Carmichael loved that verse, and she tried to live it. She was a strong woman, and she ran Dohnavur with a firm hand. But she wanted the children to know, above all, that they were carried. She held the babies, played with the toddlers, made up games and songs, and gave each child a name that meant something. The names were Tamil, chosen with care, and they often expressed a hope or a prayer for the child’s life. She insisted that every child be treated as an individual, known and loved, not as one of a crowd.

It was not always possible. As the numbers grew, from a handful to dozens and then to more than a hundred, she could no longer know every child as she had known Preena and the Elf. She came to depend on the women who worked with her, Indian and British, and she gave great thought to how the children could be cared for in small groups, each with its own “mother.” But the ideal remained: a family, not an institution, and a family that reflected the gentleness of the Good Shepherd.

A Growing Family

By 1913 there were about a hundred and thirty children at Dohnavur. That was a remarkable growth from the single child who had climbed onto Amy’s knee twelve years before. It was also, by any standard, a large household to run, and it raised questions that Amy had not had to face before. How would the children be educated? What would happen to them when they grew up? Who would care for them if Amy fell ill or died? How would the work be paid for?

The last question had a clear answer, at least in principle. Amy had decided, following Hudson Taylor and George Müller, that Dohnavur would not appeal for money. Its needs would be made known to God in prayer, and the household would trust him to supply them. Gifts came, from friends in Britain and elsewhere, often unsolicited and sometimes at the very moment of need. Amy kept records of these answers to prayer, and they became an important part of the story she told about Dohnavur. She believed that the work was God’s, and that he would provide for it as long as he wanted it to continue.

The other questions were harder, and they would occupy her for the rest of her life. But in the years around 1909, when Lotus Buds was published, the main feeling at Dohnavur seems to have been one of joy. The children were growing. The nurseries were full of noise. And Amy, who had once thought her work would be preaching in the villages, had found herself the mother of a family she could never have imagined.

fields.title: Amma
fields.body_html:
“But we were gentle in the midst of you, as when a nurse cherisheth her own children: even so, being affectionately desirous of you, we were well pleased to impart unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were become very dear to us.”

— 1 Thessalonians 2:7-8, ASV

A Name

The children of Dohnavur called Amy Carmichael Amma. In Tamil the word means “mother,” and it is also, as she explained in the glossary to her first book, an ordinary word that women use in speaking to one another and that girls use to older women. For a child at Dohnavur it meant both things at once. It was a word of courtesy, and it was a word of belonging. Amy did not want to be called “Miss Carmichael,” or “madam,” or by any of the titles that missionaries in India usually bore. She wanted to be a mother to the children, and she wanted them to know it.

She was not, of course, their mother in the ordinary sense, and she knew it. Many of the children had mothers living, and some kept in touch with them. Some had been brought by their mothers. And as the family grew, Amy could not be a mother to each child in the way that a woman with a few children can be. But the name expressed what she hoped Dohnavur would be: not an orphanage, but a home.

Becoming Indian

From her early years in Tinnevelly, Amy wore Indian dress, and at Dohnavur she asked those who joined her to do the same. The women wore saris; the household ate Indian food, cooked in the Indian way; Tamil was the language of daily life. The children were given Tamil names, and they grew up in Tamil culture, learning Tamil songs and stories and the courtesies of Tamil life. Amy wrote many Tamil hymns and songs for them, and set Scripture to Tamil tunes.

This was not common among missionaries at the time. Many mission schools and orphanages in India gave their children English names, dressed them in European clothes, taught them English, and raised them to be, in effect, little Englishmen and Englishwomen. The aim was often sincere, and the results were mixed. Such children could find themselves strangers in their own country, cut off from their families and communities, and dependent on the mission for the rest of their lives. Amy wanted to avoid that. She wanted the children of Dohnavur to be Indian Christians, not Westernised Indians.

There was one Indian custom, however, that she would not adopt, and that was caste. The children who came to Dohnavur came from many communities, high and low, and Amy insisted that within the family those distinctions counted for nothing. The children ate together, played together, slept in the same nurseries, and were taught that they were sisters. For children from high-caste families this could be a hard lesson, as it had been for Pearl-eyes on her first night, when she drew herself up and refused food that would break her caste. For the families and communities outside, it was one of the most offensive things about Dohnavur, because it meant that a child who went there could never go back into her caste. Amy knew this, and she did not flinch from it. She believed that in Christ there was neither high caste nor low, and that a Christian family which kept caste was not fully Christian.

It would be wrong to exaggerate the extent of her adaptation. She remained in many ways a woman of her own culture. She thought and prayed and wrote in English. Her books were addressed to British readers, and her theology was that of Keswick. Dohnavur was run according to her ideas of order and discipline, and those ideas were shaped by a Victorian upbringing. Some later observers felt that, for all its Indian dress and Tamil songs, Dohnavur was at heart a very British institution. There is truth in that, as there is in most such judgements. But for her time she went further than most, and she did it on principle.

The Accals

The real work of caring for the children was done, in large part, by Indian Christian women. They were known as the accals, from the Tamil word for “elder sister,” and that name too was chosen with care. They were not servants or employees in the usual sense, but members of the family, responsible for the children in their care. Some of them were converts who had come out of Hindu homes, like Arulai; some were widows, like Ponnammal; some came from Christian families in the district; and in time many were girls who had grown up at Dohnavur themselves.

Ponnammal, the young widow who had led the band, became one of the chief pillars of the household. But those who stayed formed a close-knit community, bound together by the work, by prayer, and by their loyalty to Amma.

Discipline and Love

Amy Carmichael was a loving mother, and she was also a strict one. She believed, as most people of her generation did, that children needed firm discipline, and that disobedience, lying and sulking should be dealt with promptly. She expected obedience, and she could be severe. Some of the children who grew up at Dohnavur remembered her with deep love and with a certain awe. Some of the adult workers found her exacting, and a few found her overbearing.

There is no need to pretend otherwise. A woman who had built a large and complex household out of nothing, against opposition, with very little help, was not likely to be meek. She had strong opinions about almost everything, from the way children should be fed to the way prayer meetings should be run, and she expected them to be followed. She could be sharp with those who disagreed, and she did not always distinguish between disagreement with her and disloyalty to the work. Those were real faults, and they caused real pain to some who loved her.

But her discipline was meant in love, and those who knew her best testified that it was received that way by most of the children. She had a gift for making each child feel important. She laughed easily, enjoyed jokes, invented games, wrote songs and stories, and loved the natural world, which she taught the children to love too: birds, butterflies, flowers, streams, the mountains. She wanted Dohnavur to be a happy place, and by most accounts it was.

Not the Gospel Only

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians. He reminds them that when he and his companions were among them, they were “gentle in the midst of you, as when a nurse cherisheth her own children.” The word translated “nurse” means a nursing mother, and the image is of a mother caring for her own baby. Paul goes on: “we were well pleased to impart unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were become very dear to us.”

That last sentence is a good description of what Amy Carmichael tried to do at Dohnavur. She did not want only to teach the children about God. She wanted to give them herself, and she wanted the women who worked with her to do the same. Her idea of Christian service was not a professional transaction, in which a missionary delivered a message and went home on furlough. It was a life given, day after day, to particular people who had become dear.

That was one of the reasons she never went home. There were other reasons too: her health, the long voyage, the cost, and later her injury. But the deepest reason was that her children were at Dohnavur, and she would not leave them. In the early years, the danger that a child might be taken back if she were away was real. Later it was simply that she could not imagine being anywhere else. Her home was where her family was.

A Mother’s Cost

Being Amma cost Amy Carmichael a great deal. It cost her the evangelistic work she had loved. It cost her the possibility of ever going home, and of seeing her own mother again. It cost her rest, and often sleep, and sometimes health. It cost her grief, because children died, and some who lived turned away from what she had taught them. And it cost her a certain kind of freedom, because a mother is never free of her children.

fields.title: The Sorrowful Years
fields.body_html:
“Jesus answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt understand hereafter.”

— John 13:7, ASV

The Dear Old Man

The first of the great losses had come some years earlier. Robert Wilson, the Quaker who had taken Amy into his home and given her his name, died in 1905. She had not seen him since she sailed for India ten years before. They had written to each other faithfully, and he had supported the work with his gifts and his prayers, but she had not been able to go home to him, and she was not with him when he died. Her early books had been published under the name Amy Wilson-Carmichael, and she went on using it for some years afterwards. It was her way of keeping faith with the old man who had been a father to her.

His death was a sorrow, but it was the kind of sorrow that missionaries far from home learned to expect. He was an old man, and he had lived a full life. The sorrows of the years between 1912 and 1915 were of a different kind. They came close together, and they took from Amy the people on whom she most depended.

Thomas Walker

In August 1912 Thomas Walker died. He had gone away from Dohnavur on a journey, and he fell ill and died within a short time, far from home. Sources give slightly different dates for his death, but all place it in the second half of August 1912.

For Amy it was a devastating blow. Walker had been her teacher, her colleague and her counsellor since 1896. He had taught her Tamil, guided her in the work, stood beside her when Preena came, and helped her to build the household at Dohnavur. He had been, in a sense, its head, the ordained missionary under whose authority the whole work went on. His scholarly mind and his steady judgement had balanced her intensity. Now he was gone, and she was left with the full responsibility for a growing family and its many workers, without the one man whose advice she trusted above all others.

Walker’s own voice can still be heard in a few places. When Amy chose quotations from missionaries to head the chapters of Things as They Are, she included one from him, about the girls of caste families who wanted to follow Christ. “In India the bitter cry is far more bitter,” he had written, “but it is stifled and smothered by the cruel gag of Caste.” It is the sentence of a man who had spent many years listening, and who did not use strong words lightly. He had been in Tinnevelly since the 1880s, and he knew its churches, its villages and its language as few foreigners did. He was, by every account, a man of prayer, and his addresses at conventions for the deepening of spiritual life had been valued all over South India. When such a man said that something was terrible, people listened. Amy had relied on that authority more than she perhaps knew, and now she would have to stand without it.

Mrs. Walker, whom Amy loved deeply, was left a widow, and the partnership of three that had carried the work since the Pannaivilai days was broken.

She grieved, and she also wrote. Four years later she published Walker of Tinnevelly, a memoir of his life and work. It is a portrait of a man she admired without reserve, written with love and with the restraint he would have wanted. She did not make him a plaster saint. She showed a disciplined, scholarly, sometimes severe man who had given his life to the Tamil church, and whose influence ran far beyond the few places where he had lived.

A Wall and a Lawyer

The troubles did not come singly. Soon after Walker’s death, while the household was still in mourning, a lawyer wrote to demand that the building of a wall around part of the compound should stop at once. The claim was that the land on which the wall was being built did not legally belong to the mission. It was the kind of dispute that could drag on for years, and it came at a time when Amy had no one with Walker’s standing to deal with it.

It was not the only legal threat of these years. The work of sheltering children who were claimed by others was always exposed to the law, and there were families and communities who had every reason to try to use it. Amy’s biographers record a case, about 1914, in which a charge of kidnapping was brought in connection with a girl named Muttammal whom the Fellowship was protecting, and in which Amy herself faced the possibility of arrest. The case was eventually dropped. The details are known chiefly from the later biographies, and this book has not been able to check them against court records. But the general picture is clear enough. To shelter children at Dohnavur was to live under the shadow of the courts.

Her Mother

On 14 July 1913 Amy’s mother died in England. Catherine Carmichael had given her daughter up twice, first to Robert Wilson and then to the mission field, and Amy had not been able to go home to her. She had followed the work with love and prayer, and she had supported it in every way she could.

We know little of how Amy received the news, beyond the fact of her grief. She had always been close to her mother, and her mother’s letter of 1892, giving her freely to God, had been one of the treasures of her life. Now the woman who had taught her to pray, and who had let her go, was gone. Amy was forty-five. Her father had been dead for nearly thirty years, the Dear Old Man for eight. She had become, in the fullest sense, an orphan herself.

Ponnammal

The last of the great losses of these years was the hardest. Ponnammal, the young widow who had led the band in the 1890s and had become one of the pillars of Dohnavur, fell ill with a long and painful illness, which the biographies describe as cancer. Amy cared for her and watched her suffer. She died in 1915.

Ponnammal had been Amy’s closest Indian friend. She had shared the early journeys, the hardships of village work, the joys and sorrows of the first converts, and the building of the household. She had cared for children, trained younger women, and given wisdom and steadiness to the whole community. Amy admired her deeply, and in later years she wrote her life, under the title Ponnammal: Her Story. Ponnammal left a daughter, whom Amy took into her own care.

Amy found Ponnammal’s suffering harder to bear than her death. She had prayed for her healing, and the prayer had not been answered. She had watched a woman she loved endure great pain, and had been unable to relieve it. It was the kind of experience that tests faith to its foundations, and Amy did not pretend that it was easy. But she came through it, as she came through so much, by holding on to the conviction that God knew what he was doing, even when she did not.

The War Years

In August 1914, between the death of her mother and the death of Ponnammal, war broke out in Europe. It was far from Dohnavur, but its effects reached even there. The cost of living rose sharply. Communications with Britain became slower and less certain. Gifts from home, on which the work depended, might have been expected to dry up, as friends faced their own hardships and anxieties. Amy and her household continued to live by prayer, making their needs known to God and not to people, and they later testified that through all those years they had never lacked what they needed.

It would be easy to make too much of that testimony, and Amy herself was careful not to suggest that God’s provision meant there was never any anxiety, or that other faithful Christians who did go without were less faithful. But it was a real part of her experience, and it strengthened her conviction that the work was God’s and not hers.

Understanding Hereafter

The words of Jesus at the head of this chapter were spoken to Peter at the Last Supper, when Jesus knelt to wash the disciples’ feet and Peter protested. “What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt understand hereafter.” They are words that Christians have clung to in times of loss, because they promise understanding without demanding it now.

Amy Carmichael did not understand why Walker had to die when the work needed him most, why her mother had to die without seeing her again, or why Ponnammal had to suffer so much. She did not pretend to understand. She wrote later about the danger of offering easy explanations to people in pain, and about the need simply to trust. In one of her poems from these years she wrote of acceptance as the place where peace is found, and many readers have found in that phrase the key to her life after 1912. She did not mean resignation, or a dull submission to fate. She meant a deliberate choice to receive from God’s hand what she could not understand, and to go on.

The years from 1912 to 1915 took from her almost everyone who had been with her at the beginning. They also left her, for the first time, fully in charge of the work she had built. What she did with that responsibility is the subject of the chapters that follow.

fields.title: Boys
fields.body_html:
“And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.”

— Genesis 21:17, ASV

A Burden for Boys

For its first seventeen years the family at Dohnavur was a family of girls. That was natural. The danger that had first moved Amy Carmichael was the dedication of girls to temples, and the children who came to her were girls who had been, or might have been, caught up in it. The women who cared for them were women. The whole life of the household was shaped around the needs of girls and small children.

But Amy came to believe that boys too were in danger. In the course of her inquiries she learned that boys also were sometimes given to temples or to the travelling dramatic companies associated with temple festivals, and that some of them were exploited in ways that were as damaging as anything that happened to the girls. The subject was even more hidden than that of the girls, and even harder to speak about. But once she knew, she could not forget it.

According to the Fellowship’s own history, the burden came to her about 1912. She began to pray that God would either take it away or show her what to do about it. It was a practical as well as a spiritual question. A household of girls and women could not simply take in boys. It would need men to care for them, separate buildings, a different kind of education, and a great deal more money. And it would need, above all, a clear sign that this was God’s will and not merely her own idea.

Waiting

The answer did not come quickly. For six years Amy prayed, and for six years nothing happened. Those were the years of Walker’s death, her mother’s death and Ponnammal’s long illness, the years of the war, the wall and the lawyer. They were not years in which a new work could easily have been begun. But the burden did not go away, and she went on praying.

Waiting was not something that came naturally to her. She was a woman of action, impatient by temperament, and her instinct when she saw a need was to meet it. But she had learned, over many years, that her instincts were not always God’s timing. In Japan she had acted quickly and come to regret it. In January 1918 a baby boy was brought to Dohnavur. The circumstances, as the Fellowship remembered them, were unexpected; nobody had gone looking for him. Amy took his coming as the answer to six years of prayer. The household took him in, and the boys’ work began.

The great need was for men. She wanted them to be Christians who could stand on their own feet in Indian society, not dependants of a foreign institution.

The danger that had brought them to Dohnavur did not disappear when they arrived, and she was determined that no boy in her care should be exposed to the influences she had fought against. That meant a protected life, inside the compound, with limited contact with the world outside. As with the girls, the protection was real and necessary in the early years. As with the girls, some observers would later wonder whether it went on longer and further than it needed to.

The boys were not the only lost sons whom Amy met in these years. In the early 1920s the countryside around Dohnavur was disturbed by a band of outlaws, led by a man whom Amy would call Raj. By her account he had been driven to the hills by injustice and persecution, and he had become a kind of Robin Hood, feared by the police and the rich and admired by many of the poor. In the course of his years as a fugitive he came into contact with the Fellowship, and Amy came to know him. He listened to the gospel, and she believed that he came to a real faith in Christ.

She urged him to give himself up and face the courts, and for a time there seemed to be hope that he might do so. It did not happen. Raj was killed by the police not long afterwards, and Amy was left to grieve for a man she had come to regard as a brother in Christ, and to face the suspicion of those who thought the mission had been too friendly with a criminal. But the story shows something about her that is easy to miss: that her compassion was not limited to small children, and that she was willing to risk her reputation for the sake of a hunted man.

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the story of Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness. Driven out of Abraham’s household, with the water gone, Hagar laid her son under a bush and went a little way off, because she could not bear to watch him die. And God heard the voice of the lad. The angel’s words are some of the most tender in Genesis: “fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.”

Where he is: not where he ought to be, or where he might have been, but in the wilderness, under a bush, dying of thirst. God heard him there. By the end of her life the boys’ side of the family had grown into a large company, and many of those who passed through it grew up to be teachers, farmers, craftsmen, nurses and Christian workers. The boys’ work is less famous than the girls’, and it is often left out of popular accounts of Amy Carmichael’s life. But it was, in its way, as remarkable an act of faith, and it was born out of six years of patient prayer.
