fields.title: A Fellowship and Its Cost
fields.body_html:
“And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and soul: and not one of them said that aught of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.”

— Acts 4:32, ASV

Sisters of the Common Life

In March 1916, in the middle of the war and the year after Ponnammal’s death, Amy Carmichael gathered a small group of the Indian women who worked with her into a fellowship she called the Sisters of the Common Life. The name was borrowed from a late medieval movement in the Low Countries, the Brethren and Sisters of the Common Life, from which had come Thomas à Kempis and The Imitation of Christ. Amy did not intend to found a religious order in the Catholic sense. There were no lifelong vows. But the Sisters committed themselves to a life of simplicity, prayer and service at Dohnavur, and to remaining unmarried for as long as they felt called to it, so that they could give themselves wholly to the children.

It was a remarkable step for a Protestant missionary in South India. In a society where marriage was almost universal for women, and where an unmarried woman was regarded as an anomaly, Amy was offering Indian Christian women a recognised way of life outside marriage, with dignity and purpose. Many of those who joined were women who had come out of Hindu homes, or who had grown up at Dohnavur, and for whom marriage within the Christian community was not always easy to arrange. For them the Sisters offered a family and a calling.

It also raised questions. Some Indian Christians, and some missionaries, were uneasy about a Protestant community of unmarried women under a foreign leader, and wondered whether it was healthy for young women to be encouraged not to marry. Amy was clear that she did not regard singleness as superior to marriage, and that the girls who grew up at Dohnavur were free to marry if they chose. Many did. But she believed that some were called to a single life of service, as she had been, and she wanted to give that calling a shape.

Leaving the Society

For nearly thirty years Amy had worked in India as a missionary of the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society, though in practice she had long run her own work with a great deal of independence. As Dohnavur grew, the arrangement became more awkward. The Fellowship included workers of many denominations, men as well as women, and Indians as well as Europeans. It had its own principles, its own way of life, and its own leader. It made no appeals for money, while the Society, like all mission societies, depended on them. Amy did not wish to be bound by the rules and decisions of a committee in London that knew little of Dohnavur.

In 1925 the connection with the Society was ended by agreement, and Dohnavur became fully independent. In 1927 it was registered as the Dohnavur Fellowship, with its own constitution and its own governing structure. Amy remained its leader, and it was clear to everyone that the Fellowship was, in large measure, what she made it.

The independence had obvious advantages. Dohnavur could follow its own principles without compromise, and Amy was free to lead as she believed God was leading her. But it also had costs. An independent work, led by a strong founder, without outside oversight, was vulnerable to the weaknesses of its leader. Decisions that might have been questioned by a committee were not questioned. And the question of what would happen when the founder died, always a hard one for such works, became more pressing.

Stephen Neill

The most painful episode of these years, and one that Amy never mentioned in her own history of the Fellowship, involved a young man who would later become one of the best-known missionary scholars of the century. Stephen Neill was a brilliant young Cambridge graduate, a fellow of Trinity College, who came to India in 1924 to work at Dohnavur. His parents, both doctors, came out too for a time. He had read Amy’s books, and he came, it seems, with high hopes of working under her.

The partnership did not last. Within a year or so Neill and Amy were at odds, and in November 1925 he left Dohnavur. The reasons are not entirely clear, and the surviving accounts reflect the views of the people who gave them. A historian who has studied the episode, Dyron Daughrity, has described it as a bitter parting. It seems that Neill disagreed with Amy over the treatment and upbringing of the boys, including the degree to which they should be allowed outside the compound, and that he did not easily submit to her authority. Amy, for her part, seems to have felt that he was undermining the work and the unity of the Fellowship. Neill’s mother blamed the friction partly on Amy’s religious outlook, and Neill himself, in an autobiography published after his death, wrote critically of his time at Dohnavur.

Neill went on to a distinguished career. He became bishop of Tinnevelly, the very diocese in which Dohnavur lay, and later one of the most respected historians of Christian missions in the world. The episode tells us something about both of them. Neill was young, gifted and sure of himself, and he may have been difficult to manage. Amy was a strong leader who did not easily share authority, and who could not always distinguish disagreement from disloyalty. A wiser handling on both sides might have kept him. Amy’s silence about him in Gold Cord, her own history of the Fellowship, suggests that the wound went deep.

Healing

One of the needs that Amy had prayed about for many years was a hospital. The children of Dohnavur were often ill, and so were the people of the villages around. The nearest proper medical care was far away, and many children had died who might have lived with better treatment. With the coming of doctors and nurses to the Fellowship, the hope of a hospital became a reality. By the end of the 1920s the Fellowship had its own hospital, which Amy named, in Tamil, the Place of Heavenly Healing. It served not only the Fellowship but the surrounding villages, Hindu and Christian alike, and it became one of the most valued parts of Dohnavur’s work.

The hospital was also, in Amy’s eyes, a place of witness. She wanted the people who came for treatment to see the love of Christ in the care they received, and to hear the gospel if they wished. She was careful that no one should be pressured, and that treatment should never depend on willingness to listen. But she believed that healing of the body and healing of the soul belonged together, as they had in the ministry of Jesus.

Books from Dohnavur

Through all these years Amy went on writing. Her books were one of the main ways in which friends at home learned about Dohnavur, and since the Fellowship made no appeals, they were also, without being designed for it, one of the ways in which friends came to share in its life. In 1922 she published a life of Thomas Ragland, the Cambridge scholar who had pioneered itinerant evangelism in the villages of North Tinnevelly in the 1850s, and whose letter about the worth of a single soul she had quoted twenty years earlier. In 1924 came Mimosa, the story of a girl from a Hindu family who spent only a short time at Dohnavur as a child, heard there that God loved her, and went home to hold on to that one truth for years with almost no Christian teaching at all. The book is a quiet one, and many readers have found it among her most moving. It is a story about the power of a little light, and about the faithfulness of God to a child whom no missionary could follow.

She also wrote songs, many of them in Tamil, for the children to sing, and verse in English, some of which was gathered into books. Her writing in these years became more devotional and less polemical than Things as They Are. She was writing less to rouse readers at home than to strengthen those who were already committed, inside and outside the Fellowship, and to set down what she had learned about prayer, suffering and obedience. That shift would become even more marked after 1931, when writing became, for a time, almost the only work she could do.

One Heart and Soul

The verse at the head of this chapter describes the earliest church in Jerusalem: “the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and soul,” and they held their possessions in common. It is an ideal that Christians have tried again and again to live out, in monasteries and religious orders, in communities and households, and it has never been easy.

Amy Carmichael tried to live it at Dohnavur. The Fellowship owned its property in common, its members received no salaries, and they shared a life of work and prayer. Unity was one of her great concerns. She wanted the Fellowship to be of one heart and soul, and she believed that disunity was one of the most dangerous threats to its life. That concern lay behind much of her strictness, and behind her difficulty with people like Stephen Neill who did not fit.

The ideal was a good one, and it produced a community of rare devotion. But the danger of such an ideal is that unity can come to mean uniformity, and that the leader’s will can come to be identified with the will of God. Amy was not blind to this danger, and she warned against it. But she did not always escape it. The story of the Fellowship in these years is the story of a remarkable community, held together by love and by a powerful leader, and it is also a reminder that even the best communities need ways of hearing those who disagree.

fields.title: The Pit at Kalakadu
fields.body_html:
“But he knoweth the way that I take; When he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.”

— Job 23:10, ASV

Sixty-Three

By 1931 Amy Carmichael was sixty-three years old. She had been in India for thirty-six years, without once going home. The household that had begun with one runaway child had become a Fellowship of several hundred people, with nurseries, schools, workshops, a boys’ compound and a hospital. She was still its leader, and she was still active: walking the compound, visiting the nurseries, teaching, writing, counselling, praying, and making decisions large and small. Outside it, in time, a bird-bath was placed, so that she could watch the birds that came to drink and bathe. She had always loved birds, and they became one of the pleasures of her confinement. It is natural to connect the fall with the prayer she had prayed, and many of those who have told her story have done so. She had asked God to do whatever would fit her for his service, and within a short time she was crippled. Was this the answer?

Amy herself came to believe that it was, in the sense that God had allowed it and would use it. She did not believe that God had pushed her into the pit, or that suffering was good in itself. But she believed that nothing came to her except through his hands, and that what came through his hands could be received as a gift, however hard. In the years that followed she wrote a great deal about suffering, about acceptance, and about the hidden purposes of God in pain, and much of it grew directly out of her own experience in that room.

It is worth being careful here, as she was. There is a kind of Christian talk about suffering that makes it too easy: that treats every disaster as a lesson, every illness as a blessing in disguise, and every unanswered prayer as part of a neat plan. Amy did not talk like that, at least not in her better moments. She admitted that she did not understand. She admitted that the pain was real and that it wore her down. She admitted that she longed to be up and about, and that the confinement was hard to bear. What she affirmed was not that she understood, but that she trusted. Amy had prayed many such prayers herself, for Ponnammal, for babies in the nurseries, for converts in danger, and she knew that “no” is also an answer. The child who had stood at a mirror in Millisle, disappointed to find her eyes still brown, now lay in a room in Dohnavur and learned the same lesson again, at much greater cost.

Losing Control

For a woman like Amy Carmichael, the hardest part of the fall may have been not the pain but the loss of control. She had always been the one who acted, who decided, who went to the nursery when a baby was ill, who walked down to the boys’ compound to settle a problem, who saw everything with her own eyes. Now she could see almost nothing except her own room and the garden outside its window. She had to depend on others to tell her what was happening, and to carry out her decisions.

That forced a change in the way the Fellowship was led. Others took on more and more of the daily work of leadership: the senior Indian and British members, among them Godfrey Webb-Peploe in the boys’ work and the doctors in the hospital. Amy remained the head of the Fellowship, consulted on everything and deciding the most important matters, and her authority was not diminished. But she could no longer be everywhere, and the Fellowship had to learn to work without her constant presence.

In the long run that was good for it. A work that depends entirely on one person is fragile, and Dohnavur would have to survive her death. The twenty years of her confinement gave others the experience and the authority they would need. Whether Amy saw it that way at the time is less clear. She found it hard to let go, and those around her sometimes found it hard to act without her.

Gold

Job’s words at the head of this chapter end with a promise: “When he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.” The image is of a refiner’s fire, in which gold is heated until the impurities rise to the surface and can be skimmed away. The fire does not destroy the gold; it purifies it.

It is the same image that had confronted Amy as a girl beside the fountain in Belfast, when the words about gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay and stubble came to her, and she learned that the fire would test what she had built. Now, at sixty-three, she was in the fire herself. What would come out of it?

The answer, as the next chapter will show, was a great deal. Out of the room to which she was confined came many of her most enduring books, a stream of letters to people all over the world, and a ministry of prayer and counsel that reached far beyond Dohnavur. Those who knew her in her last years spoke of a gentleness and a tenderness that had not always been so evident in the active years. The fire had done its work. fields.title: A Room at Dohnavur
fields.body_html:
“And he hath said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”

— 2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV

Twenty Years in a Room

For the last twenty years of her life, Amy Carmichael lived mostly in one room. It was not a sickroom in the gloomy Victorian sense. It had a window onto a garden, a bird-bath outside where she could watch the birds, books, flowers, and a constant coming and going of children and members of the Fellowship. But it was a room she could rarely leave. She was often in pain. She slept badly. There were long periods when she was too ill to do much at all. And she was aware, all the time, of the life of the Fellowship going on outside, in places she could no longer reach.

She did not waste those years. Out of that room came a stream of writing that has outlasted almost everything else she did, at least in the knowledge of the wider Christian world. And out of it came also a ministry of prayer, counsel and encouragement that held the Fellowship together and reached thousands of people far beyond it.

Gold Cord

The first major book she wrote after her fall was Gold Cord, published in 1932. It was her own history of the Dohnavur Fellowship, from Preena’s coming to the early 1930s. The title came from an image she loved: a cord of gold that bound the members of the Fellowship to God and to one another, made of many strands twisted together. The book is not a full or impartial history. It leaves out much, including, as we have seen, the episode with Stephen Neill, and it tells the story as Amy saw it, as an unfolding of God’s faithfulness. But it is the single most important source for the inner life of Dohnavur, and it shows the Fellowship as its founder wanted it to be seen.

It also shows how much she had come to depend on the community. The book is full of other people: the accals, the Sisters, the doctors and nurses, the boys’ workers, the children themselves. Amy was its narrator, but she was not its hero. She wanted the reader to see a family, held together by a golden cord, and not a missionary surrounded by admirers.

Books for the Suffering

In 1933 she published Rose from Brier, a book of letters and meditations for people who were ill or in pain. It grew out of notes she had written to patients in the Dohnavur hospital and to others who were suffering, and out of her own experience in the years since her fall. She had noticed, she said, that most books of comfort for the sick were written by people who were well, and that they often missed their mark. She wanted to write as one sufferer to another, honestly, without pretending that pain was easy or that faith made it painless.

The book was widely read, and it brought her letters from all over the world from people in hospitals and sickrooms who felt that she understood. She answered many of them. In the years that followed she wrote other books of meditation, verse and counsel, some drawn from the notes she wrote almost daily to members of the Fellowship. Many of these were collected and published after her death.

Notes and Letters

Much of what Amy wrote in these years was never meant for publication at all. Unable to walk the compound, she kept in touch with the members of the Fellowship by writing to them: short notes, often daily, sent across the compound by hand, offering a verse, a word of encouragement, a gentle rebuke, or simply a greeting. Members kept these notes, sometimes for decades, and many of them were later gathered into books. They show a leader who knew her people well and cared about the smallest details of their lives, and who could be tender and funny as well as searching.

She also wrote to friends and strangers outside the Fellowship, many of whom had written to her because of her books. Some were missionaries in difficulty; some were ill; some were young people trying to discern a call. She could not answer them all, but she answered many, and those letters carried her influence far beyond Dohnavur. A whole generation of evangelical missionaries, especially women, grew up reading her, and some of them went to the field because of her. Among her readers was a schoolgirl in America named Elisabeth Howard, who would later, as Elisabeth Elliot, write her life.

All of this was done from a bed or a chair, often through pain, and often on days when she could manage only a few lines. It was not the work she would have chosen. But it was work, and she did it faithfully.

If

The best known of all her books is a small one, published in 1938, with a one-word title: If. It grew, by the usual account, out of a conversation with a fellow worker about a difficulty in the Fellowship, and about what it means to love as Christ loved. Amy went away and wrote down, one after another, a series of short sentences, each beginning with the word “if,” each describing some small failure of love, and each ending with the same refrain, which measures that failure against the love of Calvary.

The sentences are searching, and they are meant to be. They do not deal with great sins but with small ones: irritation, sarcasm, self-pity, the wish to be noticed, the readiness to talk about another person’s faults, the reluctance to forgive. They hold up each of these against the love shown on the cross, and they leave the reader, as they left the writer, with nowhere to hide. Amy wrote them first for herself and her Fellowship, and she was aware that they condemned her as much as anyone. Their power lies partly in that. They are not the words of a saint looking down on sinners, but of a woman who knew her own temper, pride and impatience, and who had learned in the furnace of pain how much she still had to learn about love.

The book is still in print and still widely read, and it is, for many Christians, the only thing of Amy Carmichael’s they know. Its sentences are not quoted here, out of respect for the rights that may still attach to them; readers should find them in her own words.

Arulai

The years in the room brought further losses. The members of the first generation, those who had been with Amy from the Pannaivilai days, were growing old and dying. The hardest of these losses was Arulai, the girl convert who had grown into one of the leaders of the Fellowship, and on whom Amy had come to rely more than on almost anyone. Arulai died, after a long illness, in 1939. Amy grieved for her as she had grieved for Ponnammal, and she felt the loss of an Indian leader whom she had hoped would carry the Fellowship into the future.

The Second World War followed. India was drawn into it, and in 1942 Japanese forces advanced through Burma towards India’s eastern frontier, and Japanese ships and aircraft raided the eastern coast. For a time there was real fear in South India. Supplies were short, prices rose, and contact with friends in Britain was disrupted. The Fellowship carried on, as it had through the First World War, trusting God for its needs. Amy, in her room, prayed and wrote and led.

Independence and the Act

In August 1947 India became independent. Amy Carmichael had lived her whole Indian life under British rule, and now she saw it end. She did not leave, as many British people did. Dohnavur was her home, and the Fellowship had long been preparing for a future in which Indians would lead it. In the years that followed, Indian members took on more and more responsibility, and the Fellowship, like the Indian churches around it, adjusted to life in a new nation.

Two months later, in October 1947, the Madras Legislature passed the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act, which made it illegal to dedicate girls to temples in the Madras Presidency. It was the culmination of decades of campaigning by Indian reformers, above all Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, and it was passed by an Indian government in the first weeks of independence. Amy had spent nearly half a century working to protect children from the practice it outlawed. She lived to see it ended in law, though she knew that law alone would not end it in practice everywhere. Some popular accounts give the date of the act as 1948, and some give Amy the credit for it. Neither is quite right. The act was passed in 1947, and it was the work of Indian legislators. But it is not wrong to see her long witness as one of the many streams that fed it.

Power Made Perfect in Weakness

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s account of what he learned when he asked three times to be freed from what he called a thorn in the flesh, and was refused. “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Paul’s response was not resignation but a strange kind of boasting: “Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”

Amy Carmichael knew that verse, and in her last twenty years she lived it. She had asked for healing, and she had not been healed. She had been an active, strong-willed leader, and she had been made weak. But out of that weakness came the books by which most of the world now knows her, a deepened gentleness that those around her noticed, and a Fellowship that learned to stand on its own. She did not pretend that weakness was pleasant. But she found, as Paul had found, that it was a place where the power of Christ could rest.

It was the culmination of decades of campaigning by Indian reformers, above all Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, and it was passed by an Indian government in the first weeks of independence. Amy had spent nearly half a century working to protect children from the practice it outlawed. She lived to see it ended in law, though she knew that law alone would not end it in practice everywhere. Some popular accounts give the date of the act as 1948, and some give Amy the credit for it. Neither is quite right. The act was passed in 1947, and it was the work of Indian legislators. But it is not wrong to see her long witness as one of the many streams that fed it. Power Made Perfect in Weakness The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s account of what he learned when he asked three times to be freed from what he called a thorn in the flesh, and was refused. “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Paul’s response was not resignation but a strange kind of boasting: “Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” Amy Carmichael knew that verse, and in her last twenty years she lived it. She had asked for healing, and she had not been healed. She had been an active, strong-willed leader, and she had been made weak. But out of that weakness came the books by which most of the world now knows her, a deepened gentleness that those around her noticed, and a Fellowship that learned to stand on its own. She did not pretend that weakness was pleasant. But she found, as Paul had found, that it was a place where the power of Christ could rest.

fields.title: God’s Garden
fields.body_html:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit.”

— John 12:24, ASV

18 January 1951

Amy Carmichael died at Dohnavur on 18 January 1951. She was eighty-three years old. She had lived in India for fifty-five years, and for the last nineteen of them she had been largely confined to her room. Her final illness was long, and in her last months she was very weak and often not fully conscious. Those who cared for her were members of the family she had built: Indian and British women and men who had grown up at Dohnavur or come to join it, and who had learned from her what it meant to give their lives for others.

She had left instructions about her funeral and her grave. She did not want a monument. She did not want a stone with her name and dates and a list of her achievements. She was buried in the Fellowship’s own burial ground, which was known as God’s Garden, among the children and workers who had gone before her. Over the grave the Fellowship placed a bird-bath, like the one she had watched from her window for twenty years, and on it they inscribed a single word: Amma.

It was exactly right. She had been called many things in her life: Miss Carmichael, Miss Wilson-Carmichael, the Missie Ammal, the child-stealing Ammal, the founder of the Dohnavur Fellowship. But the name that mattered to her, and to the people who loved her, was the one the children had given her. She had been their mother.

The Fellowship After Her

The great test of any work built around a strong founder is what happens when the founder dies. Many such works decline or collapse, because no one can take the founder’s place and the community cannot agree on how to go on without her. Amy had thought about this for many years, and the twenty years of her confinement had given others the experience they needed to lead. The Dohnavur Fellowship survived her death, and it continues today.

It has changed, as it was bound to. Indian leadership, which Amy had long intended, became complete. The temple dedication that first brought children to Dohnavur was outlawed, and the needs of the children and families it serves have changed with the times. The Fellowship today works in Tamil Nadu with children and families, offering care, education and medical help in a Christian setting, on the land at the foot of the mountains where Amy lived. The hospital still serves the villages around. The work is smaller in some respects and different in many, but it is recognisably the same family.

The Books

Amy Carmichael’s books have also outlived her. Many of them are still in print, and they continue to be read by Christians all over the world, especially those drawn to her teaching on prayer, suffering, obedience and love. If remains the best known. Gold Cord and Rose from Brier are still read. The early books, Things as They Are and Lotus Buds among them, are now in the public domain, and they are read today both as Christian classics and as historical documents of missionary life in South India at the turn of the twentieth century.

Her influence on later missionaries has been considerable. A generation of women missionaries, in particular, found in her an example of a single woman who did serious and lasting work, who refused to be confined to the roles that missionary societies expected of women, and who wrote about the cost of discipleship without sentimentality. Elisabeth Elliot, whose life is told in the previous volume of this series, was one of them, and her biography of Amy Carmichael introduced her to a new generation of readers in the 1980s.

Remembered at Home

She never went back to Ireland, but Ireland has not forgotten her. In Belfast the congregation that grew from the Welcome Hall still meets off the Shankill Road, and it has opened a centre in her name where visitors can learn her story. The Ulster History Circle, which marks the places associated with notable people from the north of Ireland, has honoured her with one of its blue plaques. In Millisle, the village by the sea where she was born, her name is known and her story is told. It is a modest kind of fame, and she would probably have disliked it. But it is a reminder that the woman who became Amma to the children of a Tamil village began as the eldest daughter of a miller in County Down, and that the faith she carried to India was first given to her there.

She is remembered in other places too, often in small ways: in the names of schools and mission houses, in hymnbooks that include her verses, and in the private libraries of Christians who keep her books by their beds. The memory that would have mattered most to her, though, is the one kept at Dohnavur, among the people who still call that place home.

Weighing the Life

A biography that has tried to be honest throughout should try to be honest at the end. How should Amy Carmichael’s life be weighed?

On one side, the achievements are great. She gave half a century to the care of children whom almost nobody else would take, and she gave them not only food and shelter but a home, a family, an education and a faith. Hundreds of children, perhaps more than a thousand in all over the years, grew up at Dohnavur who might otherwise have faced lives of exploitation, neglect or early death. She did it without salary, without appeals, and without ever going home. She built a community that has outlasted her by more than seventy years. And she wrote books that have helped many thousands of Christians to pray, to endure suffering, and to love more truly.

On the other side, there are shadows, and this book has tried not to hide them. Her writing about Hinduism was often harsh and sometimes unfair, and it contributed to a picture of Indian religion and of the women of the temple communities that did harm. She ran Dohnavur with an authority that some found overbearing, and she did not easily share power or tolerate disagreement, as the episode with Stephen Neill shows. The protective walls of Dohnavur, necessary in the early years, may have stayed high longer than they needed to, and some of the children who grew up there found it hard to make their way in the world outside. She was a woman of her time and her empire, and she shared some of its blind spots.

Those shadows are real, and they should not be explained away. But they do not cancel the light. Every human life, including every Christian life, is a mixture of faithfulness and failure, insight and blindness, love and self-will. The question is not whether Amy Carmichael was perfect, but whether she was faithful, and whether God worked through her. On both counts the answer seems clear.

A Grain of Wheat

The verse at the head of this chapter was spoken by Jesus in the last week of his life, when some Greeks came asking to see him. He answered with a saying about a grain of wheat: unless it falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. He was speaking first of himself, and of the death he was about to die. But he went on at once to speak of his followers: “He that loveth his life loseth it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal” (John 12:25, ASV).

Amy Carmichael took that saying as a pattern for her life. The phrase most often associated with her, that missionary life is simply a chance to die, is an echo of it. She did not mean that missionaries should seek death, or despise life. She meant that the missionary’s calling is to let go of self: of comfort, of home, of reputation, of control, of the life one would have chosen. She let go of a great deal. She let go of Belfast and the Welcome Hall, of Robert Wilson and Broughton Grange, of Japan and the village work she loved, of her mother, of her health, and finally of her active leadership. Each time, something died. And each time, she believed, something grew.

Amma

This book began with a verse about a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to look for one that is lost, and with the words of Jesus: “it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.” It is fitting to end there.

Amy Carmichael’s great work began with one child. Preena did not come to Dohnavur as part of a programme or a strategy. She came because she had heard that there was a woman who took children in, and she walked through the dark to find her. Amy took her in, at some risk, because she believed that this one child mattered to God. Everything else followed from that: the nurseries, the boys’ compound, the hospital, the Fellowship, the books. But it began with one.

The bird-bath over her grave in God’s Garden bears one word, and it is not her name. It is the name that one runaway child, and hundreds after her, gave to the woman who opened the door. Amy Carmichael would not have wanted to be remembered as a heroine, a saint, or a legend. She would have wanted to be remembered, if at all, as a mother, and as a witness to the Father who does not will that one of these little ones should perish. That is how she is remembered at Dohnavur still.

fields.title: Appendix a: Lessons from the Life of Amy Carmichael
fields.body_html:
“Remember them that had the rule over you, men that spake unto you the word of God; and considering the issue of their life, imitate their faith.”

— Hebrews 13:7, ASV

The lessons below gather up the themes of this book so that readers can return to them. Amy Carmichael would not have wanted her life to be a pattern. She would have wanted it to point beyond herself to the God who, she believed, had led her every step of the way. Each lesson therefore rests on Scripture, not on her example alone. The letter to the Hebrews tells us to consider how those who went before us lived and died, and to imitate their faith, not every detail of their lives. Some of the lessons below come from her failures as well as her faithfulness.

1. No Is Also an Answer

The child who prayed for blue eyes learned that God hears every prayer, and that he is free to say no. She learned the same lesson again in a sickroom sixty years later. “What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt understand hereafter” (John 13:7, ASV).

2. Faith Must Become One’s Own

Amy grew up in a home full of faith, but at fifteen, at a children’s mission in Harrogate, she received the love of God for herself. “Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee” (Jeremiah 31:3, ASV).

3. Build With What Will Last

An old woman’s bundle, carried through the streets of Belfast, taught her that respectability is stubble and love is gold. “The fire itself shall prove each man’s work of what sort it is” (1 Corinthians 3:13, ASV).

4. Christ Is the Keeper

At a convention in Glasgow she learned that the Christian life is not a strain after holiness but a trust in the one who is able to keep us. “Now unto him that is able to guard you from stumbling … be glory” (Jude 24-25, ASV).

5. Go Where the Poor Are

She built a hall for girls too poor to wear hats, and lived in a slum to be near the mill girls of Manchester. “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor” (Luke 14:21, ASV).

6. God Sets the Solitary in Families

An old Quaker took her into his home when she was worn out, and she spent her life doing the same for children with nowhere to go. “God setteth the solitary in families” (Psalm 68:6, ASV).

7. A Shut Door Is Not a Withdrawn Call

The China Inland Mission turned her down, her health failed in Japan, and she was called home from Ceylon. She went on believing that she had been sent. “Trust in Jehovah with all thy heart, And lean not upon thine own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5, ASV).

8. Do Not Let Your Clothes Get in the Way

A pair of fur gloves taught her that foreign habits can distract from the gospel. She wore a kimono in Japan and a sari in India. “I am become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22, ASV).

9. Faithfulness, Not Success

Most days in the villages ended as they began. She held on to the text that says stewards must be found faithful, and thanked God that it did not say successful. “Here, moreover, it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2, ASV).

10. Tell the Truth

Things as They Are told readers at home what they did not want to hear. Honesty about the cost and slowness of the work was, she believed, the foundation of true prayer. “For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth” (2 Corinthians 13:8, ASV).

11. Speak Fairly of Those You Oppose

Her writing about Hinduism was often harsh, and it gave real offence. A Christian witness is weakened, not strengthened, by caricature of others’ faith. “But speaking truth in love, may grow up in all things into him, who is the head, even Christ” (Ephesians 4:15, ASV).

12. Count the Cost, and Do Not Hide It

Converts in caste India often lost home, family and inheritance. She did not hide that cost from them or from her readers. “If any man would come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23, ASV).

13. One Child Matters

Her great work began with a single runaway girl who climbed onto her knee. “Whosoever shall receive one of such little children in my name, receiveth me” (Mark 9:37, ASV).

14. Speak for Those Who Cannot Speak

She gave her life to protecting children whose futures had been decided for them before they could understand. “Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate” (Proverbs 31:8, ASV).

15. Honour Those Who Fought Beside You

The end of temple dedication was won above all by Indian reformers. Christians should be glad to honour the good done by others, and slow to claim credit for themselves. “Love vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up” (1 Corinthians 13:4, ASV).

16. Let the Plan Go

She came to India to preach in the villages, and found herself caring for babies. She let her own plan go and took the work God gave her. “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might” (Ecclesiastes 9:10, ASV).

17. Wait for God’s Time

She prayed for six years about the boys before the first boy came. “Wait for Jehovah: Be strong, and let thy heart take courage; Yea, wait thou for Jehovah” (Psalm 27:14, ASV).

18. Tell Your Needs to God

Dohnavur made no appeals for money and testified that it never lacked what it needed. Those who follow her in this should beware of asking by not asking. “And my God shall supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19, ASV).

19. Lead Without Lording It

Her strength built Dohnavur, and her difficulty in sharing authority cost it Stephen Neill and caused others pain. “Neither as lording it over the charge allotted to you, but making yourselves ensamples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3, ASV).

20. In Christ There Is No Caste

At Dohnavur children of every community ate, slept and prayed together as sisters and brothers. “There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, ASV).

21. Weakness Is Not Wasted

Twenty years in a room produced her most enduring books and a deeper gentleness. “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV).

22. Love Is Tested in Small Things

Her best-known book measures small failures of love against the love of Calvary. “Love suffereth long, and is kind; love envieth not … seeketh not its own, is not provoked, taketh not account of evil” (1 Corinthians 13:4-5, ASV).

23. Except a Grain of Wheat Die

She let go of home, work, health and control, and believed that each letting go bore fruit. “Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit” (John 12:24, ASV).

24. Be Remembered as Love

Over her grave there is no name, only the word the children gave her. The greatest honour a Christian can receive is to have loved well. “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13, ASV).

Those who follow her in this should beware of asking by not asking. “And my God shall supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19, ASV). 19. Lead Without Lording It Her strength built Dohnavur, and her difficulty in sharing authority cost it Stephen Neill and caused others pain. “Neither as lording it over the charge allotted to you, but making yourselves ensamples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3, ASV). 20. In Christ There Is No Caste At Dohnavur children of every community ate, slept and prayed together as sisters and brothers. “There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, ASV). 21. Weakness Is Not Wasted Twenty years in a room produced her most enduring books and a deeper gentleness. “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV). 22. Love Is Tested in Small Things Her best-known book measures small failures of love against the love of Calvary. “Love suffereth long, and is kind; love envieth not … seeketh not its own, is not provoked, taketh not account of evil” (1 Corinthians 13:4-5, ASV). 23. Except a Grain of Wheat Die She let go of home, work, health and control, and believed that each letting go bore fruit. “Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit” (John 12:24, ASV). 24. Be Remembered as Love Over her grave there is no name, only the word the children gave her. The greatest honour a Christian can receive is to have loved well. “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13, ASV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

— James 1:22, ASV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty-four weeks. Its purpose is not to make Amy Carmichael an object of admiration, but to let her life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer. Some chapters, especially those on Things as They Are and on temple dedication, raise hard questions about mission, culture and the way Christians speak of other faiths. They are meant to be discussed honestly and charitably, not settled quickly.

Introduction - The Legend and Her Own Books

Central idea

The real Amy Carmichael, as her own books and the record show her, is more instructive than the legend that has grown around her.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 13:8; John 8:32.

Reflection

1. Which stories about Christian heroes have you heard that may have grown in the telling? 2. Why does it matter whether a story is accurate, if it inspires?

Chapter 1 - Brown Eyes

Central idea

A strong-willed child in a home of faith learned that God hears every prayer and is free to say no.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 139:13-14; Matthew 7:9-11.

Reflection

1. Can you remember a prayer that was answered with no? How did you receive it? 2. What did your own upbringing give you that you still use?

Chapter 2 - Harrogate

Central idea

At fifteen, at a children’s mission, a girl who had always known about Christ received his love for herself.

Scriptures to revisit

Jeremiah 31:3; Mark 10:13-16.

Reflection

1. When did faith become your own, rather than your parents’? 2. How seriously does your church take the faith of children?

Chapter 3 - Gold, Silver, Costly Stones

Central idea

A moment of embarrassment in a Belfast street and a prayer in a Glasgow hall gave her a direction and a source of strength.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Corinthians 3:10-15; Jude 24-25.

Reflection

1. What are you building with your life, and how will it stand the fire? 2. Where does fear of others’ opinion keep you from doing good?

Chapter 4 - The Shawlies

Central idea

She went out to the mill girls the churches overlooked and built them a hall called the Welcome.

Scriptures to revisit

Luke 14:15-24; James 2:1-9.

Reflection

1. Who are the “shawlies” of your town? 2. What would it take for them to feel truly welcome in your church?

Chapter 5 - The Dear Old Man

Central idea

Broken in health in Manchester, she was taken into Robert Wilson’s home and given a new family.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 68:5-6; Ruth 1:16-17.

Reflection

1. Who has been a spiritual father or mother to you? 2. How might you set someone solitary in a family?

Chapter 6 - “Go Ye”

Central idea

A familiar command became a personal call, and it cost her mother and Robert Wilson as much as it cost her.

Scriptures to revisit

Mark 16:15; Luke 14:25-33.

Reflection

1. How do you discern between a call from God and your own desire? 2. What does it cost those who love us when we obey God?

Chapter 7 - Sunrise Land

Central idea

Fifteen months in Japan taught her about identification, slowness, and the faithfulness of God in loneliness.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 113:3; Psalm 34:22; 1 Corinthians 9:19-23.

Reflection

1. What might be the “fur gloves” in your witness? 2. How do you face the fear of loneliness?

Chapter 8 - A Door Shut, a Door Opened

Central idea

After Ceylon and a summons home, a new society sent her to India, where she would stay for fifty-five years.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 3:5-6; Acts 16:6-10.

Reflection

1. Looking back, can you see guidance in what seemed at the time like false starts? 2. Where do you need to submit your sense of God’s leading to the counsel of others?

Chapter 9 - Bangalore

Central idea

Dismayed by the comfortable life of a missionary station, she resolved not to be pressed into its mould, and found a teacher in Thomas Walker.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 12:1-2; Philippians 2:5-8.

Reflection

1. Where has the culture around you pressed your faith into its mould? 2. Is it possible to resist one mould only to be pressed into another?

Chapter 10 - The Starry Cluster

Central idea

With a band of Indian women she travelled the villages, and learned that most days end as they began.

Scriptures to revisit

Daniel 12:3; 1 Corinthians 4:1-2.

Reflection

1. How do you keep going when there are no visible results? 2. What is the place of “simple witness” in your life?

Chapter 11 - The Cost of One Soul

Central idea

Converts in caste India often lost everything, and some died young; she believed it was worth it.

Scriptures to revisit

Mark 10:28-31; Matthew 10:34-39.

Reflection

1. What has following Christ cost you? 2. How can Christians honour the grief of families who lose a child to another faith?

Chapter 12 - Pearl-Eyes

Central idea

A runaway child walked through the dark to find the “child-stealing Ammal,” and Amy took the risk of keeping her.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 10:14-18; Matthew 18:10-14.

Reflection

1. Where do you see God’s care in the timing of events in your life? 2. What risks would you take for one child?

Chapter 13 - Dohnavur

Central idea

A village founded as a refuge became the home of a new family, and Amy let her own plan go.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 16:5-6; Numbers 35:9-15.

Reflection

1. Have you had to give up a work you loved for one you did not choose? 2. What makes a place a true refuge?

Chapter 14 - Things as They Are

Central idea

Her first India book told the truth about the work, and was both doubted and confirmed.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 4:1-2; Ephesians 4:15.

Reflection

1. Why do we prefer encouraging stories to true ones? 2. How would a Hindu reader have felt reading this book, and what can we learn from that?

Chapter 15 - Servants of the Gods

Central idea

The system of temple dedication, its history, its abuses, and the Indian reformers who ended it in law.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 24:11-12; Isaiah 1:17.

Reflection

1. Once we know of an injustice, what is our responsibility? 2. How can Christians oppose an evil without slandering the people caught up in it?

Chapter 16 - Lotus Buds

Central idea

Babies began to come, and the household grew into a family that she loved and delighted in.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 40:11; Mark 10:13-16.

Reflection

1. What can children teach adults about faith? 2. How do you hold together strength and gentleness?

Chapter 17 - Amma

Central idea

She tried to make Dohnavur a home, not an institution, and to give the children Indian lives in Christ.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Thessalonians 2:7-12; Galatians 3:28.

Reflection

1. What is the difference between a home and an institution? 2. Where do strictness and love meet, and where do they part?

Chapter 18 - The Sorrowful Years

Central idea

Between 1912 and 1915 she lost Walker, her mother and Ponnammal, and faced the shadow of the courts.

Scriptures to revisit

John 13:1-7; 2 Corinthians 1:3-7.

Reflection

1. How do you go on when those you depend on are taken? 2. What is the difference between acceptance and resignation?

Chapter 19 - Boys

Central idea

She prayed six years about the boys before the first came, and befriended a hunted outlaw.

Scriptures to revisit

Genesis 21:14-20; Psalm 27:14.

Reflection

1. What have you been praying about for years? 2. Whom are you inclined to write off as beyond help?

Chapter 20 - A Fellowship and Its Cost

Central idea

The Sisters of the Common Life, independence, the hospital, and the painful parting with Stephen Neill.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 4:32-35; 1 Peter 5:1-5.

Reflection

1. How can a strong community hear those who disagree? 2. Is unity the same as uniformity?

Chapter 21 - The Pit at Kalakadu

Central idea

A fall in 1931 laid her aside for the rest of her life, and forced others to lead.

Scriptures to revisit

Job 23:8-10; Romans 8:28.

Reflection

1. How do you respond when God answers a prayer of surrender in a way you did not expect? 2. What would happen to the work you lead if you were laid aside tomorrow?

Chapter 22 - A Room at Dohnavur

Central idea

From one room came her most lasting books, a ministry of letters, and a gentleness the fire had refined.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 12:7-10; 1 Corinthians 13:4-7.

Reflection

1. What small failures of love would you have to confess? 2. How can weakness become a place of fruitfulness?

Chapter 23 - God’s Garden

Central idea

She died in 1951 and was buried under one word; her life is weighed with its light and its shadows.

Scriptures to revisit

John 12:23-26; Hebrews 13:7.

Reflection

1. What would you want written over your grave? 2. Which part of her faith, not her methods, is God calling you to imitate?

For the Whole Book

Central idea

A life given to one child at a time, with its faithfulness and its failures, points beyond itself to the Father who does not will that one of these little ones should perish.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 18:10-14; 2 Corinthians 4:7.

Reflection

1. What has this life taught you about the cost and the joy of following Christ? 2. What one thing will you do differently because you have read it?

fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of Amy Carmichael
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.”

— Psalm 90:12, ASV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Dates given in Amy Carmichael’s own early books, or agreed by the main sources, are given plainly. Where the sources disagree, the disagreement is noted. Where a date rests only on the later biographies, it is marked as such.

1820s - Dohnavur Founded

The German missionary Charles Rhenius, of the Church Missionary Society, founds Dohnavur in the Tinnevelly district as a refuge for persecuted converts, named after a Prussian benefactor, Count Dohna.

1859 - The Ulster Revival

A great religious revival sweeps the Presbyterian north of Ireland, shaping the piety of the generation into which Amy is born.

1867 - Birth

Amy Beatrice Carmichael is born on 16 December at Millisle, County Down, the eldest of seven children of David Carmichael, miller, and Catherine Jane Filson. The Children’s Special Service Mission is founded the same year.

1875 - The Keswick Convention

Canon T. D. Harford-Battersby and Robert Wilson found the Keswick Convention for the deepening of spiritual life.

c. 1880-1883 - Harrogate

Amy attends a Methodist girls’ boarding school in Harrogate, Yorkshire.

1883 - Conversion

At about fifteen she puts her trust in Christ at a children’s mission in Harrogate. Some sources give 1882; most give 1883.

c. 1883 - Belfast

The family, whose milling business is in decline, moves to Belfast. Accounts differ on the exact year.

1885 - Her Father’s Death

David Carmichael dies, leaving the family in financial difficulty. About this time Amy begins to suffer from neuralgia.

Mid-1880s - The Fountain and the Shawlies

On a Sunday morning in Belfast the words of 1 Corinthians 3:12-14 confront her as she helps an old woman with a bundle. She begins a Sunday class for the shawlies, the mill girls, at Rosemary Street Presbyterian Church.

1886 - Glasgow

At a convention in Glasgow she receives an assurance, from the words of Jude 24, that Christ is able to keep her.

1887 - Keswick

She attends the Keswick Convention and hears Hudson Taylor. She probably first meets Robert Wilson about this time.

1887 or 1889 - The Welcome Hall

An iron hall for the shawlies, paid for by a gift of five hundred pounds, is opened at Cambrai Street, Belfast, and named the Welcome. Some sources give 1887; others give the opening as January 1889.

1889 - Manchester

Amy and her mother move to Manchester to work among mill girls. Amy lives in a poor district, and her health breaks down.

1890 - Broughton Grange

She goes to live with Robert Wilson at Broughton Grange, Cumberland, as his companion and adopted daughter in all but law, and later takes the name Wilson-Carmichael.

1892 - The Call

On 13 January, at Broughton Grange, she becomes convinced that she is called to go overseas. She applies to the China Inland Mission and is rejected on medical grounds. The Keswick Convention agrees to send her as its first missionary.

1893-1894 - Japan

She sails in March 1893 and joins Barclay Buxton’s band at Matsue, Japan. She stays about fifteen months, and leaves in the summer of 1894 in poor health.

1894 - Ceylon and Home

A short stay in Ceylon ends when news reaches her late in the year that Robert Wilson has had a stroke. She returns to England by the end of 1894.

1895 - India

From Sunrise Land is published. Accepted by the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society, she sails for India in October and arrives at Madras in November. She goes to Bangalore to learn Tamil.

1896 - Tinnevelly

She joins Thomas Walker of the Church Missionary Society and his wife in the Tinnevelly district, first at Palamcottah and then at Pannaivilai.

1897-1901 - The Band

With Ponnammal and other Indian women she travels the villages as an itinerant band. A small number of converts, among them Arulai, join the household. Part of 1900 is spent at Dohnavur.

1901 - Preena

A seven-year-old girl who has run away from a temple household arrives at Pannaivilai; she is brought to Amy, by the usual date, on 7 March. Later that year the household settles at Dohnavur.

1901-1902 - Visitors

Two friends from home visit and persuade her to make her letters into a book.

1903 - Things as They Are

Published in April by Morgan and Scott, with a preface by Eugene Stock; reprinted in August 1903 and in following years. A later edition adds confirmatory notes from missionaries and from Pandita Ramabai.

c. 1904 - Babies

Babies begin to be brought to Dohnavur, and nurseries are built over the following years.

1905 - Robert Wilson’s Death

The Dear Old Man dies in England.

1906 - Overweights of Joy

A sequel to Things as They Are, telling the joys of the work.

1909 - Lotus Buds

Published in November with fifty photographs of the children of Dohnavur.

1912 - Walker’s Death

Thomas Walker dies in August, away from Dohnavur. A dispute over land and a compound wall follows. About this time Amy begins to pray about boys in danger.

1913 - Her Mother’s Death

Catherine Carmichael dies in England on 14 July. About a hundred and thirty children are now in the family at Dohnavur.

c. 1914 - A Charge of Kidnapping

According to the later biographies, a charge is brought in connection with a girl named Muttammal, and Amy faces possible arrest; the case is eventually dropped. The First World War begins in August.

1915 - Ponnammal’s Death

Ponnammal dies after a long illness.

1916 - Sisters of the Common Life; Walker of Tinnevelly

In March Amy forms the Sisters of the Common Life. Her memoir of Thomas Walker is published.

1918 - The First Boy

In January a baby boy is brought to Dohnavur, and the boys’ work begins. Ponnammal: Her Story is published about this time.

Early 1920s - Raj

She comes to know the outlaw she calls Raj, who is later killed by the police. Raj, Brigand Chief follows in 1927. Ragland, Spiritual Pioneer is published in 1922 and Mimosa in 1924.

1924-1925 - Stephen Neill

Stephen Neill works at Dohnavur and leaves in November 1925 after a painful disagreement.

1925-1927 - Independence

The link with the Zenana Society ends in 1925. The Dohnavur Fellowship is registered in 1927.

Late 1920s - The Hospital

With doctors among its members, the Fellowship opens its own hospital, named in Tamil the Place of Heavenly Healing.

1930 - Reform Stalls

Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, who has brought forward proposals to end temple dedication in the Madras Legislative Council, resigns her seat in protest at Gandhi’s arrest; the bill lies dormant.

1931 - The Fall

On 24 October she falls into an uncovered pit in a building being prepared for the work, at Kalakadu according to her biographers, breaking her leg, dislocating her ankle and injuring her spine. She is largely confined to her room for the rest of her life.

1932-1938 - Books from a Room

Gold Cord (1932), Rose from Brier (1933) and If (1938), among others.

1939 - Arulai’s Death

Arulai, one of the leaders of the Fellowship, dies after a long illness. The Second World War begins.

1947 - Independence and the Madras Act

India becomes independent on 15 August. On 9 October the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act is passed, outlawing the dedication of girls to temples in the Madras Presidency. Popular accounts sometimes give 1948.

1951 - Death

Amy Carmichael dies at Dohnavur on 18 January, aged eighty-three, and is buried in God’s Garden under a bird-bath inscribed Amma.

1953 and After

Frank Houghton’s Amy Carmichael of Dohnavur is published (1953), followed in later decades by Elisabeth Elliot’s A Chance to Die (1987) and Iain Murray’s Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes (2015). The Dohnavur Fellowship continues its work in Tamil Nadu under Indian leadership.

Amy lives in a poor district, and her health breaks down. 1890 - Broughton Grange She goes to live with Robert Wilson at Broughton Grange, Cumberland, as his companion and adopted daughter in all but law, and later takes the name Wilson-Carmichael. 1892 - The Call On 13 January, at Broughton Grange, she becomes convinced that she is called to go overseas. She applies to the China Inland Mission and is rejected on medical grounds. The Keswick Convention agrees to send her as its first missionary. 1893-1894 - Japan She sails in March 1893 and joins Barclay Buxton’s band at Matsue, Japan. She stays about fifteen months, and leaves in the summer of 1894 in poor health. 1894 - Ceylon and Home A short stay in Ceylon ends when news reaches her late in the year that Robert Wilson has had a stroke. She returns to England by the end of 1894. 1895 - India From Sunrise Land is published. Accepted by the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society, she sails for India in October and arrives at Madras in November. She goes to Bangalore to learn Tamil. 1896 - Tinnevelly She joins Thomas Walker of the Church Missionary Society and his wife in the Tinnevelly district, first at Palamcottah and then at Pannaivilai. 1897-1901 - The Band With Ponnammal and other Indian women she travels the villages as an itinerant band. A small number of converts, among them Arulai, join the household. Part of 1900 is spent at Dohnavur. 1901 - Preena A seven-year-old girl who has run away from a temple household arrives at Pannaivilai; she is brought to Amy, by the usual date, on 7 March. Later that year the household settles at Dohnavur. 1901-1902 - Visitors Two friends from home visit and persuade her to make her letters into a book. 1903 - Things as They Are Published in April by Morgan and Scott, with a preface by Eugene Stock; reprinted in August 1903 and in following years. A later edition adds confirmatory notes from missionaries and from Pandita Ramabai. c. 1904 - Babies Babies begin to be brought to Dohnavur, and nurseries are built over the following years. 1905 - Robert Wilson’s Death The Dear Old Man dies in England. 1906 - Overweights of Joy A sequel to Things as They Are, telling the joys of the work. 1909 - Lotus Buds Published in November with fifty photographs of the children of Dohnavur. 1912 - Walker’s Death Thomas Walker dies in August, away from Dohnavur. A dispute over land and a compound wall follows. About this time Amy begins to pray about boys in danger. 1913 - Her Mother’s Death Catherine Carmichael dies in England on 14 July. About a hundred and thirty children are now in the family at Dohnavur. c. 1914 - A Charge of Kidnapping According to the later biographies, a charge is brought in connection with a girl named Muttammal, and Amy faces possible arrest; the case is eventually dropped. The First World War begins in August. 1915 - Ponnammal’s Death Ponnammal dies after a long illness. 1916 - Sisters of the Common Life; Walker of Tinnevelly In March Amy forms the Sisters of the Common Life. Her memoir of Thomas Walker is published. 1918 - The First Boy In January a baby boy is brought to Dohnavur, and the boys’ work begins. Ponnammal: Her Story is published about this time. Early 1920s - Raj She comes to know the outlaw she calls Raj, who is later killed by the police. Raj, Brigand Chief follows in 1927. Ragland, Spiritual Pioneer is published in 1922 and Mimosa in 1924. 1924-1925 - Stephen Neill Stephen Neill works at Dohnavur and leaves in November 1925 after a painful disagreement. 1925-1927 - Independence The link with the Zenana Society ends in 1925. The Dohnavur Fellowship is registered in 1927. Late 1920s - The Hospital With doctors among its members, the Fellowship opens its own hospital, named in Tamil the Place of Heavenly Healing. 1930 - Reform Stalls Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, who has brought forward proposals to end temple dedication in the Madras Legislative Council, resigns her seat in protest at Gandhi’s arrest; the bill lies dormant. 1931 - The Fall On 24 October she falls into an uncovered pit in a building being prepared for the work, at Kalakadu according to her biographers, breaking her leg, dislocating her ankle and injuring her spine. She is largely confined to her room for the rest of her life. 1932-1938 - Books from a Room Gold Cord (1932), Rose from Brier (1933) and If (1938), among others. 1939 - Arulai’s Death Arulai, one of the leaders of the Fellowship, dies after a long illness. The Second World War begins. 1947 - Independence and the Madras Act India becomes independent on 15 August. On 9 October the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act is passed, outlawing the dedication of girls to temples in the Madras Presidency. Popular accounts sometimes give 1948. 1951 - Death Amy Carmichael dies at Dohnavur on 18 January, aged eighty-three, and is buried in God’s Garden under a bird-bath inscribed Amma. 1953 and After Frank Houghton’s Amy Carmichael of Dohnavur is published (1953), followed in later decades by Elisabeth Elliot’s A Chance to Die (1987) and Iain Murray’s Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes (2015). The Dohnavur Fellowship continues its work in Tamil Nadu under Indian leadership.

fields.title: Appendix D: Notes on Sources and Method
fields.body_html:
“it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write unto thee in order … that thou mightest know the certainty concerning the things wherein thou wast instructed.”

— Luke 1:3-4, ASV

This appendix explains where the story told in this book comes from, how the sources were weighed, and which popular claims have been corrected or qualified. It is written for readers who want to check the story for themselves, and for anyone who will retell it.

Her Own Books

The first source for Amy Carmichael’s life is her own writing. This book has quoted directly only from her books published before 1929, which are in the public domain in the United States, and almost all the quotations come from one of them: Things as They Are: Mission Work in Southern India (London: Morgan and Scott, 1903), the text of which is in the Ochorus library. That book was written from the field in 1901 and 1902, and its account of Preena’s arrival, given under the name Pearl-eyes, is the earliest that survives. Quotations from it have been checked against the Ochorus text, including the later edition’s confirmatory notes and Eugene Stock’s preface.

Her other early books, From Sunrise Land (1895), Overweights of Joy (1906), Lotus Buds (1909), Walker of Tinnevelly (1916) and Ragland, Spiritual Pioneer (1922), are named and described but not quoted. Her later books, including Gold Cord (1932), Rose from Brier (1933) and If (1938), may still be in copyright in some countries, and they are named so that readers can find them, but they are not quoted. Where this book reports the substance of them, it does so in its own words.

Her books must be read as what they are: writing for supporters, shaped by a strong evangelical conviction, often using translated or changed names, and openly selective. She said repeatedly that she was leaving much out. Where this book relies on her account, it says so.

The Biographies

Frank Houghton, Amy Carmichael of Dohnavur (1953), and Elisabeth Elliot, A Chance to Die: The Life and Legacy of Amy Carmichael (1987), are the standard lives, and Iain H. Murray, Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes (2015), is a more recent one. All are in copyright. This book has used them, and summaries of them, only as guides to facts and dates, and has neither quoted them nor followed their wording. Several details in this book rest chiefly on them, and are marked in the text with phrases such as “her biographers record”: among them the comet at Harrogate, the fountain in Belfast, the Glasgow convention, the fur gloves in Japan, the cave, the coffee-stained skin, the Muttammal case, the place of her fall, and the story of Raj.

Scholarship and Reference

For the controversy with Stephen Neill, this book has drawn on Dyron B. Daughrity, “A Dissonant Mission: Stephen Neill, Amy Carmichael, and Missionary Conflict in South India,” International Review of Mission (2008). For the history of temple dedication and its abolition, it has drawn on the general literature on the devadasi reform movement in the Madras Presidency, and in particular on the arguments of Davesh Soneji, Unfinished Gestures: Devadasis, Memory, and Modernity in South India (2012), together with standard accounts of the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of 1947, Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy and Moovalur Ramamirtham. Reference works, encyclopedia entries, the Dohnavur Fellowship’s own published material, and the materials of the Welcome Evangelical Church in Belfast have been used for orientation. None of these modern works is reproduced here.

Corrections and Qualifications

The burned hands. Popular accounts say Preena’s hands were branded as a punishment for her first escape. Amy’s 1903 account says that the temple woman burned the child’s fingers for “some childish fault,” after which she ran away to her mother. This book follows the 1903 account.

The date of Preena’s coming. The usual date, 7 March 1901, is that of her being brought to the bungalow; some accounts give 6 March for her escape the evening before. Amy’s own early account gives no date.

“Temple prostitutes.” Popular accounts sometimes say that Amy rescued a thousand temple prostitutes. Most of the children at Dohnavur were infants or small girls, many of them received because they were thought to be in danger of dedication, and many for other reasons. This book avoids the phrase.

The 1947 Act. The dedication of girls to temples was outlawed in the Madras Presidency by the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act, passed on 9 October 1947, not in 1948 and not for all India at once; other states legislated later. The campaign was led by Indian reformers, and the law should not be credited to Amy Carmichael, though her witness was part of the wider movement.

Her mother’s death. Catherine Carmichael died on 14 July 1913, not in 1912. Thomas Walker died in August 1912 (sources give the 20th or the 24th).

The Welcome Hall. Sources give 1887 or January 1889 for its opening. This book notes both.

Conversion. Most sources give 1883, when she was fifteen; some give 1882.

The fall. Most popular accounts place it at Dohnavur; the biographies place it in a building at Kalakadu being prepared for the work. The date, 24 October 1931, is agreed.

“Missionary life is simply a chance to die.” The saying is widely attributed to Amy Carmichael and gave Elisabeth Elliot her title, but it is seldom given with a source or date, and it is mentioned here as attributed.

Blue eyes and coffee. Both stories are told in popular accounts. The first comes from her own recollection, and the ages given for it vary. The second is consistent with her known practice of wearing Indian dress, but its details are uncertain.

Thirty-five books. Counts of her books vary widely, depending on whether booklets, collections of verse and posthumous compilations are included. This book does not give a number.

What This Book Has Not Done

This book has not invented dialogue, scenes, names, dates or numbers. Where a story rests on one source, it says so. It has not drawn on unpublished archives, and it has not been able to check court records or the Fellowship’s registers. Readers who wish to go further are encouraged to read Amy Carmichael’s own books, beginning with Things as They Are, and the biographies by Houghton and Elliot, and to listen to the Indian voices, Christian and Hindu, who have written about the same years from their own side.

Scripture

All Scripture is quoted from the American Standard Version of 1901, which is in the public domain. Where Amy Carmichael remembered a verse in the Authorised Version and the wording differs, this is noted in the text. The quotations from Scripture inside her own writings are given as she printed them.
